name: System Design for Builders
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Senior engineers, architects and founders who design, build and run production systems with small teams.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of estimation, trade-off, failure-mode and design-review questions.

domains.name: Requirements, estimation and reliability targets
domains.summary: Turning vague asks into numbers: functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope QPS, storage and bandwidth estimates, availability math with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, tail latency and Little's law, and the consistency models behind CAP and PACELC.

domains.name: Data storage, replication and caching
domains.summary: Choosing and running the data layer: relational first and when other stores fit, leader-follower and quorum replication and their lag anomalies, sharding and hot keys, isolation and optimistic versus pessimistic concurrency, and caching from cache-aside to CDN and HTTP caching.

domains.name: Scalability and resilience patterns
domains.summary: Keeping services up under load: L4 and L7 load balancing, stateless horizontal scaling, timeouts and retries with backoff, jitter and retry budgets, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding, rate-limiting algorithms, and idempotency keys for safe write retries.

domains.name: Asynchronous and distributed systems
domains.summary: Building on queues, logs and consensus: delivery semantics and ordering, the transactional outbox and change data capture, sagas versus 2PC, event sourcing and CQRS, Raft-style leader election with leases and fencing tokens, and why wall clocks lie.

domains.name: APIs, multi-tenancy and security
domains.summary: Designing APIs people can build on safely: REST, gRPC, GraphQL, webhooks and SSE, pagination, versioning and errors, OAuth 2.0, OIDC and JWT pitfalls, pooled versus siloed multi-tenancy with row-level security, and least privilege, secrets, encryption and the OWASP Top 10.

domains.name: Design case studies, observability and cost
domains.summary: Putting it together: classic designs such as feeds, chat and notifications, search and upload pipelines, an LLM gateway and RAG service, observability with RED, USE and SLO burn-rate alerts, and cost-aware architecture that a team of one to three can run.

scenarios.title: Designing a multi-tenant SaaS backend
scenarios.description: Many customers share one product. Choose pooled or siloed data per tier, enforce tenant isolation with row-level security and scoped tokens, and keep one noisy tenant from slowing everyone else down.

scenarios.title: Scaling a read-heavy API 100x
scenarios.description: Traffic is about to grow a hundredfold. Estimate the new QPS and storage, add read replicas, caching and a CDN where they pay off, and protect the database from stampedes and hot keys.

scenarios.title: Building a payments or order pipeline
scenarios.description: Orders and payments must never be lost or charged twice. Use idempotency keys, a transactional outbox and sagas with compensation, and plan for retries, duplicates and partial failure at every step.

scenarios.title: Designing an LLM gateway and RAG service
scenarios.description: Several teams call LLMs through one service. Route across model deployments, handle 429s and spillover, stream responses, ground answers with retrieval, and track cost and latency per tenant.

scenarios.title: A senior system design interview
scenarios.description: Forty-five minutes, one vague prompt. Pin down requirements, size the system with quick estimates, sketch a design a small team could run, then defend its trade-offs and failure modes.

lessons.title: From vague asks to numbers: requirements and estimation
lessons.summary: Split functional from non-functional requirements, turn adjectives like "fast" and "always up" into measurable targets, and size a system with back-of-the-envelope arithmetic before choosing any technology.

sections.heading: Functional vs non-functional requirements
sections.body:
**Functional requirements** say what the system does: "a user can upload a photo", "an admin can deactivate an account", "a buyer can export orders as CSV". They are features you can demo.

**Non-functional requirements** say how well it does it: latency, availability, durability, throughput, recovery objectives, security and cost. They decide the architecture far more than the feature list does. Two products with identical features can need completely different designs if one must answer in 100 ms at the 99th percentile across regions and the other can answer in 5 s from one box.

A useful interview and design-review habit is to list three to five core functional requirements, then spend most of the time pinning down the non-functional ones, because those are where the trade-offs live.

sections.heading: Turning adjectives into numbers
sections.body:
Stakeholders say "fast", "reliable" and "never lose data". Translate each into a measurable target tied to a user journey:

| Vague ask | Measurable target |
|---|---|
| "Checkout must be fast" | p99 checkout API latency under 400 ms, measured at the load balancer, over 28 days |
| "Always up" | 99.9% of valid checkout requests succeed, per 30-day window |
| "Never lose orders" | RPO of 0 for committed orders; RTO of 15 minutes for the region |

The SRE book frames this as an **SLI** (a carefully defined quantitative measure, such as request latency or error rate) and an **SLO** (a target value or range for that SLI). Azure Well-Architected adds the recovery targets: **RTO** is the maximum acceptable time the application can be unavailable after an incident, and **RPO** is the maximum acceptable duration of data loss.

Prefer percentiles over averages for latency, name the measurement point, and name the window. A target with no window cannot be checked.

sections.heading: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
sections.body:
Estimation turns requirements into load. The SRE Workbook's non-abstract design chapter argues designers must "continuously exercise the muscle" of turning a whiteboard design into concrete resource estimates.

A day has 86,400 seconds; round it to about $10^5$ for quick work.

- **Average QPS** = requests per day / 86,400. For 100M requests/day: $10^8 / 86{,}400 \approx 1{,}157$ req/s.
- **Peak QPS** = average × a peak factor. Traffic is not flat; daily peaks of 2× to 5× the average are a common planning assumption, and launches or events can be higher. Size for the peak, not the average.
- **Storage** = items/day × bytes/item × retention × replication factor. 500k uploads/day × 2 MB = 1 TB/day; one year ≈ 365 TB; three copies ≈ 1.1 PB.
- **Bandwidth** = QPS × bytes per response. 2,000 req/s × 250 KB = 500 MB/s = **4 Gbps** (multiply bytes by 8 for bits).

State every assumption out loud (DAU, requests per user, object size, peak factor). The answer only needs to be right to within a small factor; the value is in seeing which resource dominates.

sections.heading: Latency numbers worth carrying
sections.body:
The SRE book's chapter on managing critical state gives round-trip times you can quote: about **1 ms** inside a datacenter, about **45 ms** across the US, and about **70 ms** from New York to London. Those figures decide whether a synchronous cross-region write fits a latency budget.

Other "numbers every engineer should know" (memory vs SSD vs disk access) are best treated as order-of-magnitude assumptions you state up front: memory is far faster than SSD, SSD far faster than spinning disk, and any network hop costs more than a local memory read. Measure your own hardware before committing to a capacity plan.

keyPoints: Functional requirements are features; non-functional requirements (latency, availability, durability, RTO/RPO, cost) drive the architecture.
Every target needs an SLI, a threshold, a measurement point and a window.
Average QPS = daily requests / 86,400; size capacity for peak QPS, not the average.
Storage = items × size × retention × replicas; bandwidth = QPS × response size, times 8 for bits.
Use round RTTs: about 1 ms in a datacenter, about 45 ms across the US, about 70 ms NY to London.

gotchas.trap: Sizing servers from average QPS.
gotchas.correct: Apply a peak factor and add headroom; averages hide the daily peak and bursts.

gotchas.trap: Quoting bandwidth in MB/s against a link rated in Gbps.
gotchas.correct: Convert bytes to bits (×8) before comparing with network capacity.

gotchas.trap: Accepting "it should be fast" as a requirement.
gotchas.correct: Rewrite it as a percentile latency SLO for a named journey, measured at a named point over a named window.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting replication when estimating storage.
gotchas.correct: Multiply raw data by the replica count and retention period.

lessons.lab: Pick a photo-sharing app with 10M daily active users. Assume each user views 50 photos and uploads 0.2 photos per day, a photo averages 2 MB, and the peak factor is 3. Compute: average and peak read QPS, average and peak write QPS, daily new storage, one-year storage with three replicas, and peak egress in Gbps if 80% of views hit a CDN. Write each assumption next to its number, then name the one resource that dominates the design.

lessons.title: Availability math, SLOs and error budgets
lessons.summary: Compute availability for serial and redundant dependencies, convert nines into minutes of downtime, and run a service on an SLO with an error budget and burn-rate alerts.

sections.heading: Defining availability
sections.body:
AWS Well-Architected defines availability as available-for-use time divided by total time, and advises against excluding planned maintenance from the total. For request-driven services, **request-based availability** is successful responses divided by valid requests, often measured over 1-minute or 5-minute periods and averaged.

The yearly downtime allowances are worth memorising (SRE availability table, no planned downtime):

| Target | Per year | Per 30 days |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | ~3.65 days | ~7.2 h |
| 99.9% | 8.76 h | 43.2 min |
| 99.95% | 4.38 h | 21.6 min |
| 99.99% | 52.6 min | 4.32 min |
| 99.999% | 5.26 min | 25.9 s |

Each extra nine cuts the allowance by 10×.

sections.heading: Serial and redundant dependencies
sections.body:
**Hard (serial) dependencies multiply.** If a request needs every component, availability is the product:

$$A_{serial} = \prod_i A_i$$

AWS's example: a 99.99% service with two independent hard dependencies at 99.99% gives $0.9999^3 \approx 99.97\%$. You cannot be more available than the product of what you hard-depend on.

**Redundant (parallel) independent components** fail only when all fail:

$$A_{parallel} = 1 - \prod_i (1 - A_i)$$

Two independent 99.9% replicas give $1 - 0.001^2 = 99.9999\%$; AWS's shortcut is to add the nines (3 + 3 = 6). The word **independent** is doing the work: replicas that share a power feed, an availability zone, a config push or a bad deploy fail together, and the math no longer applies.

**MTBF and MTTR**: $A = \frac{MTBF}{MTBF + MTTR}$. AWS's example: MTBF of 150 days and MTTR of 1 hour gives about 99.97%. Cutting MTTR (faster detection, rollback, failover) is often cheaper than raising MTBF.

sections.heading: SLIs, SLOs and SLAs
sections.body:
- **SLI**: a quantitative measure of service level, such as the fraction of requests served successfully or the fraction faster than 300 ms.
- **SLO**: a target for an SLI over a window, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days.
- **SLA**: a contract with users that carries consequences (often financial) when missed. The SRE book recommends a safety margin: a tighter internal SLO than the one advertised to users, so the team can react to chronic problems before users notice. Azure Well-Architected adds that SLOs and SLAs are controlled independently: an SLA is a business and legal commitment, and its value is a business decision.

Azure Well-Architected notes that a composite SLO is the product of its contributing factors (for example $99.95\% \times 99.99999\% \approx 99.95\%$), but the stated SLO should reflect the business target for the user flow, not just whatever the dependencies happen to deliver.

sections.heading: Error budgets and burn-rate alerts
sections.body:
The **error budget** is $1 - SLO$. The SRE book's example: at 2.5M requests per day and a 99.99% target, the budget is 250 failed requests per day. The budget is shared between product and SRE; while budget remains, teams can ship and take risks, and when it is spent, releases slow or stop until reliability recovers. The SRE Workbook publishes an example error budget policy that writes this down in advance.

The SRE book also shows why 100% is the wrong target: on 1M dollars of revenue, moving from 99.9% to 99.99% is worth only about 900 dollars (0.09% of revenue), which must exceed the cost of the extra nine.

**Burn rate** is how fast you consume budget relative to the SLO window. Budget consumed = burn rate × alert window / SLO period, and the error-rate threshold = burn rate × (1 − SLO). The Workbook's recommended multiwindow alerts for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days:

| Action | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget consumed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Page | 1 h | 5 min | 14.4 | 2% |
| Page | 6 h | 30 min | 6 | 5% |
| Ticket | 3 days | 6 h | 1 | 10% |

At burn rate 14.4 the error rate is $14.4 \times 0.001 = 1.44\%$. The short window makes the alert stop firing soon after the problem is fixed.

keyPoints: Serial hard dependencies multiply; redundancy gives 1 − product of failure probabilities, only if failures are independent.
99.9% allows 43.2 minutes per 30 days; 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes.
Availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR); shrinking MTTR is a strong lever.
Error budget = 1 − SLO; spending it slows or halts releases under an agreed policy.
Page on fast burn (e.g. 14.4× over 1 h with a 5 min short window), ticket on slow burn.

gotchas.trap: Adding nines for two replicas that live in the same zone or share a deploy pipeline.
gotchas.correct: Redundancy math assumes independent failures; correlated replicas give far less than the formula suggests.

gotchas.trap: Setting the internal SLO equal to the customer SLA.
gotchas.correct: The SRE book advises a safety margin: keep the internal SLO tighter than what is advertised to users, so you can act before they feel the problem.

gotchas.trap: Paging whenever the error rate exceeds 1 − SLO for one minute.
gotchas.correct: Alert on burn rate over multiple windows so you page on budget-threatening burns and avoid noise.

gotchas.trap: Aiming for 100% availability.
gotchas.correct: Pick the SLO users need; each extra nine costs more and restricts dependencies and release speed.

lessons.lab: A checkout API (99.95%) calls an auth service (99.99%), a payments provider (99.9%) and a database cluster built from two independent 99.9% replicas. Compute the composite availability and the monthly downtime it implies. Then write a one-page SLO document for checkout with an SLI definition, a 30-day SLO, the error budget in minutes and in failed requests (assume 3M requests per day), and the two paging burn-rate rules from the SRE Workbook table.

lessons.title: Latency: percentiles, tail latency and queueing
lessons.summary: Measure latency as a distribution, understand why fan-out turns rare slow responses into common ones, and use Little's law to reason about concurrency, timeouts and queues.

sections.heading: Percentiles, not averages
sections.body:
The SRE book's monitoring chapter warns that averages hide the tail: a service handling 1,000 requests per second with a 100 ms **mean** could still have 1% of requests taking 5 seconds. Users experience the tail, and a heavy user making many requests hits it often.

Record latency in **histograms** and report percentiles: p50 (typical), p95/p99 (tail), p99.9 for high-volume or fan-out paths. The SRE book suggests exponentially spaced buckets about 3× apart (0–10, 10–30, 30–100, 100–300 ms). Percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts; aggregate the histograms, then compute the percentile.

Latency is one of the four golden signals, with traffic, errors and saturation. Track the latency of failed requests separately, since fast errors can make a latency graph look healthy.

sections.heading: Tail latency and fan-out
sections.body:
Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" explains why large services must tolerate variability rather than eliminate it. The core arithmetic: if each backend is slow 1% of the time and a request must wait for all of $n$ backends, the chance the request is slow is

$$P(\text{slow}) = 1 - 0.99^{n}$$

For $n = 10$ that is about 9.6%; for $n = 100$ it is about 63%. A p99 problem on one server becomes a median problem for the fan-out request.

Mitigations: reduce fan-out, set per-call deadlines, return partial results where the product allows, and send a backup ("hedged") request to another replica when the first is slow, which the paper discusses as a tail-tolerant technique. Hedging adds load, so bound it.

sections.heading: Little's law and concurrency
sections.body:
Little's law relates the average number of requests in a system ($L$), the arrival rate ($\lambda$) and the average time each spends there ($W$):

$$L = \lambda W$$

At 2,000 req/s and 50 ms latency, about 100 requests are in flight. If a dependency slows to 1 s, the same traffic holds about 2,000 in flight: 20× more threads, connections and memory. The Builders' Library dependency-isolation article states the same relation (concurrency equals arrival rate times latency) and recommends a separate concurrency bulkhead for each dependency. That is how a slow dependency exhausts a caller that has no limit on concurrency, and why the Builders' Library ties timeout choice to the latency distribution of the downstream (for example, choosing a timeout from an acceptable false-timeout rate such as the p99.9).

sections.heading: Queueing intuition
sections.body:
As utilisation approaches 100%, queueing delay grows sharply, so plan headroom rather than running hot. A queue does not add capacity; it only converts overload into latency.

The SRE book's cascading-failures chapter gives the numbers: a queue of 10× the thread count with 100 ms handling time adds about 1 s of waiting when full. For steady traffic it recommends keeping queues small (about 50% of the thread pool or less) so the server rejects early instead of serving requests whose clients have already given up. It also discusses LIFO or CoDel-style queueing and propagating deadlines so work that cannot finish in time is dropped.

keyPoints: Report p50/p95/p99 from histograms; never average percentiles across hosts.
With fan-out n and per-backend slow probability p, P(slow) = 1 − (1 − p)^n; 1% slow at n = 100 gives about 63%.
Little's law: in-flight = arrival rate × latency; slowdowns multiply concurrency.
Queues trade overload for latency; keep them short and fail fast near saturation.
Set timeouts from the downstream latency distribution, and propagate deadlines.

gotchas.trap: Using mean latency as the SLI.
gotchas.correct: Use a percentile or "fraction of requests under X ms" SLI built from a histogram.

gotchas.trap: Averaging p99 values from 20 hosts to get a fleet p99.
gotchas.correct: Merge the histograms (or raw samples), then compute the percentile.

gotchas.trap: Adding a large request queue to absorb a slow dependency.
gotchas.correct: Bound the queue and concurrency; a long queue only adds waiting time and serves requests whose clients already timed out.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a 1% slow backend only affects 1% of user requests.
gotchas.correct: With fan-out, nearly every request can wait on at least one slow backend.

lessons.lab: Write a short script that simulates a service fanning out to n backends, where each backend takes 10 ms with probability 0.99 and 1 s with probability 0.01. For n = 1, 10, 50 and 100, report the p50 and p99 of the overall request latency. Then add a hedged request sent after 50 ms to a second replica and compare p99 and total backend load. Finally, use Little's law to compute how many threads the caller needs at 2,000 req/s for each case.

lessons.title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
lessons.summary: Use CAP and PACELC to frame replication trade-offs, and choose the weakest consistency model that still meets the product requirement, from linearizable down to eventual.

sections.heading: CAP in one paragraph
sections.body: When replicas cannot talk to each other (a network **partition**), a replicated system must choose: refuse some requests to stay consistent (**C**), or keep answering and risk returning stale or conflicting data (**A**). Partitions are not optional in a distributed system, so CAP is really a statement about behaviour during a partition. It is a theorem about a narrow definition of consistency (linearizability) and availability (every non-failed node answers), not a label for a whole product.

sections.heading: PACELC: the trade-off you pay every day
sections.body:
PACELC (Abadi, 2012) extends CAP: if there is a **P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse, in normal operation, choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Partitions are rare; the latency cost of strong consistency is paid on every request.

The Azure Cosmos DB consistency-levels documentation frames its choices exactly this way, as trade-offs among consistency, availability, latency and throughput "as defined by the PACELC theorem". It notes that linearizable strong consistency increases write latency, because data must replicate and commit across large distances, and reduces availability during failures. With cross-region RTTs around 45–70 ms, a synchronous multi-region commit adds tens of milliseconds to every write.

sections.heading: The consistency spectrum
sections.body:
From strongest to weakest, the models you will meet:

- **Linearizable (strong)**: every operation appears to take effect atomically at one point between its start and end, consistent with real time. A read after a completed write, from any client, sees that write.
- **Sequential**: all clients see operations in one total order consistent with each client's program order, but that order need not match real time.
- **Causal**: operations that are causally related (a reply after the post it answers) are seen in that order by everyone; concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
- **Session guarantees**: within a client session, **read-your-writes**, monotonic reads and related guarantees. Cosmos DB's session level guarantees read-your-writes and write-follows-reads within a session.
- **Consistent prefix**: readers may lag, but never see writes out of order.
- **Eventual**: replicas converge if writes stop; Cosmos DB notes a client may even read values older than ones it read before.

Cosmos DB names five levels in this spirit: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix and Eventual. Bounded staleness lets reads lag by at most K versions or T time. Note that Cosmos DB scopes its consistent-prefix level narrowly: writes in a transactional batch are always seen together and in order, while single-document writes behave as eventual. The general model above is the textbook definition.

sections.heading: Choosing a model
sections.body:
Start from the product requirement and pick the weakest model that satisfies it:

- A user edits their profile and must see the change on reload: **read-your-writes** (route the user's reads to the leader for a short time, or carry a session token / version and have followers wait until they catch up; the Follower Reads pattern describes serving reads from followers and the staleness that brings).
- Comments in a thread must never appear before the post they reply to: **causal** or **consistent prefix**.
- Account balance checks that guard money, uniqueness constraints and leader election: **linearizable**, typically via a majority quorum or consensus.
- Like counters, view counts, recommendation feeds: **eventual** is usually fine.

Strong consistency everywhere is the safe-sounding default that quietly costs latency and availability; eventual consistency everywhere is the fast default that quietly produces anomalies. Decide per data item and per operation.

keyPoints: CAP is about behaviour during a partition: stay consistent by refusing, or stay available and risk staleness.
PACELC adds the normal-case trade-off: latency vs consistency, paid on every request.
Roughly, from strongest to weakest: linearizable > sequential > causal > session guarantees / consistent prefix > eventual.
Read-your-writes is a per-session guarantee; it does not require global linearizability.
Pick the weakest model that meets each requirement, per data item and operation.

gotchas.trap: Calling a database "CP" or "AP" as if that settles the design.
gotchas.correct: CAP only describes partition behaviour under narrow definitions; many systems offer tunable consistency per request.

gotchas.trap: Reading from an async follower right after a write and expecting the new value.
gotchas.correct: Follower reads can be stale; use leader reads, session tokens or version checks for read-your-writes.

gotchas.trap: Making every read linearizable "to be safe".
gotchas.correct: Strong consistency adds cross-replica latency on every operation and lowers availability during failures; reserve it for invariants that need it.

gotchas.trap: Assuming eventual consistency means reads only lag a little and move forward.
gotchas.correct: Without session or monotonic guarantees a client can read an older value after a newer one.

lessons.lab: For a social app, list ten data items or operations (profile edit, post creation, comment thread, like count, follower count, username uniqueness, password change, DM delivery order, feed ranking, payment balance). For each, choose the weakest consistency model that meets the product need, say how you would implement it on a leader-follower database with async replicas, and name the anomaly a user would see if you picked one level weaker.

lessons.title: Choosing storage: relational first, then specialise
lessons.summary: Start with a relational database as the system of record, and add key-value, document, wide-column, search or object storage only when a specific access pattern or data lifecycle demands it.

sections.heading: Why relational is the default
sections.body:
A relational database gives you **ACID transactions across rows**, joins, constraints (unique, foreign key, check) and mature tooling. The Azure data store guide lists its strengths as multi-row transactional consistency, complex joins and strong constraints, with typical workloads such as order management, inventory, ledgers and billing.

Its main consideration is scale-out: horizontal scale "generally requires sharding or partitioning". For most products that is a problem for later. A single well-indexed PostgreSQL primary with read replicas carries a long way, and it keeps one source of truth.

PostgreSQL also covers several "NoSQL" needs without a second system:

- `jsonb` columns hold flexible, per-row attributes and can be indexed.
- Built-in full text search handles basic keyword search with ranking.
- Declarative partitioning splits very large tables on one server.

sections.heading: When another model earns its place
sections.body:
The Azure guide's advice is to **combine models only where access patterns or life cycles clearly diverge**, and to choose the best-fit model "instead of combining models in a way that complicates operations". Good reasons to add a store:

| Model | Fits when | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Key-value | Every access is by a known key; the value is opaque; latency matters most | Sessions, caches, feature flags, rate counters |
| Document | Data is read and written as one self-contained aggregate with a varying shape | Product catalogues, content, profiles |
| Wide-column (column-family) | Very high write throughput; queries always use a designed row key | IoT telemetry, event histories |
| Search index | Full-text relevance scoring, fuzzy (typo-tolerant) matching, filters and facets | Product or document search |
| Object storage | Large binary or file data | Images, video, backups, exports |

Each extra store adds a deployment, a backup story, a security surface and a consistency boundary.

sections.heading: Object storage for blobs
sections.body:
Do not put large files in database rows. Store the bytes in object storage and keep the **object key plus metadata** (owner, size, content type, checksum) in the relational database. Amazon S3, for example, documents strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE of objects, so a reader that sees the metadata row can fetch the object it points to.

Uploads can go straight from the client to object storage with a short-lived pre-signed URL (the Valet Key pattern, covered in the design case studies domain), so your API servers never stream gigabytes.

sections.heading: Derived stores and the source of truth
sections.body: A search index, cache or analytics store is usually **derived data**: rebuilt from the system of record through change data capture or an outbox. That makes it eventually consistent with the database, and it means you can drop and rebuild it. Decide explicitly which store is the system of record for each entity. Writing to two stores from application code without a transaction (a "dual write") will leave them inconsistent after a partial failure.

sections.heading: Keys and identifiers
sections.body: Primary key choice affects write locality. Random UUIDv4 keys scatter inserts across a B-tree index. RFC 9562 defines **UUIDv7**, a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits, and notes that time-ordered keys improve index locality. PostgreSQL 18 ships a native `uuidv7()` function. On a sharded store, though, a time-ordered key used as the shard key concentrates writes; see the partitioning lesson.

keyPoints: Default to one relational database as the system of record; add stores for clearly divergent access patterns.
jsonb, full text search and table partitioning let PostgreSQL absorb many early "NoSQL" needs.
Key-value fits access by known key; document fits self-contained aggregates; wide-column fits high-write, row-key-shaped queries.
Put large files in object storage and keep the key and metadata in the database.
Search indexes and caches are derived data, eventually consistent with the source of truth.

gotchas.trap: Picking a database per microservice feature on day one "for scale".
gotchas.correct: Every store adds operations, backups and consistency boundaries. Add one when a measured access pattern needs it.

gotchas.trap: Making the search cluster the system of record because it holds every field.
gotchas.correct: Keep the relational database authoritative and rebuild the index from it via CDC or an outbox.

gotchas.trap: Storing uploaded videos in a bytea column.
gotchas.correct: Store bytes in object storage; store the object key and metadata in the database.

lessons.lab:
Take a small marketplace (users, listings, orders, listing photos, listing search).

1. Model users, listings and orders in PostgreSQL. Put free-form listing attributes in a `jsonb` column with a GIN index.
2. Store photo bytes in an object store bucket; store only the key, size and checksum in a `listing_photos` table.
3. Implement keyword search with PostgreSQL full text search. Write down one requirement (for example typo tolerance or facet counts) that would justify a dedicated search index, and sketch how you would feed it from the database through an outbox.

lessons.title: Replication: leaders, quorums and lag
lessons.summary: How leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication work, what asynchronous lag does to readers, and how quorums and synchronous commits trade latency for durability.

sections.heading: Leader and followers
sections.body:
In single-leader replication every write goes to one node, which records it in a replicated log and ships it to followers (the Fowler/Joshi patterns **Leader and Followers** and **Replicated Log**). Followers can serve reads (**Follower Reads**) to add read throughput and reduce latency.

PostgreSQL streaming replication is the standard example. The docs state it is **asynchronous by default**: there is a small delay between a commit on the primary and the change becoming visible on the standby. You can measure the lag by comparing `pg_current_wal_lsn()` on the primary with the received or replayed LSN on the standby.

sections.heading: Asynchronous vs synchronous commit
sections.body:
With asynchronous replication, if the primary crashes, "some transactions that were committed may not have been replicated to the standby server, causing data loss", and the loss is proportional to the replication delay at failover.

Synchronous replication makes each commit wait for confirmation from one or more synchronous standbys. The PostgreSQL docs note the **minimum extra wait is the round-trip time between primary and standby**. You can require a quorum of standbys, for example `synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)'`, so commits wait for any two of the three.

Durability is not the same as read freshness. The default synchronous mode waits for the standby to flush WAL, not to apply it. Only `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` makes the commit wait until the change is visible to queries on the standby.

sections.heading: Replication lag anomalies
sections.body:
When reads go to asynchronous followers, users can see anomalies even though nothing is "broken":

- **Read-your-writes violation**: a user saves a change, reloads, and the read hits a lagging replica that does not yet have it. Fix: read from the leader for that user for a short window after a write, or make the replica wait until it has replayed the LSN the write returned.
- **Non-monotonic reads**: successive reads hit replicas with different lag, so data appears and then disappears. Fix: pin a user's reads to one replica (for example by hashing the user ID).
- **Consistent prefix violation**: in partitioned systems, an answer can be seen before its question. Fix: keep causally related writes in the same partition, or track causal dependencies.

sections.heading: Multi-leader replication
sections.body:
Multi-leader setups accept writes in several places, often one leader per region. They tolerate a region outage and give local write latency, but two leaders can accept **conflicting concurrent writes** to the same record.

Last-write-wins by wall-clock timestamp resolves the conflict by silently discarding one update, and clocks drift. Safer options:

- Route all writes for a given record to one "home" leader, so conflicts cannot happen for that record.
- Detect concurrency with **version vectors** (one counter per node, a Fowler/Joshi pattern) and merge, or keep both versions for the application to resolve.
- Design data types whose updates commute, such as counters and sets.

sections.heading: Leaderless quorums
sections.body:
In leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication a client writes to N replicas and waits for W acknowledgements, and reads from R replicas and takes the newest version. If **R + W > N**, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum, so at least one replica in the read set has the latest acknowledged write. A common setting is N=3, W=2, R=2.

Caveats: "sloppy" quorums that accept writes on stand-in nodes during failures (with hinted handoff) weaken the overlap guarantee, and concurrent writes still need version tracking. Replicas that missed writes catch up through read repair and background anti-entropy.

keyPoints: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default; failover can lose recently committed transactions.
Synchronous replication adds at least one primary-standby round trip to every commit.
Synchronous durability (flush) is not read freshness; remote_apply is what waits for visibility on the standby.
Lag causes read-your-writes, monotonic-read and consistent-prefix anomalies; fix them with routing, pinning or LSN waits.
Multi-leader writes conflict; LWW by wall clock silently drops data.
Leaderless quorums need R + W > N for overlap; sloppy quorums weaken it.

gotchas.trap: Adding read replicas and routing every read to them, including the page shown right after a save.
gotchas.correct: Route post-write reads for that user to the leader or wait for the replica to replay the write LSN.

gotchas.trap: Believing synchronous replication means standby reads are always current.
gotchas.correct: Default synchronous commit waits for WAL flush on the standby; only remote_apply waits until the change is visible there.

gotchas.trap: Resolving multi-region conflicts with last-write-wins timestamps.
gotchas.correct: Give each record a home leader, or detect concurrency with version vectors and merge.

gotchas.trap: Setting N=3, W=1, R=1 for speed and expecting fresh reads.
gotchas.correct: R + W must exceed N for quorums to overlap; use W=2, R=2 for N=3.

lessons.lab:
Run a PostgreSQL primary and one streaming standby (containers are fine).

1. Insert a row on the primary and immediately query the standby in a loop; record how often the row is missing.
2. Compare `pg_current_wal_lsn()` on the primary with `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` on the standby to measure lag.
3. Enable synchronous replication for the standby and measure commit latency before and after. Then set `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` and repeat step 1.
4. Write a short read-routing rule for your app: which reads may go to the standby, and for how long after a write a user is pinned to the primary.

lessons.title: Partitioning and sharding without hot spots
lessons.summary: Choosing a shard key, hash vs range vs lookup strategies, handling hot keys, and rebalancing with consistent hashing or fixed virtual partitions.

sections.heading: The shard key is the big decision
sections.body:
Sharding splits a data store into horizontal partitions with the same schema, each holding a distinct subset of the data. The Azure Sharding pattern calls the shard key "the most critical design decision" because changing it later usually means migrating all data.

A good shard key, per that pattern:

- is **immutable**,
- has **high cardinality**,
- spreads data **and load** evenly, and
- matches the dominant query pattern so most requests hit **one shard**.

Avoid monotonically increasing values (auto-increment IDs, timestamps), low-cardinality attributes (booleans, small enums) and values that change often. If no single attribute works, use a composite key. For lookups by non-key attributes, maintain an index table.

sections.heading: Hash, range, lookup and geographic
sections.body:
- **Hash**: shard = f(hash(key)). It spreads load well and needs no map, but range queries must fan out to every shard.
- **Range**: contiguous key ranges per shard. Range scans are cheap, but sequential keys pile new writes onto the newest shard.
- **Lookup (directory)**: a map from key, often tenant ID, to shard. It gives full control and lets you move a tenant, at the cost of a lookup and a map that must be highly available and cacheable.
- **Geographic**: shard by region for residency and latency. It is often uneven, so combine it with hash or lookup inside each region.

Partitioning tables inside one PostgreSQL server (declarative partitioning) is a different tool. It helps with pruning and dropping old data, but it does not add servers.

sections.heading: Rebalancing and consistent hashing
sections.body:
With `hash(key) mod N`, changing N reassigns **most** keys and triggers a mass migration. Two common fixes:

- **Consistent hashing** places nodes and keys on a hash ring, so adding a node moves only the keys in the arc it takes over. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth the distribution.
- **Fixed partitions** (a Fowler/Joshi pattern, also the Azure "virtual shards" idea): create many more partitions than nodes up front, for example 1,024, and move whole partitions between nodes. The key-to-partition mapping never changes; only the partition-to-node map does.

When you move data, also invalidate or refresh caches that hold the old location.

sections.heading: Hot keys and hot partitions
sections.body:
Even a good key distribution has outliers: one celebrity account, one viral product, one huge tenant. The DynamoDB guidance is to design for uniform activity across partition keys, and it documents a per-partition throughput ceiling, so one hot key cannot be fixed by adding capacity elsewhere.

Remedies:

- **Write sharding**: append a suffix (random or computed) to the hot key, such as `2014-07-09.1` through `.200`, so writes spread out; reads then query every suffix and merge.
- **Read hot keys**: serve them from a cache or replicas.
- **Isolate big tenants**: the Azure pattern suggests giving volatile or high-value tenants their own shards.

sections.heading: Containing blast radius with shuffle sharding
sections.body: Plain sharding means one bad tenant can take down everyone on its shard. **Shuffle sharding** (Amazon Builders' Library) assigns each customer a small random combination of workers, for example 2 of 8. Two customers rarely share the same combination, so a "poison" customer that breaks its workers leaves almost every other customer with at least one healthy worker. Pair it with per-partition circuit breakers so one overloaded partition reduces availability partially rather than totally.

keyPoints: A good shard key is immutable, high-cardinality, evenly loaded and aligned with the main query.
Monotonic keys (timestamps, sequences) create a hot newest shard under range sharding.
hash mod N reshuffles most keys on resize; consistent hashing or fixed partitions move only a fraction.
Hot keys need write sharding, caching or isolation; more total capacity does not fix one hot partition.
Shuffle sharding limits how many customers a single bad customer can affect.

gotchas.trap: Sharding an event table by created_at so recent queries are fast.
gotchas.correct: All current writes land on one shard; use a hash or composite key such as (bucket, time).

gotchas.trap: Using shard = hash(id) % node_count and planning to "just add a node".
gotchas.correct: Pre-split into many fixed partitions or use consistent hashing so resizing moves little data.

gotchas.trap: Raising table-wide throughput to fix one throttled celebrity key.
gotchas.correct: Per-partition limits still apply; spread the key with suffixes or serve reads from cache.

lessons.lab: Write a script that assigns 100,000 keys to 10 nodes with `hash mod N`, then to 11 nodes, and count how many keys moved. Repeat with a consistent-hash ring with 100 virtual nodes per server, and with 1,024 fixed partitions reassigned to the new node. Compare the moved fractions, then simulate one key receiving 30% of writes and show how a 10-way suffix changes the per-node load.

lessons.title: Transactions and isolation in practice
lessons.summary: The anomalies each isolation level allows in PostgreSQL, why lost updates and write skew slip through, and when to use atomic updates, row locks, optimistic versions or Serializable with retries.

sections.heading: PostgreSQL isolation levels
sections.body:
PostgreSQL's default is **Read Committed**. Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, so there are three distinct levels:

| Level | Dirty read | Nonrepeatable read | Phantom read | Serialization anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read Committed | No | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable Read | No | No | No in PostgreSQL | Possible |
| Serializable | No | No | No | No |

Repeatable Read is implemented as **snapshot isolation**. Serializable uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) with non-blocking predicate locks. Both can abort a transaction with **SQLSTATE 40001** (serialization failure), and the application must **retry the whole transaction**.

sections.heading: Lost updates
sections.body:
A lost update happens when two transactions read a value, compute in application code, and write back, so one write overwrites the other. Under Read Committed this is common in "read, modify in code, write" handlers.

Fixes, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Do it in one statement**: `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND qty >= 1`, then check the affected row count.
2. **Lock the row** while you decide: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside the transaction.
3. **Optimistic version check**: `UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`; zero rows means someone else won, so reload and retry.
4. Run at Repeatable Read or Serializable and retry on 40001.

sections.heading: Write skew
sections.body:
Write skew is the anomaly snapshot isolation allows. Two transactions read an overlapping set of rows, each checks a rule ("at least one doctor stays on call"), and each updates a **different** row. Neither sees the other's write, both commit, and the rule is broken.

The PostgreSQL docs warn that enforcing business rules under Repeatable Read needs explicit locks. Options:

- Run at **Serializable**, which detects the dangerous read/write dependency and aborts one transaction with 40001.
- Lock the rows the rule depends on (`FOR UPDATE`), or a single parent row that represents the rule.
- Turn the rule into a constraint the database enforces, such as a unique or exclusion constraint.

sections.heading: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency
sections.body:
**Pessimistic** concurrency takes locks before acting (`FOR UPDATE`, table locks, advisory locks). It suits short transactions with high contention, but locks held for long periods block others and can deadlock.

**Optimistic** concurrency does not lock. It detects conflicts at write time with a version column, or over HTTP with an `ETag` and `If-Match`, which returns **412 Precondition Failed** when the resource changed (RFC 9110 conditional requests). It suits low contention and long "think time", such as a user editing a form for minutes. Never hold a database lock open while waiting for a human.

Serializable is optimistic at the database level: it lets transactions run and aborts one on conflict, so it needs retry logic and works best with short transactions.

sections.heading: Queue-like tables and SKIP LOCKED
sections.body: For a Postgres-backed job queue, workers can claim jobs with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1`. Each worker skips rows another worker has locked instead of waiting. The PostgreSQL docs describe SKIP LOCKED as a way "to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table", and warn it is not suitable for general-purpose work because it returns an inconsistent view of the data.

keyPoints: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation; Serializable is SSI.
Serialization failures return SQLSTATE 40001; retry the whole transaction, not one statement.
Prefer single-statement atomic updates for counters and stock; check the affected row count.
Snapshot isolation allows write skew; use Serializable, row locks on the rule, or a database constraint.
Optimistic checks (version column, ETag/If-Match then 412) fit long think time; pessimistic locks fit short, contended work.
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the tool for multiple workers on a queue table.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the default isolation level prevents lost updates in read-modify-write code.
gotchas.correct: Read Committed allows them; use an atomic UPDATE, FOR UPDATE, or a version check.

gotchas.trap: Retrying only the failed statement after a 40001 error.
gotchas.correct: Roll back and rerun the entire transaction, including its reads.

gotchas.trap: Believing Repeatable Read enforces "at least one row must stay X" rules.
gotchas.correct: It allows write skew; use Serializable or lock the rows the rule reads.

gotchas.trap: Holding SELECT ... FOR UPDATE while a user edits a form.
gotchas.correct: Use an optimistic version or ETag check at save time.

lessons.lab:
In two psql sessions:

1. Under Read Committed, have both sessions read `qty`, then each run `UPDATE stock SET qty = <read value - 1>`. Observe the lost update. Repeat with `SET qty = qty - 1` and note the difference.
2. Create an `on_call` table with two doctors on call. In both sessions at Repeatable Read, check `count(*) >= 2` and take a different doctor off call. Both commit: write skew.
3. Repeat step 2 at Serializable and capture the 40001 error. Write a retry wrapper that reruns the whole transaction with backoff.

lessons.title: Caching: patterns, invalidation and HTTP
lessons.summary: Cache-aside vs inline caches, TTLs and invalidation, stampedes and request coalescing, the cache-as-capacity trap, eviction policy, and HTTP and CDN caching headers.

sections.heading: Cache-aside vs read-through and write-through
sections.body:
In **cache-aside** the application owns the cache: read the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the value, return it. On update, **write the database, then invalidate the cache entry**. The Azure pattern notes cache-aside does not guarantee consistency: between the write and the next read a reader can see stale data or miss.

**Inline** caches (read-through and write-through) put cache management behind the data access API. Write-through updates the store and the cache in the same operation, so readers see the new value right after a successful write. Write-behind (write-back) acknowledges after the cache write and flushes later, which is faster but risks losing writes.

sections.heading: TTLs, invalidation and staleness
sections.body:
Every cached value is eventually inconsistent with its source, so caching only works when the service and its clients tolerate staleness. Use a TTL on every entry as a backstop, even when you also invalidate on write; it bounds how long a missed invalidation can hurt.

The Azure pattern warns against TTLs so short that the cache keeps refetching and so long that data goes stale. Useful refinements from the Amazon Builders' Library article:

- **Soft and hard TTL**: refresh after the soft TTL; if the downstream is failing, keep serving the old value until the hard TTL.
- **Negative caching**: cache "not found" or error responses with a different, usually shorter, TTL so a missing key does not hammer the database.
- **Jitter** expiry times so keys written together do not expire together.

sections.heading: Stampedes, cold starts and the capacity trap
sections.body:
A **thundering herd** (cache stampede) is many clients requesting the same uncached item at once, after expiry or when a new server joins with an empty cache. **Request coalescing** ensures "only one pending request is out for uncached resources"; the rest wait for its result.

The deeper risk is a service **"addicted to its cache"**: the backend is sized for the miss rate, so a cache flush, a fleet-wide deploy of in-process caches, or a shift in key distribution sends full load to a backend that cannot take it. The SRE book makes the same point: prefer latency caches over capacity caches. Make sure the backend can survive a cold cache, or that the service throttles and sheds load when the hit rate drops.

External caches (a separate cache fleet) avoid per-server cold starts and fleet-wide coherence problems, but they are another dependency to scale and monitor.

sections.heading: Eviction policy
sections.body: Caches have finite memory. Redis's eviction docs list policies including `noeviction` (return errors on writes when full), `allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`, `volatile-lru` and `volatile-ttl`. They recommend **`allkeys-lru` as a good default** when a subset of keys is hot. The `volatile-*` policies evict only keys that have a TTL, and behave like `noeviction` when no keys have one. If you mix persistent keys and cache keys, the docs suggest considering two separate instances.

sections.heading: HTTP and CDN caching
sections.body:
RFC 9111 defines the cache directives that browsers and CDNs follow:

- `no-store`: do not store the response at all. This is the directive for sensitive data.
- `no-cache`: may store, but **must revalidate** with the origin before each reuse. It does not forbid storage.
- `private`: shared caches (CDNs, proxies) must not store it; the browser may.
- `s-maxage`: freshness lifetime for shared caches only; overrides `max-age` there.
- Revalidation uses `ETag` with `If-None-Match`, answered by **304 Not Modified**.
- `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` come from **RFC 5861**.

For static assets, put a content hash or version in the file name and serve it with a long `max-age` (MDN calls this cache busting; `immutable` avoids reload revalidation). CloudFront documents both invalidation and versioned file names for updating cached files; versioned names avoid waiting on invalidations and keep old and new releases separable. Keep the HTML entry page short-lived or revalidated so it can point at new asset names.

keyPoints: Cache-aside: write the database first, then invalidate; keep a TTL as a backstop.
Write-through gives read-after-write freshness; write-behind risks data loss.
Request coalescing and jittered or soft TTLs prevent stampedes; negative caching protects against repeated misses.
Do not let the backend depend on the hit rate for capacity; plan for a cold cache.
allkeys-lru is a good Redis default; volatile-* policies act like noeviction when no keys have TTLs.
no-cache means revalidate, not "do not store"; no-store forbids storage; private keeps CDNs out.
Hash-named static assets with long max-age beat per-deploy CDN invalidations.

gotchas.trap: Setting Cache-Control: no-cache to keep account pages out of caches.
gotchas.correct: no-cache still allows storage; use no-store for sensitive responses and private for per-user ones.

gotchas.trap: Updating the cache first and then writing the database.
gotchas.correct: If the database write fails, the cache now holds a value that never existed; write the database, then invalidate.

gotchas.trap: Sizing the database for the cache miss rate.
gotchas.correct: A cold or flushed cache sends full traffic to it; size for that or shed load.

gotchas.trap: Using volatile-lru on a cache whose keys have no TTL.
gotchas.correct: Nothing is evictable, so writes fail like noeviction; use allkeys-lru or set TTLs.

lessons.lab:
Put a Redis cache-aside layer in front of a slow `GET /products/:id` endpoint.

1. Add a TTL with ±10% jitter and invalidate the key after each successful database update.
2. Load test with 500 concurrent requests for one key right after expiry; count database queries. Add single-flight request coalescing and measure again.
3. Add a soft TTL: return the stale value while one background refresh runs, and keep serving it if the database is down until a hard TTL.
4. Serve the product page's JS bundle with a content-hashed name and `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`, and the HTML with `no-cache`. Check the 304 responses in browser dev tools.

lessons.title: Load balancing, stateless services and autoscaling
lessons.summary: How L4 and L7 balancers differ, why horizontal scaling needs stateless instances, how health checks and draining keep the pool honest, and how to pick an autoscaling metric that actually tracks load.

sections.heading: L4 vs L7 load balancers
sections.body:
A **Layer-4** balancer works on TCP/UDP flows. It picks a backend per connection and never parses HTTP, which makes it fast and protocol-agnostic. Azure describes its Load Balancer as a Layer-4 service for all TCP and UDP traffic, built for very low latency.

A **Layer-7** balancer is a proxy that terminates HTTP(S) and sees every request. That buys features an L4 device cannot offer: TLS offload, path-based routing, a WAF, and session affinity.

Use this rule of thumb:
- **L4** for raw throughput, non-HTTP protocols, or when TLS must pass through to the backend.
- **L7** when routing depends on the request (path, header, host), or when you need per-request balancing of multiplexed protocols such as HTTP/2 and gRPC.

An L4 balancer pins a long-lived HTTP/2 connection to one backend, so every request on that connection lands on the same instance.

sections.heading: Balancing policies and health
sections.body:
Policies range from blind to load-aware. The SRE book contrasts simple **Round Robin**, which ignores backend state, with **Least-Loaded Round Robin** and **Weighted Round Robin**, which use information about the backends.

Health checking has two failure modes:
- **Too shallow:** the process answers on its port but cannot do useful work.
- **Too deep:** a dependency check fails on every host at once and the balancer empties the pool.

The Builders' Library describes **fail open** for the second case. When *all* targets fail their health check, the balancer keeps sending traffic to all of them rather than to none.

Drain before you stop. The SRE book's **lame duck** state means "still serving, but asking clients to send new requests elsewhere". On SIGTERM a task enters lame duck, finishes in-flight work, and then exits.

sections.heading: Stateless services
sections.body:
Horizontal scaling only works if any instance can serve any request. Keep per-user state out of the instance's memory: put sessions, carts and uploads in a shared store (a database, a cache cluster or object storage).

**Sticky sessions** (session affinity) are a crutch, not a design:
- Scale-in or a crash loses the sessions on that instance.
- Load skews toward instances holding heavy users.
- New instances receive little traffic until old sessions expire.

Stateless instances also make deploys, autoscaling and zone failover simple, because any instance is disposable.

sections.heading: Autoscaling that tracks load
sections.body:
**Target tracking** keeps a metric near a target, for example average CPU at 50%. Scale out above it, scale in below it.

The AWS docs set firm rules for the metric:
- It must describe how busy an instance is, and it must **change proportionally to the number of instances**. CPU utilization and request count per target qualify.
- Load-balancer latency does not, because it rises with load but not in proportion. Raw queue depth does not either. **Queue messages per instance** can work.
- With several policies, the group scales **out if any** policy asks and scales **in only if all** agree, because availability comes first.
- Set an **instance warmup** time. Until it expires, a new instance does not count toward the group's aggregated metrics.

The SRE book warns that **QPS is a poor capacity unit**, because requests vary widely in cost. Model capacity in resources such as CPU and memory instead.

Autoscaling takes minutes, so keep headroom for the ramp. It also does nothing for a shared bottleneck: adding web servers in front of a saturated primary database adds load to the database.

sections.heading: Zones and cross-zone balancing
sections.body:
Spread targets across at least two availability zones. Cross-zone balancing changes how traffic divides.

Take the ELB guide's example: two zones, 2 targets in zone A and 8 in zone B. Each balancer node receives 50% of client traffic.
- **Cross-zone on:** every one of the 10 targets gets 10%.
- **Cross-zone off:** each zone-A target gets 25% and each zone-B target gets 6.25%.

Uneven zone capacity plus cross-zone off is a classic source of hot instances.

keyPoints: L4 balances connections; L7 terminates HTTP and balances, routes and inspects per request.
Horizontal scaling requires stateless instances; move session state to a shared store.
Health checks: avoid both shallow and fleet-wide deep failures; fail open when every target fails.
Drain with a lame-duck or deregistration step before shutting an instance down.
Target-tracking metrics must scale proportionally with instance count; use queue backlog per instance, not raw queue depth.
Model capacity in resources (CPU, memory), not raw QPS.

gotchas.trap: Enabling sticky sessions so in-memory sessions survive autoscaling.
gotchas.correct: Externalize session state; affinity still loses sessions on scale-in and skews load.

gotchas.trap: Autoscaling a worker fleet on raw queue depth or on request latency.
gotchas.correct: Use a metric proportional to fleet size, such as backlog per instance or CPU.

gotchas.trap: A health check that fails every host whenever a shared dependency blips.
gotchas.correct: Keep dependency checks careful and rely on fail-open behaviour when all targets fail.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an L4 balancer spreads gRPC requests evenly.
gotchas.correct: L4 pins each connection; use L7 or client-side per-request balancing for multiplexed protocols.

lessons.lab: Take a toy HTTP service that keeps a counter in memory. Run three instances behind a local L7 proxy and show that the counter is inconsistent. Move the counter to Redis and show it is now correct whichever instance serves the request. Then compute the per-target traffic shares for 3 targets in zone A and 6 in zone B, with cross-zone balancing on and off.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries, backoff and retry budgets
lessons.summary: Choose timeouts from latency percentiles, propagate deadlines, back off with jitter, and cap retries per request and per client so that retries do not turn a blip into an outage.

sections.heading: Choosing timeouts
sections.body:
A call without a timeout can hold a thread, a connection and memory indefinitely. The Azure Circuit Breaker page describes those blocked requests exhausting resources that unrelated work needs.

The Builders' Library sets timeouts from an **acceptable false-timeout rate**. If you can tolerate 0.1% of good calls timing out, set the timeout near the downstream's **p99.9** latency.

Both extremes hurt:
- **Too short** fails healthy calls and causes retries.
- **Too long** lets the queue fill during a slowdown. By Little's law, concurrency = arrival rate × latency.

sections.heading: Deadline propagation
sections.body:
Pass the **remaining** time budget down the call chain instead of giving each hop its own fixed timeout. The SRE book's example: a 30 s deadline with 7 s already used leaves 23 s for downstream work, minus a few hundred milliseconds for the trip back.

If the deadline has already passed when a request leaves a queue, drop it. Nobody is waiting for that answer.

sections.heading: Retry amplification and storms
sections.body:
Retries multiply down the stack. If each of *k* layers makes up to *a* attempts, the bottom layer can see up to $a^k$ attempts for one user request.

- The SRE book: three retrying layers that each make 4 attempts (1 try + 3 retries) give $4^3 = 64$ attempts at the database.
- The Builders' Library: in a five-deep call stack where every layer retries, a failing database can see **243×** the load ($3^5$). That figure counts 3 attempts per layer across 5 layers, while the SRE figure above counts retries plus the first try ($(r+1)^k$), so check which convention a number uses before comparing.

The fix is structural. **Retry at a single point in the stack**, which the SRE book phrases as retrying only at the layer directly above the failing backend. Have overloaded servers return an explicit "overloaded; don't retry" signal.

A **retry storm** happens when many clients fail together and retry together, keeping an overloaded dependency overloaded after the original trigger has gone.

sections.heading: Exponential backoff and jitter
sections.body:
Back off exponentially between attempts, and **cap** the backoff so that waits do not grow unbounded. Capping alone leaves every client retrying in lockstep at the cap, so add **jitter**: a random component that spreads retries out in time.

Jitter is not only for retries. The Builders' Library adds jitter to timers and periodic jobs too. For scheduled work it uses a **consistent per-host offset** (the same number every time on the same host) rather than a fresh random value. That keeps load spread out and makes any spike reproducible.

sections.heading: Retry budgets
sections.body:
The SRE book bounds retries two ways:
- a **per-request** limit of 3 attempts;
- a **per-client retry budget**, under which a client retries only while retries stay below **10%** of its requests.

In the worst case the per-request cap alone still allows about 3× load growth. The 10% budget cuts that to about **1.1×**. AWS SDKs similarly limit local retries with a token bucket.

Retry only errors that may be transient. Never retry validation errors, and honour `Retry-After` on 429 and 503 responses.

Finally, retry a call with side effects only if it is idempotent. The idempotency lesson covers how.

keyPoints: Set timeouts from an acceptable false-timeout rate, e.g. 0.1% maps to downstream p99.9.
Propagate the remaining deadline; drop work whose deadline has passed.
Up to a^k attempts reach the bottom of k layers that each make a attempts; retry at a single layer.
Use capped exponential backoff with jitter; jitter periodic jobs with a consistent per-host offset.
Retry budget: at most 3 attempts per request and retries under 10% of a client's requests (about 1.1x growth instead of 3x).

gotchas.trap: Every layer retries 3 times "to be safe".
gotchas.correct: Retries multiply; retry at one layer and propagate a do-not-retry signal upward.

gotchas.trap: Fixed-interval retries after an outage.
gotchas.correct: Capped exponential backoff with jitter, so clients do not retry in lockstep.

gotchas.trap: Using a library default 30 s timeout for a 20 ms call.
gotchas.correct: Derive the timeout from the downstream latency distribution and the caller's deadline.

gotchas.trap: Picking a fresh random offset for hourly cron jobs on every run.
gotchas.correct: Use a consistent per-host offset, such as a hash of the host ID.

lessons.title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and degradation
lessons.summary: Stop calling what is failing, isolate resources per dependency, reject excess load early to protect goodput, and degrade features instead of failing whole requests.

sections.heading: Circuit breakers
sections.body:
A circuit breaker is a proxy that tracks recent failures. The Azure pattern defines three states:
- **Closed:** calls pass through. A *time-based* failure counter trips the breaker when failures exceed a threshold within an interval.
- **Open:** calls fail immediately. A timeout timer starts.
- **Half-Open:** a *limited* number of trial calls pass through. Enough consecutive successes close the breaker; any failure reopens it.

Half-Open exists so that a recovering service is not flooded. When the breaker is open, it can return a **meaningful default value** instead of an exception.

Breakers and retries are different tools: retry expects eventual success, while a breaker prevents calls that are likely to fail. If you combine them, the retry logic must stop when the breaker reports a non-transient fault.

sections.heading: Scope and caveats
sections.body:
Scope breakers to independent failure units. The Azure page's example is a sharded data store: if one shard's errors trip a single shared breaker, the client also stops using the healthy shards. Use one breaker per shard, partition or endpoint.

The Builders' Library warns that breakers introduce **modal behaviour**, which is hard to test. Prefer simple, always-on limits such as retry token buckets where they suffice, and test breaker transitions deliberately.

sections.heading: Bulkheads
sections.body:
A **bulkhead** partitions resources so that one failing dependency cannot drain capacity everyone shares.

The classic form is a separate connection or thread pool per downstream service. If Service A hangs, only work in A's pool waits, and calls to B and C continue. You can also partition service instances per consumer, so a noisy client exhausts only its own slice.

Azure suggests combining bulkheads with retry, circuit breaker and throttling.

sections.heading: Load shedding and goodput
sections.body:
Under overload, **throughput** (requests sent) and **goodput** (requests answered correctly and fast enough to be useful) diverge. Without shedding, latency climbs until clients time out and goodput collapses toward zero.

**Load shedding** rejects excess requests quickly so that the accepted ones stay fast. In the ideal overload test, goodput plateaus near full utilization and stays flat as offered load keeps rising.

Shedding is not free: rejecting still costs CPU, so shed as **early and cheaply** as possible. Concretely:
- Return 503 once in-flight requests pass a limit.
- Keep queues bounded.
- Prefer LIFO or CoDel-style queues over FIFO during overload, so you do not serve requests whose clients already gave up.

Prioritize traffic by **criticality**. The SRE book uses CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS and SHEDDABLE, and sheds the sheddable classes first.

sections.heading: Graceful degradation
sections.body:
Fail partially, not totally. The SRE book: redirect when possible, serve **degraded results** when necessary, and handle resource errors transparently when all else fails.

Typical degradations:
- Render a product page without recommendations.
- Serve slightly stale cached data.
- Disable an expensive search filter.
- Switch to a cheaper algorithm.

Decide the degraded modes in advance, make them testable, and alert when they activate.

keyPoints: Circuit breaker states: Closed (counting failures), Open (fail fast), Half-Open (limited trial calls).
Scope breakers per shard, partition or endpoint so one bad unit does not cut off healthy ones.
Bulkheads isolate pools per dependency or per consumer to stop resource exhaustion from cascading.
Load shedding protects goodput; shed early, cheaply and by criticality.
Graceful degradation serves reduced functionality instead of failing whole requests.

gotchas.trap: One shared connection pool for all downstream calls.
gotchas.correct: A pool per dependency (a bulkhead), each with its own timeout.

gotchas.trap: Retrying through an open circuit breaker.
gotchas.correct: Retry logic should stop when the breaker reports the fault is not transient.

gotchas.trap: An unbounded FIFO queue absorbing an overload.
gotchas.correct: Bound the queue, drop expired work and prefer LIFO or CoDel under overload.

gotchas.trap: Returning 500 for the whole page when an optional widget fails.
gotchas.correct: Degrade: omit the widget or serve a cached or default value.

Put it in front of a fake dependency that fails 100% of calls for 10 s and then recovers. Log the state transitions and show that Half-Open lets only a few calls through.

lessons.title: Rate limiting algorithms and distributed limits
lessons.summary: Fixed and sliding windows, token and leaky buckets, the right status codes, and how to enforce one limit across many servers without races.

sections.heading: Window algorithms
sections.body:
The Redis rate-limiting tutorial compares the common algorithms.

- **Fixed window:** count requests per discrete interval, with the window number in the key. It is the simplest and uses one counter. Because the counter resets at each boundary, a client can send nearly **2× the limit** around a boundary.
- **Sliding window log:** store a timestamp per request and count those inside the rolling window. It is exact with no boundary bursts, but memory grows with the request count (O(n) per client).
- **Sliding window counter:** keep the current and previous fixed-window counters and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the rolling window. It is near-exact with two counters, and the tutorial calls it the best default for most APIs.

sections.heading: Token bucket and leaky bucket
sections.body:
A **token bucket** has a refill rate and a capacity. Each request takes a token, and an empty bucket means reject. The capacity is the **burst**: tokens saved while idle can be spent at once. API Gateway throttles this way, where a *rate* (tokens added per second) plus a *burst* (bucket capacity) define the limit.

The Builders' Library warns that a large burst defeats the limit. It suggests **chaining** a low-rate/high-burst bucket with a high-rate/low-burst bucket.

A **leaky bucket** drains at a fixed rate and comes in two variants:
- **Shaping:** queue requests and forward them at the drain rate, delaying bursts.
- **Policing:** drop requests that arrive faster than the drain rate.

Use it when the downstream needs a strictly even rate.

sections.heading: Responding to limited clients
sections.body:
Use the right status code:
- **429 Too Many Requests** (RFC 6585) means *this client* exceeded its quota.
- **503 Service Unavailable** means *the server* is out of capacity.

The Builders' Library draws the same 4xx-vs-5xx line. Include `Retry-After` so that well-behaved clients wait.

The `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers are still an **IETF draft**, not an RFC. Treat them as optional.

sections.heading: Distributed limits
sections.body:
A per-tenant limit across N servers needs coordination. There are three options.

1. **Split the quota locally.** Give each server limit/N. It is cheap, but it breaks when traffic is uneven: a tenant pinned to two of ten servers gets only 20% of its quota. The Builders' Library uses relaxed burst values or distributed admission control for non-uniform traffic.
2. **Use a central counter store**, such as Redis. It needs **atomic** read-check-update. A separate GET then SET is a TOCTOU race that lets concurrent requests bypass the limit. Redis runs Lua scripts atomically. In Redis Cluster, every key a script touches must hash to the same slot, so use hash tags for two-key algorithms.
3. **Route each key to one owner** with consistent hashing, or have servers share observed rates. This is approximate but avoids a hot central store.

When *you* are the client of a throttled service, rate-limit yourself. The Azure Rate Limiting pattern's example: blind retry-on-error sent 30,000 records to ingest 10,000. Its fix is to write records to a durable queue and have job processors drain it at a controlled rate under the limit.

keyPoints: A fixed window is simple but allows about 2x the limit across a boundary.
A sliding window log is exact but O(n) memory; a sliding window counter is near-exact with two counters.
Token bucket = refill rate + capacity (the burst); leaky bucket = constant drain (shape or police).
429 means the client exceeded its quota; 503 means the server is out of capacity.
Distributed counters must update atomically (for example a Redis Lua script); local splits break under skew.

gotchas.trap: Implementing a Redis limiter as GET, compare, then SET.
gotchas.correct: Make check-and-increment atomic, for example with a Lua script.

gotchas.trap: Returning 503 when a tenant exceeds its quota.
gotchas.correct: Return 429 with Retry-After; keep 503 for server capacity problems.

gotchas.trap: Setting a token-bucket burst equal to a whole day's quota.
gotchas.correct: Keep the burst bounded, or chain a second high-rate, low-burst bucket.

gotchas.trap: Calling the RateLimit headers a published standard.
gotchas.correct: They are still an IETF Internet-Draft.

Replay a trace that sends 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00, and count how many each limiter admits. Then make the token bucket atomic in Redis with a Lua script, and fire 50 concurrent requests to show it never over-admits.

lessons.title: Idempotency keys and safe retries
lessons.summary: Which HTTP methods are safe to retry, how idempotency keys make POSTs and payments retryable, and how consumers deduplicate at-least-once deliveries.

sections.heading: Method semantics
sections.body:
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as **safe**. PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are **idempotent**; POST and PATCH are not.

On retries the RFC is explicit:
- A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it knows the request is idempotent.
- A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests.

Idempotent means the *effect on the server* is the same however many times the request runs. The response may differ: a second DELETE can return 404.

sections.heading: Idempotency keys
sections.body:
To make a POST retryable, the client generates a **unique key per logical operation**, such as a UUID, and sends the same key on every retry. The server then works as follows:

1. Look up the key. If it is unseen, process the request and **store the key with the outcome atomically with the side effect**. The Builders' Library calls out the failure modes to avoid: recording the token but failing to create the resource, or creating the resource but failing to record the token.
2. If the key was seen and the request completed, return a **semantically equivalent response**, the same meaning as the first response.
3. If the key was seen **with different parameters**, reject it. The Builders' Library returns a validation error. The IETF Idempotency-Key draft suggests **422**.
4. If the key was seen and the original is **still in flight**, the draft suggests **409 Conflict**.

Keys expire after a documented window. The `Idempotency-Key` header itself is still an **IETF draft**, not an RFC.

sections.heading: Payments and timeouts
sections.body:
A timeout tells you nothing about whether the charge happened. The only safe recovery is to **retry with the same key**.

Generating a new key per attempt, or "checking status, then charging again", can double-charge whenever the first attempt is still in flight or its result is not yet visible.

Claim the key with a unique constraint or a set-if-absent write, so that two concurrent requests cannot both proceed.

sections.heading: Idempotent consumers and deduplication
sections.body:
At-least-once delivery means duplicates. The Azure **Idempotent Consumer** pattern prescribes four rules:
- Use a **stable deduplication key**: a producer-assigned message ID or a business idempotency key, *not* a correlation ID shared by related messages.
- **Claim the key atomically**, with an insert that fails on conflict or a set-if-absent.
- **Commit the dedup marker and the business side effects in the same transaction**. Check, process, then record as separate steps leaves a crash window that reprocesses the message.
- If several consumers share a dedup store, key it on **consumer identity + message identity**.

keyPoints: Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. Idempotent: those plus PUT and DELETE. Not idempotent: POST, PATCH.
Proxies must not auto-retry non-idempotent requests.
Send one idempotency key per logical operation and reuse it on every retry.
Same key with a different payload means reject (422 in the IETF draft); same key still in flight means 409.
Record the key and the side effect atomically; consumers commit the dedup marker in the same transaction.

gotchas.trap: Generating a fresh idempotency key on each retry attempt.
gotchas.correct: The key identifies the logical operation; every retry reuses it.

gotchas.trap: Writing the order to the database, then the key to a cache in a separate step.
gotchas.correct: Store the key and the effect in one transaction, or claim the key atomically first.

gotchas.trap: Deduplicating messages on a correlation ID.
gotchas.correct: Use a stable per-message or per-operation identifier.

gotchas.trap: Calling Idempotency-Key an HTTP standard.
gotchas.correct: It is an IETF Internet-Draft.

Write tests for a first call, a retry after completion (same response), a retry with a different amount (422), and two concurrent calls with the same key (one gets 409, one charge recorded).
