lessons.title: Queues, logs and delivery semantics
lessons.summary: How queues and partitioned logs differ, what at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once really promise, and why ordering only exists per partition.

sections.heading: Queues versus logs
sections.body:
A **queue** hands each message to one worker and forgets it once it is acknowledged. Workers compete for messages, so adding workers adds throughput (the Competing Consumers pattern), but there is no durable history to re-read.

A **log** (Kafka is the common example) is an append-only, retained sequence of records split into **partitions**. Consumers track their own position (the offset). Because the data stays for the retention period (Kafka's topic default `retention.ms` is 7 days), a new consumer can replay history, and several independent consumer groups can read the same topic.

| | Queue | Partitioned log |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of parallelism | Message | Partition (per consumer group) |
| Replay | Usually no | Yes, within retention |
| Ordering | Weak once you have many workers | Per partition |
| Fan-out to many readers | Needs topics/subscriptions | Each consumer group reads independently |

Kafka 4.2 and later also offer **share groups** (KIP-932, "Queues for Kafka"), where consumers can outnumber partitions and records are acknowledged individually. Treat this as queue-style consumption on top of a log, and check the current release notes for details.

sections.heading: Delivery semantics come from where you record progress
sections.body:
The Kafka design docs define the three guarantees:

- **At-most-once:** messages "may be lost but are never redelivered".
- **At-least-once:** messages "are never lost but may be redelivered".
- **Exactly-once:** each message is "processed once and only once".

For a consumer, the choice comes from *when it saves its position*:

1. Save the offset, **then** process. If you crash after saving, the message is skipped: **at-most-once**.
2. Process, **then** save the offset. If you crash after processing, the message is processed again: **at-least-once**.

At-least-once is the usual default, so **handlers must be idempotent**. The Idempotent Consumer pattern records processed message IDs, or makes the write naturally idempotent (an upsert keyed on the event ID), so a redelivery has no extra effect.

sections.heading: Effectively-once and its limits
sections.body:
Kafka's idempotent producer (producer ID plus sequence numbers) stops retries from writing duplicates to a partition. Kafka transactions write atomically across partitions, and consumers that use `isolation.level=read_committed` see only committed data (the default is `read_uncommitted`). Together these give exactly-once for read-process-write pipelines that stay **inside Kafka**.

Once the output leaves Kafka, the docs are explicit: exactly-once "for other destination systems generally requires cooperation with such systems". In practice that means one of:

- store the consumer position **in the same transaction** as the output (for example, the offset in the same database row update), or
- make the destination write idempotent, keyed on a stable message ID.

This is why many teams say "effectively-once": delivery is at-least-once, and idempotent processing makes the *effect* happen once.

sections.heading: Ordering, partitions and keys
sections.body:
Kafka guarantees order **only within a partition**. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a consumer group, so:

- Records that must stay in order (all events for one account, one order, one device) need the **same key**, so that they land in the same partition.
- Parallelism in a classic consumer group is capped by the partition count. With 6 partitions and 10 consumers, 4 consumers sit idle.
- A hot key creates a hot partition. Ordering per key and spreading load are in tension.

**Durability settings.** The 4.4 producer defaults are `acks=all` and `enable.idempotence=true`. The topic default `min.insync.replicas` is **1**, so with `acks=all` a write can still be acknowledged when only the leader holds it. For durable topics, use replication factor 3 with `min.insync.replicas=2`. Writes are then rejected, not silently under-replicated, once the in-sync replica set (ISR) shrinks below 2.

keyPoints: A queue distributes messages to competing workers; a log retains records and lets each consumer group track its own offset and replay.
Commit the offset before processing gives at-most-once; process then commit gives at-least-once.
Exactly-once in Kafka covers Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines; external sinks need idempotent writes or offsets stored with the output.
Order is guaranteed only within a partition; key by the entity whose events must stay ordered.
For durability use RF=3, `acks=all` and `min.insync.replicas=2`; the topic default for min ISR is 1.

gotchas.trap: "We turned on Kafka exactly-once, so our database sink can never see duplicates."
gotchas.correct: Kafka transactions cover Kafka topics and offsets. A write to an external database still needs an idempotent upsert or the offset stored in the same database transaction.

gotchas.trap: Adding consumers beyond the partition count to go faster.
gotchas.correct: In a classic consumer group each partition goes to one consumer, so extra consumers sit idle. Add partitions, or use share groups when per-key order does not matter.

gotchas.trap: Assuming `acks=all` alone guarantees a write is on several replicas.
gotchas.correct: `acks=all` waits for the current ISR, which can shrink to just the leader. Set `min.insync.replicas=2` on the topic.

lessons.title: Dual writes, the outbox and CDC
lessons.summary: Why "write to the database, then publish an event" is broken, and how the transactional outbox and change data capture fix it.

sections.heading: The dual-write problem
sections.body:
A service that must both **update its database** and **publish an event** has two independent systems to write to. Without a transaction spanning both, any crash or timeout between the two writes leaves them disagreeing:

- DB commit succeeds, publish fails or the process dies: the state changed, but nobody downstream hears about it.
- Publish succeeds, DB commit fails: downstream acts on a change that never happened.

**Reordering the two writes does not help.** It only changes which inconsistency you get. Retrying the second write helps only until the process itself crashes. The fix is to make **one atomic write** the source of truth.

sections.heading: The transactional outbox
Change data capture as the relay
sections.body:
Instead of polling the outbox table, a **change data capture (CDC)** connector can tail the database's transaction log and turn committed changes into events. In PostgreSQL the mechanism is **logical decoding**, which streams committed changes from the write-ahead log through a replication slot.

CDC has two common uses:

1. **CDC on the outbox table.** You still choose explicit, versioned event payloads, but you drop the polling query. This is usually the best of both.
2. **CDC on the business tables directly.** This works for replicating data into search indexes or warehouses. It is a weaker choice for domain events, because it exposes your internal schema as a public contract.

Logical replication slots hold back WAL until they are consumed, so a stalled CDC consumer can fill the disk. Monitor slot lag.

sections.heading: Anti-patterns to recognise
sections.body:
- **Publish inside the DB transaction** (calling the broker before `COMMIT`): the publish can succeed and the commit then fail.
- **A database trigger that makes an HTTP call**: the same dual write again, now hidden.
- **"We'll use a distributed transaction across the DB and the broker"**: many brokers and cloud databases cannot take part in XA/2PC, and where they can, it couples availability. See the saga lesson.
- **Non-idempotent consumers behind an outbox**: duplicates are expected, not exceptional.

keyPoints: A dual write to a database and a broker cannot be made safe by ordering or retrying the two writes.
Outbox: write state and the event row in one local transaction; a relay publishes afterwards.
The relay is at-least-once, so consumers must dedupe on a stable event ID.
CDC (PostgreSQL logical decoding) can replace polling by tailing committed changes from the WAL.
Prefer CDC on an outbox table over CDC on internal tables for domain events.

gotchas.trap: "Publish first, then write the DB, and the problem goes away."
gotchas.correct: Either order leaves a window where one write succeeded and the other did not. Only a single atomic write plus asynchronous publication removes it.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the outbox gives exactly-once delivery.
gotchas.correct: The relay can publish and then crash before marking the row as sent. Expect duplicates and make consumers idempotent.

gotchas.trap: Leaving a CDC replication slot unmonitored.
gotchas.correct: A slot that is not consumed retains WAL. Alert on slot lag and disk use.

2. Redesign it with an outbox table. Write the DDL and the single transaction.
3. Write the relay loop, and mark the step where a crash causes a duplicate.

lessons.title: Sagas, 2PC, event sourcing and CQRS
lessons.summary: Coordinating a business transaction across services with sagas and compensation instead of two-phase commit, and when event sourcing and CQRS are worth their cost.

sections.heading: Two-phase commit and why services avoid it
sections.body:
**Two-phase commit (2PC)** makes several participants commit atomically. A coordinator asks every participant to **prepare** (make the change durable and promise to commit). Only if all vote yes does it tell them to **commit**; otherwise it tells them to abort.

The costs:

- **Blocking.** A participant that has prepared cannot decide on its own. If the coordinator fails after prepare, participants hold locks until it recovers.
- **Availability coupling.** Every participant must be up for any transaction to commit.
- **Support.** Many brokers, SaaS APIs and NoSQL stores cannot take part at all.

2PC still exists inside single systems and databases. Across microservices that each own their data, the usual answer is a saga.

sections.heading: Sagas: compensable, pivot and retryable steps
sections.body:
A **saga** is a sequence of local transactions, each in one service, where each step publishes an event or message that triggers the next. If a step fails, the saga runs **compensating transactions** that semantically undo the earlier steps, for example "refund the payment" or "release the reservation". Compensation is a new business action, not a rollback.

The Azure saga guidance classifies steps as:

- **Compensable**: can be undone by a compensating transaction.
- **Pivot**: the point of no return. Once it succeeds, the saga must run to completion.
- **Retryable**: follow the pivot, are idempotent, and are retried until they succeed.

Put steps that are hard to undo (charging a card, sending a physical shipment) at or after the pivot, and put cheap, reversible steps (reservations) before it.

**Choreography vs orchestration.** With choreography, each service reacts to events with no central coordinator. This suits a few steps, but it gets hard to follow as the saga grows and risks cyclic dependencies. With orchestration, a coordinator tells each participant what to do. That makes the workflow explicit and suits complex sagas, but it adds a component that holds the workflow logic and must itself be reliable.

sections.heading: Saga anomalies and countermeasures
sections.body:
Sagas give up isolation: other transactions can see intermediate state. The Azure guidance lists **lost updates**, **dirty reads** and **fuzzy (non-repeatable) reads**, and these countermeasures:

- **Semantic lock**: mark records as in progress (for example `status = PENDING`) so other operations treat them carefully.
- **Commutative updates**: design updates so that their order does not matter (increment and decrement, not set).
- **Pessimistic view**: reorder steps so that dirty reads cause the least harm.
- **Reread value**: check that data is unchanged before updating it.
- **Version file**: record operations so that they can be reordered or replayed.
- **Risk-based concurrency**: choose the mechanism per operation by business risk.

sections.heading: Event sourcing and CQRS at a working level
sections.body:
**Event sourcing** stores the **sequence of events** that happened to an entity in an append-only store, instead of its current state. Current state is derived by **replaying** events, often from a snapshot. You get a full audit trail, temporal queries and the ability to build new views later. Events are immutable, so you correct a mistake by appending a compensating event. The costs are event schema versioning, replay time and a harder mental model.

**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the **write model** (commands, invariants) from one or more **read models** that are optimised for queries. It pairs naturally with event sourcing, where projections consume the event stream to build read models. Once the read store is separate and updated asynchronously, **reads are eventually consistent**: a client may not see its own write right away. Design for that, for example by returning the new version from the command, showing a pending state, or reading the write side for the user's own data.

Use either pattern for complex domains with real audit or scaling needs, not as a default for simple CRUD.

keyPoints: 2PC blocks prepared participants if the coordinator fails, and couples the availability of every participant.
A saga is a series of local transactions with compensating transactions to undo completed steps.
Steps before the pivot are compensable; the pivot is the point of no return; steps after it are retryable and idempotent.
Sagas lack isolation; use semantic locks, commutative updates and rereads to contain anomalies.
With CQRS and a separate, asynchronously updated read store, queries are eventually consistent.

gotchas.trap: Treating a compensating transaction as a database rollback.
gotchas.correct: Compensation is a new, visible business action (a refund, a release). Other parties may already have seen the intermediate state.

gotchas.trap: Compensating after the pivot step succeeded.
gotchas.correct: After the pivot, the saga runs forward: retry the idempotent remaining steps until they succeed.

gotchas.trap: Adopting event sourcing and CQRS for a simple CRUD service.
gotchas.correct: Both add versioning, replay and eventual-consistency costs. Use them where audit, temporal queries or very different read and write shapes justify it.

1. Classify each step as compensable, pivot or retryable, and write each compensation.
2. Draw it once as choreography (events) and once as orchestration (a coordinator), and note which is easier to change.
3. Identify one dirty-read risk and choose a countermeasure.

lessons.title: Consensus, leases and time
lessons.summary: Raft and majority quorums at a working level, why leases need fencing tokens, and why wall clocks cannot order events.

sections.heading: Consensus with Raft
sections.body:
**Consensus** lets a group of servers agree on a sequence of values (a replicated log) even if some of them fail. **Raft** was designed to be understandable. It elects a **leader** that accepts commands and replicates log entries to followers, and an entry is committed once a **majority** has stored it.

- A cluster of **2f + 1** servers tolerates **f** failures: 3 tolerates 1, and 5 tolerates 2. A 4-node cluster still tolerates only 1, because a majority of 4 is 3.
- The Google SRE book recommends **5 replicas** for critical state, so you can take one down for maintenance and still survive a failure.
- If too many servers fail, the cluster **stops making progress, but it never returns incorrect results**.
- Each election starts a new **term** (a generation clock). Servers reject messages from stale terms, which stops a deposed leader from overwriting newer decisions.
- Election timeouts are randomised so that split votes resolve quickly.

**Cost.** A commit needs about one round trip to a quorum plus a durable disk write. That is cheap within a datacenter (an RTT of about 1 ms) and expensive across regions (about 70 ms from New York to London, per the SRE book).

In practice, you rarely implement Raft yourself. You use a coordination service or a database built on it (the "consistent core" pattern), and keep the large data elsewhere.

sections.heading: Leader election, leases and fencing tokens
Why wall clocks lie
sections.body:
Each machine's clock drifts. NTP adjusts it, sometimes by **stepping it backwards or forwards**, and leap seconds and VM pauses add more jumps. Therefore:

- **Never order events across machines by wall-clock timestamp.** With last-write-wins on wall-clock time, a node whose clock is a few hundred milliseconds fast silently overwrites newer updates.
- **Measure durations with a monotonic clock** (timeouts, lease expiry, latency). Redis notes that its key TTL is not based on a monotonic clock, so wall-clock jumps can make a lock expire early or late.
- Use wall-clock time **for humans** (logs, display), not for correctness. The Builders' Library makes the same point about Amazon's systems.

sections.heading: Logical clocks
sections.body:
- **Lamport clock:** each node keeps a counter, increments it on every event, and on receipt sets it to max(local, received) + 1. If a happened before b, then L(a) < L(b). The **converse does not hold**: L(a) < L(b) does not prove causality, and the events may have been concurrent. Lamport clocks give a total order consistent with causality (break ties by node ID).
- **Version vectors** (vector clocks) keep one counter per node. Comparing two vectors tells you whether one version **descends from** the other or whether they are **concurrent**, which is what you need to detect conflicting writes in multi-leader or leaderless stores.
- **Hybrid logical clocks** combine physical time with a logical counter. Timestamps stay close to wall-clock time but still respect causality.
- **Clock-bound wait:** systems that expose a bounded clock uncertainty can wait out that bound before acknowledging a write, so timestamp order matches real-time order.

keyPoints: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures; even-sized clusters add cost without adding fault tolerance.
Raft loses availability, not correctness, when it loses a majority.
Leases are measured with local elapsed time; expect zero or two leaders during failures.
Fencing tokens make the protected resource reject writes from stale lease holders.
Use monotonic clocks for durations, and logical or vector clocks, not wall clocks, to order events.

gotchas.trap: "The leader checks its lease right before writing, so two leaders cannot both write."
gotchas.correct: A pause between the check and the write still lets a stale leader write. The resource must enforce a fencing token.

gotchas.trap: Running 4 or 6 consensus nodes "for extra safety".
gotchas.correct: 4 nodes tolerate 1 failure (like 3), and 6 tolerate 2 (like 5). Use odd sizes.

gotchas.trap: Resolving conflicts with last-write-wins on server wall-clock time.
gotchas.correct: Clock skew silently drops newer writes. Use version vectors to detect concurrency, or a single ordered log.

gotchas.trap: Concluding causality from L(a) < L(b).
gotchas.correct: Lamport clocks only guarantee the forward direction. Use version vectors to tell concurrency from causality.

2. Simulate a 30-second GC pause on the leader, and write out what each node and the job table see.
3. Add a fencing token column to the job table, and write the conditional UPDATE that rejects the stale leader.

lessons.title: API styles: REST, gRPC, GraphQL, webhooks and SSE
lessons.summary: What each API style is good at, what it costs, and how to pick one from the shape of the traffic: who calls whom, how often, and over which network.

sections.heading: Start from the interaction, not the fashion
sections.body:
Pick an API style by asking three questions:

1. **Who starts the conversation?** The client asks (request/response), the server pushes (streaming), or a third party calls you back (webhook).
2. **Who is the client?** A browser, a mobile app, another service you own, or a partner you do not control.
3. **What is the contract?** Is it a loose, human-readable JSON contract that many outsiders read, or a strict, generated contract between teams that deploy together?

Most products end up with more than one style. For example: a public REST API, gRPC between internal services, SSE for live progress in the browser and webhooks to notify partners.

sections.heading: REST over HTTP
sections.body:
REST models the system as **resources** (`/orders/123`) and uses HTTP methods for actions on them. Its strengths come from HTTP itself:

- Every client and proxy understands it.
- Method semantics (safe, idempotent) are standardised in RFC 9110.
- GET responses can be cached by URL.
- Status codes and headers carry meaning without a custom protocol.

It is the default for public and partner APIs. Its main cost is that the server fixes the shape of each response. One client may get more fields than it needs (over-fetching), and another may have to make several calls to build one screen (under-fetching).

sections.heading: gRPC for service-to-service calls
sections.body:
Microsoft's gRPC comparison sums up the trade-off:

- gRPC **requires a contract** (a `.proto` file) and generates client code from it.
- It runs on **HTTP/2** and sends **Protobuf**, a compact binary format.
- It supports client, server and **bidirectional streaming**.

The costs:

- Browsers cannot call gRPC directly; you need **gRPC-Web** or a translating proxy.
- Binary payloads are harder to inspect by hand.

That makes gRPC a strong fit for internal, high-volume calls between services you own. It is a weak fit for a public API that third parties call with curl.

sections.heading: GraphQL for client-shaped reads
sections.body:
GraphQL is a query language and a specification. It usually runs over a **single HTTP endpoint**, and the client names exactly the fields it wants. AWS's comparison frames its main benefit as avoiding **over-fetching and under-fetching**. One query can gather nested data that would take several REST round trips.

It fits when many client screens need different slices of a rich, connected data model, typically on mobile networks. The costs move to the server:

- Every resolver needs its own authorization.
- You must limit query depth and cost, because one query can touch a lot of data.
- Per-URL HTTP caching no longer happens on its own.

sections.heading: Push: server-sent events and webhooks
sections.body:
**Server-sent events (SSE)** are a one-way stream from server to browser over plain HTTP. MDN describes them this way:

- The response uses the `text/event-stream` media type.
- The browser's `EventSource` **reconnects automatically**. The server can set the `retry` delay and an event `id`, which the browser remembers as the last event ID.
- It is **one-way**: the client cannot send messages back on the stream.
- Over HTTP/1.1 the browser allows only about **6 connections per domain**, shared across tabs. Over HTTP/2, streams are multiplexed.

SSE fits progress bars, live logs and token-by-token LLM output. If you need two-way, low-latency messaging, use WebSockets.

**Webhooks** are HTTP callbacks from a provider to a URL the consumer registers. Azure Event Grid's documentation shows the usual contract:

- **At-least-once delivery** with retries, so **duplicates can arrive**.
- **No ordering guarantee.**

Many providers also ask the receiver to prove it owns the URL (an endpoint-validation handshake) before events flow.

A receiver should therefore authenticate each delivery, acknowledge quickly with a 2xx, put the work on a queue, and process **idempotently**, keyed on the event ID.

keyPoints: Choose by interaction shape: request/response (REST, gRPC, GraphQL), server push to a browser (SSE), or callbacks to a third party (webhooks).
gRPC: required .proto contract, HTTP/2, Protobuf, bidirectional streaming; browsers need gRPC-Web.
GraphQL: single endpoint, client-selected fields, fewer round trips; authorization and query-cost limits move into the server.
SSE is one-way over HTTP with automatic reconnect; over HTTP/1.1 it is limited to about 6 connections per browser per domain.
Webhooks are typically at-least-once and unordered: dedupe by event ID, acknowledge fast, process asynchronously.

gotchas.trap: Calling a gRPC service directly from browser JavaScript.
gotchas.correct: Browsers do not support gRPC natively. Use gRPC-Web or a proxy, or expose REST, GraphQL or SSE at the edge.

gotchas.trap: Treating each webhook delivery as unique and in order.
gotchas.correct: Providers retry, so the same event can arrive twice and out of order. Store processed event IDs, and use timestamps or versions in the payload to order state changes.

gotchas.trap: Polling every second for job progress from thousands of browsers.
gotchas.correct: Use SSE (or WebSockets when you need two-way traffic) so the server pushes only when something changes.

lessons.title: API design: pagination, versioning, errors and idempotent methods
lessons.summary: The contract details that decide whether an API survives growth and retries: cursor vs offset pagination, versioning without breaking clients, RFC 9457 errors, and RFC 9110 method semantics.

sections.heading: Pagination: offset vs cursor
sections.body:
**Offset pagination** (`?limit=25&offset=50`) is simple, and the Azure API guide uses it in its examples, with a server-side cap on `limit`. It has two problems at scale:

- **Cost.** PostgreSQL's docs say that rows skipped by an OFFSET clause "still have to be computed inside the server", so a large OFFSET can be inefficient. Page 10,000 costs far more than page 1.
- **Drift.** If rows are inserted or deleted between requests, the window shifts. Clients then see duplicates or miss items.

**Cursor (keyset) pagination** returns an opaque token that encodes where the last page ended, for example the last `(created_at, id)`. The next query asks for rows *after* that key using an index. Microsoft Graph works this way: it returns an `@odata.nextLink` URL with a skip token, and the client follows it until no link comes back.

Rules that apply either way:

- Always sort on a **unique, stable order**. PostgreSQL warns that without a unique ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an unpredictable subset.
- Cap the page size.
- Keep the cursor opaque so you can change its encoding later.

sections.heading: Versioning without breaking clients
sections.body:
The Azure guide lists four ways to carry a version: **URI** (`/v2/orders`), **query string**, a **custom header**, or the **media type**. Google's API design guide puts a **major version** in the URI path (`v1`) and never exposes minor or patch numbers. Backward-compatible changes ship in place.

The practical rule:

- **Additive changes** (a new optional field, a new endpoint, a new optional parameter) are not breaking, as long as clients ignore fields they do not recognise.
- **Removing, renaming or changing the meaning or type of a field** is breaking. It needs a new major version and a deprecation period for the old one.

sections.heading: Errors: status codes plus Problem Details
sections.body:
Use the status code for the class of failure, and a machine-readable body for the details.

**Status codes** (RFC 9110 unless noted):

- **400**: malformed request.
- **401 / 403**: not authenticated / not allowed.
- **404**: not found.
- **409 Conflict**: conflicts with the current state.
- **412 Precondition Failed**: a conditional request such as If-Match failed.
- **422 Unprocessable Content**: well-formed but semantically invalid.
- **503 Service Unavailable**: overloaded or down. It may carry Retry-After.
- **429 Too Many Requests**: comes from **RFC 6585**, not RFC 9110.

**The body.** RFC 9457 (which **obsoletes RFC 7807**) defines `application/problem+json` with these members:

- `type`: a URI that identifies the problem type. It defaults to `about:blank`.
- `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`.

Never return 200 with an error inside the body. Caches, retries and monitoring all read the status code.

sections.heading: Safe and idempotent methods (RFC 9110)
sections.body:
RFC 9110 §9.2 defines two properties:

- **Safe** methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) are read-only by contract.
- **Idempotent** methods are the safe ones plus **PUT and DELETE**. Repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once.
- **POST is not idempotent**, and neither is PATCH.

The RFC says a client **SHOULD NOT** automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it knows the request is idempotent, and a proxy **MUST NOT** do so.

How to make creates safe to retry:

- Let the client choose the identifier and `PUT /orders/{id}`.
- Or accept a client-supplied idempotency key on POST. The `Idempotency-Key` header is still an **IETF draft**, not an RFC.

**Conditional requests stop lost updates.** The server returns an `ETag`. The client sends `If-Match: <etag>` with PUT or DELETE. If someone else changed the resource in the meantime, the server answers **412 Precondition Failed**. RFC 9110 names this "lost update" avoidance.

keyPoints: Large OFFSET values are computed and then discarded; cursor/keyset pagination seeks straight to the next key and does not drift when rows are inserted.
Always paginate on a unique, stable sort order and cap the page size.
Additive changes are compatible; removing, renaming or retyping a field needs a new major version.
RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json) replaced RFC 7807; type defaults to about:blank.
Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. Idempotent: those plus PUT and DELETE. POST and PATCH are not idempotent.
ETag + If-Match gives optimistic concurrency over HTTP; a stale write gets 412.

gotchas.trap: "Our clients can retry any request that times out."
gotchas.correct: Only idempotent requests are safe to retry blindly. A retried POST can create a duplicate unless the API takes an idempotency key or the create is a PUT to a client-chosen ID.

gotchas.trap: Citing RFC 7807 as the current error format.
gotchas.correct: RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 7807. The media type application/problem+json is unchanged.

gotchas.trap: Saying 429 is defined in RFC 9110.
gotchas.correct: 429 Too Many Requests is defined in RFC 6585. RFC 9110 defines 409, 412, 422 and 503.

gotchas.trap: Paginating with ORDER BY created_at alone.
gotchas.correct: Timestamps can tie. Add a unique tie-breaker such as id, or pages can repeat or skip rows.

Rewrite it as cursor pagination: define the sort key, the cursor contents, the SQL predicate and the response shape (items plus next link). Then design the error body for "order already shipped, cannot cancel" as RFC 9457 Problem Details and pick its status code.

lessons.title: Authentication and authorization: sessions, OAuth 2.0, OIDC and JWTs
lessons.summary: Sessions vs tokens, which OAuth 2.0 flows current best practice allows (RFC 9700, RFC 10017), what OIDC adds, and the JWT validation mistakes that turn into breaches.

sections.heading: Authentication vs authorization
sections.body:
- **Authentication** proves who the caller is.
- **Authorization** decides what that caller may do with *this* object.

Many serious API breaches are authorization bugs. The caller is genuinely logged in, but the API never checks that invoice 123 belongs to the caller's tenant. That is why **Broken Access Control** is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025.

Authenticate once at the edge. Authorize on every object access, as close to the data as you can.

sections.heading: Sessions vs tokens
sections.body:
**Server-side sessions.**

- The browser holds a random session ID in a cookie, and the server holds the state.
- Revocation is immediate: delete the session.
- OWASP's session cheat sheet asks you to:
  - set cookies `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite`;
  - **renew the session ID after login** or any privilege change, which defeats session fixation;
  - avoid `localStorage` for session identifiers, because any script on the page, including injected script, can read it.

**Self-contained tokens (JWTs).**

- The token carries signed claims, so any service can check it without a lookup.
- The cost is that a token stays valid until it expires unless you add server-side state, such as a deny list or introspection.
- The usual answer is short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens.

For browser apps, **RFC 10017** (OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications) ranks the architectures from most to least secure:

1. **Backend for Frontend (BFF)**: a backend does all the OAuth work, keeps the tokens, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie.
2. A token-mediating backend.
3. A browser-only client.

sections.heading: OAuth 2.0 flows that are still allowed
sections.body:
**RFC 9700**, the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (January 2025), sets the current baseline:

- Use **Authorization Code with PKCE**.
  - PKCE is required for public clients (SPAs, mobile and desktop apps) and recommended for confidential clients.
  - Use the `S256` challenge method.
- **Do not use the implicit grant.**
- The **resource owner password credentials (ROPC)** grant **MUST NOT** be used.
- The authorization server matches redirect URIs by **exact string**. The only exception is the port of a localhost redirect for native apps.
- **Audience-restrict** access tokens, so a token minted for API A is rejected by API B.
- Prefer **sender-constrained** tokens, using mTLS (RFC 8705) or DPoP (RFC 9449).
- Public clients' refresh tokens must be sender-constrained or **rotated**.
- For machine-to-machine calls, use the client credentials grant.

**OAuth 2.1** folds these rules into one document, but it is still an **IETF draft**. Do not cite it as an RFC.

sections.heading: What OpenID Connect adds
JWT pitfalls (RFC 8725)
sections.body:
RFC 8725, the JWT Best Current Practices, lists real attacks:

- **`alg: none`**: an attacker strips the signature, and a naive library accepts the token.
- **Algorithm confusion**: an RS256 token is re-signed as HS256 with the public key used as the HMAC secret.
- **Weak HMAC keys**: they can be brute-forced offline.
- **Trusting header fields**: `kid`, `jku` and `x5u` come from the attacker. Using them leads to injection or SSRF.

Mitigations:

- **Pin an allowlist of algorithms.** Never take the algorithm from the token header.
- Validate **`iss`**, check that the key belongs to that issuer, and validate **`aud`**. Reject the token if `aud` is missing or wrong.
- Check `exp` and `nbf`.
- Use **explicit typing** (`typ`) so one kind of JWT cannot be swapped for another.
- Fetch keys only from configured issuer URLs.

A successor to RFC 8725 is in progress as a draft. RFC 8725 is still the current BCP.

keyPoints: Authorize every object access; authentication alone does not stop Broken Access Control (OWASP A01:2025).
Server sessions revoke instantly; JWTs verify without a lookup but live until expiry, so keep access tokens short-lived.
RFC 9700: Authorization Code + PKCE (S256), no implicit, ROPC MUST NOT be used, exact redirect URI matching, audience-restricted tokens.
RFC 10017 ranks BFF as the most secure browser architecture: tokens stay server-side.
ID tokens are for the client (aud = client_id); APIs accept access tokens issued for them.
JWT: allowlist algorithms, reject none, validate iss and aud, never trust kid/jku/x5u blindly.

gotchas.trap: Letting the JWT header pick the verification algorithm.
gotchas.correct: Configure the expected algorithm(s) per issuer and key. RFC 8725 describes the alg:none and RS256-to-HS256 attacks this prevents.

gotchas.trap: Using the implicit grant for a single-page app because it has no backend.
gotchas.correct: RFC 9700 says not to use implicit. Use Authorization Code with PKCE, and preferably a BFF (RFC 10017).

gotchas.trap: Sending the OIDC ID token to your API as a bearer token.
gotchas.correct: The ID token's audience is the client. The API should require an access token issued for its own audience.

gotchas.trap: Calling OAuth 2.1 "the new RFC".
gotchas.correct: OAuth 2.1 is still an Internet-Draft. RFC 9700 is the published security BCP.

For each, mark where the access token and refresh token live, what an XSS bug could steal, and which cookie attributes the BFF session cookie needs.

lessons.title: Multi-tenancy: pooled vs siloed, row-level security and noisy neighbours
lessons.summary: How to lay out tenants across infrastructure and data, enforce isolation in a shared database with PostgreSQL row-level security, and keep one tenant from degrading everyone else.

sections.heading: Tenancy models from silo to pool
sections.body:
Azure's multitenant guide describes a spectrum of tenancy models:

- **Automated single-tenant (silo).** Each tenant gets a dedicated deployment.
  - Strongest isolation, simple per-tenant compliance, no noisy neighbours.
  - Cost and operational work grow with every new customer.
- **Fully multitenant (pool).** All tenants share every component.
  - Cheapest per tenant and one deployment to run.
  - Needs careful isolation and fairness.
  - One shared resource can become a hard scaling limit.
- **Vertically partitioned.** Most tenants are pooled, and premium or regulated tenants get dedicated resources.
- **Horizontally partitioned.** Some tiers (for example the database) are per tenant, and others (for example the web tier) are shared.

Groups of tenants are often placed on **deployment stamps**: identical, independently deployable copies of the stack. A stamp caps the blast radius and gives you a unit of scale.

sections.heading: Data isolation options
sections.body:
The Azure storage guide compares three approaches:

- **Shared tables with a tenant identifier column.** Cheapest and simplest to run at scale. Restoring a single tenant is hard: you restore the whole database elsewhere and copy that tenant's rows back.
- **Database (or schema) per tenant.** Clean backups, restores and offboarding per tenant, but many objects to migrate and monitor.
- **Sharded databases.** Groups of tenants per database.

The same guide warns against per-tenant schema customisations and manual schema changes. Automate migrations whichever approach you choose.

sections.heading: Row-level security in a pooled PostgreSQL database
sections.body:
PostgreSQL row-level security lets the database enforce tenant filtering, as a second line of defence behind the application. From the PostgreSQL docs:

- `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` turns it on. If no policy exists, access is **default-deny**: no rows are visible or changeable.
- **Superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` always bypass RLS.**
- **Table owners normally bypass it too**, unless you run `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. If the application connects as the owner, RLS silently does nothing. This is a classic multi-tenant bug.
- Referential-integrity checks (unique, primary key, foreign key) bypass RLS. They can leak whether a value exists.

*Course illustration (not from the PostgreSQL docs):* set the tenant per transaction with `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '...'` and write the policy as `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)`. With `true`, an unset setting returns NULL, so the policy matches no rows instead of raising an error.

Take the tenant ID from the **authenticated identity on the server**. Never take it from a header or body field that the client controls.

sections.heading: Noisy neighbours and fairness
sections.body:
Azure's Noisy Neighbor antipattern describes the problem: one tenant's activity degrades other tenants' performance on shared resources. Its suggested mitigations:

- Monitor usage **per tenant**, not just in total.
- Apply resource governance through the **Throttling** or **Rate Limiting** patterns.
- Scale up or out, and move heavy non-urgent work to off-peak.
- Rebalance heavy tenants across stamps, or restrict resource-intensive operations.

The Amazon Builders' Library article on fairness describes how Amazon does it:

- Enforce **quotas per tenant or per workload**, so a spike from one tenant is rejected for that tenant rather than slowing everyone.
- Return **429** when a tenant exceeds its quota. That is different from the service itself running out of capacity, which is a 503.

**Shuffle sharding** assigns each tenant a random combination of a few workers out of many. A tenant that poisons its workers then shares its whole set with very few other tenants.

keyPoints: Silo = isolation and per-tenant cost; pool = efficiency and shared risk; vertical and horizontal partitioning mix the two.
A shared database makes single-tenant restore and offboarding harder; plan for it up front.
RLS with no policy is default-deny; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass; table owners bypass unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.
Derive the tenant from the authenticated identity on the server, never from client-supplied input.
Per-tenant quotas with 429 contain noisy neighbours; monitor usage per tenant.

gotchas.trap: "We enabled RLS, so tenants are isolated" while the app connects as the table owner.
gotchas.correct: Owners bypass RLS unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Better still, connect as a non-owner role without BYPASSRLS.

gotchas.trap: One global rate limit protecting a shared service.
gotchas.correct: A global limit lets one heavy tenant use up everyone's allowance. Enforce quotas per tenant, and size the global limit to capacity.

gotchas.trap: Putting every tenant in a dedicated stack "for safety" with thousands of small customers.
gotchas.correct: Cost and operations grow with every tenant. Pool the long tail and give dedicated resources only to tenants that need them.

lessons.title: Security by design: least privilege, secrets, encryption and the OWASP Top 10
lessons.summary: The security defaults a system design review expects: least-privilege identities, managed and rotated secrets, encryption in transit and at rest with envelope keys, and the 2025 OWASP Top 10 as a checklist.

sections.heading: Least privilege
sections.body:
AWS Well-Architected (SEC03-BP02) states the principle: identities should be allowed "the smallest set of actions necessary to fulfill a specific task".

In a design this means:

- Each service gets **its own identity**, scoped to specific actions on specific resources.
- Workloads use **temporary credentials** through roles, not long-lived keys.
- Production is separated from development.
- Permission boundaries cap what teams can grant themselves.

Least privilege also limits the **blast radius**. A compromised thumbnail service should not be able to read the billing database.

sections.heading: Secrets management
sections.body:
OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet makes these points:

- **Centralise** secrets in a secrets manager or vault, never in source code, images or plain config files.
- **Control and audit** who can read each secret.
- **Automate rotation** and plan for revocation and expiry.
- Where you can, use **dynamic or short-lived credentials** instead of static ones.

A leaked secret has to be **rotated and revoked**. Deleting the commit that leaked it is not enough, because the old value lives on in clones, forks and logs.

sections.heading: Encryption in transit and at rest
sections.body:
**In transit.** Use TLS on every hop, including traffic between your own services. AWS's Security Pillar treats internal traffic as part of data in transit.

**At rest.** Use **envelope encryption**, as Azure's encryption-at-rest overview describes:

- A **data encryption key (DEK)** encrypts the data.
- A **key encryption key (KEK)**, held in a key vault or HSM with identity-based access and auditing, encrypts the DEK.
- Because only the DEKs are wrapped by the KEK, replacing the KEK means re-wrapping DEKs rather than re-encrypting all the data.

Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks and backups. It does **not** protect against an application that is allowed to decrypt and then leaks the data. Access control still matters.

sections.heading: OWASP Top 10:2025 as a design checklist
sections.body:
The current edition is **OWASP Top 10:2025**:

1. **A01 Broken Access Control**
2. **A02 Security Misconfiguration**
3. **A03 Software Supply Chain Failures** (new)
4. **A04 Cryptographic Failures**
5. **A05 Injection**
6. **A06 Insecure Design**
7. **A07 Authentication Failures**
8. **A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures**
9. **A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures**
10. **A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions** (new)

Use it as a checklist in design reviews:

- **A01**: is every object access authorized, tenant included?
- **A02**: are defaults safe?
- **A03**: are dependencies pinned and verified?
- **A10**: do error paths **fail closed**?

Do not quote the 2021 list as current.

keyPoints: Least privilege: per-service identities, scoped actions and resources, temporary credentials.
Secrets live in a managed store with access control, auditing and automated rotation.
A leaked secret must be rotated or revoked; deleting it from history is not enough.
TLS on every hop, internal traffic included; envelope encryption (DEK wrapped by a KEK in a vault) at rest.
OWASP Top 10:2025: A01 Broken Access Control, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures (new), A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (new).

gotchas.trap: Storing the encryption key in the same database as the data it protects.
gotchas.correct: Keep keys in a key vault or HSM with separate access control, and wrap data keys with a key encryption key.

gotchas.trap: Granting a service broad admin access "to unblock the launch".
gotchas.correct: Grant the specific actions on the specific resources. Broad grants turn a small compromise into a full one.

gotchas.trap: Treating TLS at the load balancer as enough.
gotchas.correct: Data in transit covers traffic between your own components too. Encrypt internal hops as well.

For each OWASP Top 10:2025 category, write one concrete risk in this design and one control. Then list every secret the system holds, where it lives, and how it rotates.

lessons.title: Classic designs: shortener, feed, chat, notifications
lessons.summary: Four interview-classic systems worked from numbers to components: where the reads and writes go, what to precompute, and which failure modes shape each design.

sections.heading: Start every design from numbers
sections.body:
A design review that stays abstract never finds the bottleneck. The SRE Workbook's **non-abstract large system design** (NALSD) approach is to pick a concrete workload, estimate it, and then ask "does this fit on the machines and links I have?" at each step.

For each classic below, write down three numbers before drawing boxes:

1. **Read:write ratio**. It decides what you precompute.
2. **Peak QPS**. Average QPS is `daily requests / 86,400`; then multiply by a peak factor you state as an assumption. For example, 100M/day is about 1,157 req/s on average.
3. **Data size per item × retention**. It decides whether one database node is enough.

Then iterate. Make a design that works, then one that scales, then one that survives failures.

sections.heading: URL shortener
sections.body:
**Shape:** extremely read-heavy. One write creates a code; millions of redirects read it.

- **Key generation.** Use a counter or a pre-allocated ID range encoded in base62, or a random code with a uniqueness check on insert. Hashing the long URL and truncating it invites collisions you still have to handle.
- **Read path.** Look up `code -> url` through a cache in front of the database (cache-aside). The working set is skewed toward popular links, so a small cache absorbs most reads.
- **301 or 302.** RFC 9110 makes a **301** response *heuristically cacheable*: browsers and intermediaries may reuse it without asking you again. That is cheap, but you stop seeing repeat clicks. A **302** is not cacheable by default, so every click reaches you and analytics stay accurate. Pick based on the requirement, and say why.
- **Abuse.** Rate-limit creation and scan targets. A shortener is a phishing tool if you let it be.

sections.heading: News feed: fan-out on write vs read
sections.body:
A feed is a **materialized view**: a precomputed, query-shaped copy of data that lives elsewhere.

| | Fan-out on write (push) | Fan-out on read (pull) |
|---|---|---|
| On post | Insert the post ID into every follower's feed list | Store the post once |
| On read | Read one precomputed list: fast | Merge recent posts from everyone you follow: slow |
| Breaks when | An account has millions of followers (one post = millions of writes) | Users follow many accounts, or reads dominate |

The common answer is a **hybrid**. Push for ordinary accounts, pull for the few very high-follower accounts, and merge the two at read time. Store post IDs in the feed, not post bodies, so edits and deletes do not require rewriting millions of lists. Rebuild a feed from source data when needed: a materialized view is disposable.

sections.heading: Chat and presence
sections.body:
- **Transport.** Clients hold a persistent connection, typically a WebSocket (RFC 6455), to a connection tier. Those servers are stateful, so you need a routing map from `user -> connection server` and a pub/sub hop between servers.
- **Ordering.** Guarantee order **per conversation**, not globally. Assign a per-conversation sequence number at the server that persists the message, and let clients sort and detect gaps.
- **Delivery.** Persist first, then push. If the recipient is offline, the message waits in storage and a notification goes out.
- **Presence** is a **heartbeat** problem. Clients ping every N seconds. A user is "online" while their last heartbeat is younger than a timeout. Keep presence in a fast store with a per-key TTL, not as a row update in your primary database on every ping. Presence is soft state: being a few seconds stale is fine, and losing it on restart is fine.
- **Fan-out of presence** to large groups is expensive. Send it only to contacts who are currently viewing, or batch it.

sections.heading: Notification system
sections.body:
Notifications are **publish-subscribe** plus unreliable third parties.

1. Producers publish an event (`order_shipped`) once. They do not know about channels.
2. A router applies user preferences, quiet hours and rate limits, then enqueues work on **separate queues per channel** (email, SMS, push). An SMS provider outage then backs up only the SMS queue.
3. Channel workers call the provider with retries and backoff.
4. Retries mean duplicates. Give every notification a stable ID and make workers **idempotent consumers**: record what was sent and skip repeats.
5. Keep a delivery log for support ("did the user get it?") and a dead-letter queue for poison messages.

keyPoints: Estimate read:write ratio, peak QPS and data size before choosing components.
A 301 is heuristically cacheable, so it can hide repeat clicks; a 302 keeps every click on your servers.
Feeds are materialized views. Use a hybrid: push for most accounts, pull for very high-follower accounts.
Order chat messages per conversation, not globally; presence is TTL-based soft state driven by heartbeats.
Notifications: publish once, route per channel queue, and make workers idempotent.

gotchas.trap: Fan-out on write for every account, including ones with millions of followers.
gotchas.correct: Pull high-follower accounts at read time and merge, so one post does not trigger millions of writes.

gotchas.trap: Writing every presence heartbeat as an UPDATE to the primary database.
gotchas.correct: Keep presence in a fast key-value store with per-key TTLs; it is soft state.

gotchas.trap: Global ordering for all chat messages.
gotchas.correct: Per-conversation sequence numbers give the ordering users actually see, without a global bottleneck.

lessons.title: Search, autocomplete, uploads and media pipelines
lessons.summary: How to add search without a new cluster on day one, keep autocomplete under a keystroke budget, and move large files and slow processing off the request path.

sections.heading: Search: start in the database you have
sections.body:
PostgreSQL ships **full text search**. `tsvector` documents and `tsquery` queries, with stemming, ranking and a GIN index, cover product search, help-centre search and admin lookups for many applications.

Move to a dedicated search engine when you need things the database does poorly: heavy relevance tuning, faceting over large corpora, many languages, or search load that would hurt OLTP traffic. When you do:

- The **database stays the source of truth**. The index is a derived copy, fed asynchronously (change events or an outbox), so search results are **eventually consistent**.
- Plan for **full reindexing** from source. Mapping changes and bugs will require it.
- Measure **indexing lag** as an SLI.

sections.heading: Autocomplete under a keystroke budget
sections.body:
Autocomplete fires on every keystroke, so its latency budget is far tighter than search's.

- **Client:** debounce input and cancel in-flight requests when the user keeps typing.
- **Server:** serve the **top-k suggestions per prefix from a precomputed structure** (a trie, or a sorted set per prefix), rebuilt offline from query logs. Do not run an open-ended scan per keystroke.
- **Caching:** short prefixes are few and very hot. Cache them at the edge or in memory.
- **Fuzzy matching:** in Postgres, the `pg_trgm` extension provides trigram similarity and index support for `LIKE`/`ILIKE` and similarity search. That is often enough before you need a separate engine.
- Filter suggestions for safety and personalisation **after** retrieval, not by maintaining one index per user.

sections.heading: Uploads: let clients talk to object storage
sections.body:
Do not stream large uploads through your application servers. That ties up threads and bandwidth that should serve API traffic.

The **Valet Key** pattern: the API authenticates the user, then issues a **short-lived, narrowly scoped token** (a pre-signed URL) that allows one operation on one object. The client uploads directly to object storage. Scope the token tightly: a single object key, write-only, a short expiry, and ideally a size and content-type limit.

After upload, object storage emits an event (or the client calls "complete"), and processing begins. Always validate the uploaded content server-side. The client's declared type is untrusted.

sections.heading: Media processing pipelines
sections.body:
Transcoding, thumbnailing and virus scanning are slow, so keep them off the request path.

- **Asynchronous Request-Reply.** Return `202 Accepted` with a status URL. The client polls it, or receives a webhook or push, until the job is done.
- **Claim Check.** Put a *reference* to the object on the queue, not the bytes. Queues have message-size limits, and large payloads make them slow and expensive.
- **Pipes and Filters.** Break processing into independent stages (scan, then transcode, then thumbnail, then publish), each with its own queue and scaling.
- **Competing consumers** on each stage queue, with **idempotent** workers, because at-least-once delivery will redeliver jobs. Write outputs to deterministic keys so a retry overwrites instead of duplicating.

keyPoints: Postgres full text search plus GIN indexes is a credible first search engine.
A dedicated search index is a derived, eventually consistent copy; plan reindexing and monitor lag.
Autocomplete: debounce, precompute top-k per prefix, and cache hot short prefixes.
Valet Key: issue short-lived, narrowly scoped pre-signed URLs so uploads bypass app servers.
Media jobs: 202 plus a status URL, claim check on the queue, pipes-and-filters stages, idempotent workers.

gotchas.trap: Running LIKE '%term%' against the main table on every keystroke.
gotchas.correct: Precompute per-prefix suggestions, or at least use a trigram index, and debounce the client.

gotchas.trap: Putting the uploaded file bytes in the queue message.
gotchas.correct: Store the object, then enqueue a reference to it (Claim Check).

gotchas.trap: A pre-signed URL valid for days with write access to a whole bucket prefix.
gotchas.correct: One object, one operation, short expiry.

lessons.title: Designing AI systems: gateways, RAG and agents
lessons.summary: The architecture of LLM-backed features: when a model gateway earns its place, how RAG splits ingestion from serving, and how to run background agents without runaway cost or latency.

sections.heading: LLM gateway: when and what
sections.body:
A gateway sits between your clients and one or more model deployments. Azure's guidance lists what it is good for:

- **Throttling-aware routing.** Model backends return `429` with `Retry-After`. The gateway should honour it and **break the circuit for that backend**, not keep hitting it, and retry the request against another backend in the pool.
- **Spillover.** Slightly underprovision reserved (provisioned) capacity so it is fully used, and let overflow "burst" to pay-as-you-go capacity.
- **Per-client token quotas** (tokens per minute) and **usage tracking for chargeback or showback**.
- **Session affinity** for stateful conversations, so one conversation stays on one backend.

Hard rule: when load-balancing or failing over, **every backend must serve the same model at the same version**. Never fail over from version X to X+1 or balance between them; client behaviour changes unexpectedly.

And the small-team rule from the same guide: **if updating client configuration is as easy as changing gateway routing, the gateway may not justify itself**. It is another component to secure, run and pay for.

sections.heading: RAG: two subsystems
sections.body:
Google Cloud's RAG reference architectures all split the system in two:

1. **Data ingestion.** Parse documents, chunk them, embed the chunks, and write them to an index. This is a batch or streaming pipeline with its own schedule, retries and backfills.
2. **Serving.** Embed the query, retrieve the top chunks (often with filters such as tenant or permissions), optionally rerank, build the prompt, call the model, and return an answer with citations.

Storage choices include a managed vector search service or **Postgres with embeddings stored next to operational data**, for example with pgvector. For a small team the Postgres option means one database, transactional updates, and access filters as ordinary `WHERE` clauses.

Apply authorisation **at retrieval time**. If the retriever can return chunks the user may not see, the model will happily quote them.

sections.heading: Background agents
sections.body:
Agents call a model in a loop with tools, so a single task can take minutes and many model calls. Design them like any long-running job:

- **Run them off the request path.** Enqueue the task, return a job ID, and stream or poll progress (Asynchronous Request-Reply). Use a queue to level load against model rate limits.
- **Checkpoint** state between steps so a crash resumes instead of restarting and re-spending tokens.
- **Budget every run.** Cap steps, tokens, wall-clock time and spend per task and per tenant, and stop cleanly when a cap is hit.
- **Make tool calls with side effects idempotent**, because steps will be retried.
- **Start simple.** Azure's agent orchestration guidance says to use the **lowest level of complexity that reliably meets your requirements**: a direct model call, then a single agent with tools, and only then multi-agent orchestration, because each level adds coordination overhead, latency and cost.

sections.heading: Cost and latency levers
sections.body:
- **Tokens are the cost unit.** Input and output tokens drive spend. Long retrieved contexts and long agent transcripts cost money on every call.
- **Route by task.** Send simple classification or extraction to a smaller, cheaper model, and save the largest model for the hard cases.
- **Cache.** Exact-match response caching is safe for deterministic, repeated requests. Semantic caching (matching similar prompts) saves more but can return a wrong answer for a subtly different question, so scope it carefully.
- **Stream** responses to improve perceived latency (time to first token). Streaming does not reduce total tokens or cost.
- **Batch** non-interactive work where the provider offers cheaper asynchronous processing. Check current provider terms; specifics change.
- **Measure per feature and per tenant**: tokens, cost, latency percentiles and error/429 rates.

keyPoints: A gateway honours Retry-After, breaks the circuit on 429, enforces per-client token quotas and tracks usage.
Never load-balance or fail over across different model versions.
Skip the gateway if changing client config is as easy as changing gateway routing.
RAG = ingestion (chunk, embed, index) + serving (retrieve, prompt, generate); filter by permissions at retrieval.
Agents: async jobs with checkpoints, hard budgets and idempotent tools; use the lowest complexity that works.

gotchas.trap: Failing over from the primary model deployment to a newer model version when the primary is throttled.
gotchas.correct: Fail over only to backends running the same model and version.

gotchas.trap: Running an agent synchronously inside an HTTP request with no step or token cap.
gotchas.correct: Queue it, checkpoint it, and cap steps, tokens, time and spend.

gotchas.trap: Assuming streaming cuts LLM cost.
gotchas.correct: Streaming improves time to first token; total tokens and cost are unchanged.

lessons.title: Observability: signals, methods and SLO burn-rate alerts
lessons.summary: Metrics, logs and traces and what each is for; the golden signals, RED and USE checklists; OpenTelemetry and sampling; and how multiwindow burn-rate alerts page on what users feel.

sections.heading: Three signals, three jobs
sections.body:
- **Metrics** are cheap numeric time series. Use them for dashboards and alerts. Keep label **cardinality** bounded: a label like `user_id` or a raw URL creates a new series per value and can make the metrics backend slow and expensive.
- **Logs** are discrete events with detail. Use them for "what exactly happened to this request". Make them structured, and include the trace ID.
- **Traces** are trees of **spans** across services, joined by **context propagation** (trace context passed in request headers). Use them for "where did the time go" in a distributed request.

**OpenTelemetry** is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three. Per its spec status page, tracing is stable (API, SDK and protocol), logs are stable, the metrics API and protocol are stable with the SDK listed as mixed, and profiles are still in development.

sections.heading: Golden signals, RED and USE
sections.body:
Three checklists that keep dashboards focused:

| Method | For | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| **Four golden signals** (SRE book) | User-facing services | Latency, traffic, errors, saturation |
| **RED** | Request-driven services | **R**ate, **E**rrors, **D**uration |
| **USE** (Brendan Gregg) | Resources: CPU, disks, pools, queues | **U**tilization, **S**aturation, **E**rrors |

RED is essentially the golden signals minus saturation. Use RED for every service endpoint and USE for every resource behind it. When RED says "slow", USE finds the resource that is saturated.

Measure latency as a **distribution**, not an average. The SRE book's example: at 1,000 req/s with a 100 ms mean, 1% of requests could take 5 s. Use histograms and report percentiles. Count the latency of failed requests separately, because fast errors make averages look good.

sections.heading: Sampling traces
sections.body:
Tracing every request is expensive at scale. OpenTelemetry describes two approaches:

- **Head sampling** decides at the start of a trace, for example keeping 5% of traces. It is simple and efficient, but it cannot guarantee that traces containing errors are kept, because the decision happens before the error.
- **Tail sampling** decides after seeing all or most of a trace's spans. You can keep every error and every slow trace plus a small sample of the rest. The cost is buffering spans, usually in a collector tier.

sections.heading: Alerting on SLO burn rate
sections.body:
Page on **symptoms users feel**, not causes. "Error budget burning fast" is a symptom; "CPU at 90%" is a cause and belongs on a dashboard.

**Burn rate** is how fast you are spending the error budget relative to the SLO period. A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the whole budget over the period.

- Budget consumed = burn rate × window ÷ period.
- Error-rate threshold = burn rate × (1 − SLO).

The SRE Workbook's recommended starting point for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days (720 h):

| Severity | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget consumed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Page | 1 h | 5 min | 14.4 | 2% |
| Page | 6 h | 30 min | 6 | 5% |
| Ticket | 3 d | 6 h | 1 | 10% |

Check: $14.4 \times 1/720 = 0.02$. The 1-hour page fires when the error rate exceeds $14.4 \times 0.001 = 1.44\%$.

**Multiwindow:** alert only when *both* the long and the short window exceed the threshold. The long window gives significance; the short window makes the alert stop soon after the problem is fixed, instead of firing for another hour.

keyPoints: Metrics for alerting, logs for detail, traces for cross-service latency; keep metric cardinality bounded.
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. RED for services, USE for resources.
Use percentiles from histograms, never averages alone.
Head sampling cannot guarantee error traces are kept; tail sampling can.
For 99.9%/30 d: page at burn rate 14.4 over 1 h (2% of budget) with a 5 min short window.

gotchas.trap: Paging on high CPU.
gotchas.correct: Page on SLO burn (symptoms); put CPU on a dashboard for diagnosis.

gotchas.trap: Adding user_id as a metric label to debug one customer.
gotchas.correct: Put user_id in logs and trace attributes; keep metric labels low-cardinality.

gotchas.trap: A single 1-hour window burn alert.
gotchas.correct: Add a short window so the alert resets quickly after recovery.

lessons.title: Cost-aware architecture for small teams
lessons.summary: Why the cheapest architecture is usually a well-run monolith on managed services, how to decide build vs buy, and how to price an extra nine before paying for it.

sections.heading: Cost is a pillar, not an afterthought
sections.body:
AWS Well-Architected has six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, **Cost Optimization** and Sustainability. Cost trades off against every other pillar, so make the trade-off explicit in each design decision.

For a small team, the dominant cost is usually **people's time**, not the cloud bill. Each extra moving part needs on-call knowledge, upgrades, security patching and dashboards.

sections.heading: Avoid premature distribution
sections.body:
The SRE book's *Simplicity* chapter calls for minimal APIs, removing unneeded code and features, and treating complexity as a cost to justify.

Applied to architecture:

- Start with **one deployable service and one relational database**. Use modules inside the codebase for boundaries.
- Split a service out only when you have a concrete reason: a different scaling profile, a different release cadence owned by a different team, or an isolation or compliance need.
- A network hop turns a function call into something that can time out, retry, partially fail and need tracing. Microservices make you pay that cost on every call.
- Scale vertically and add read replicas or caches before sharding.

sections.heading: Managed services and build vs buy
sections.body:
Prefer **managed services** for undifferentiated heavy lifting: databases, queues, object storage, auth, email delivery, observability backends. You pay a premium on the bill to avoid paying in engineering time and on-call load.

Build when the capability **is your product's differentiator**, or when no offering meets a hard requirement (data residency, latency, cost at your real scale). When you buy, check:

- **Exit cost.** Can you export your data in a standard format?
- **Pricing shape.** How does price grow with your growth driver (users, requests, GB, tokens)?
- **Limits.** Quotas and rate limits that will bite at 10x.

Do not add a component that clients could handle themselves. Azure's gateway guide makes exactly this point about LLM gateways.

sections.heading: Price the nines
sections.body:
Availability is not free. AWS notes that higher targets restrict which dependencies you can use and slow down change. Serial hard dependencies multiply: three at 99.99% give about 99.97%.

The SRE book's test: an extra nine is worth funding only if its value exceeds its cost. In its example, moving from 99.9% to 99.99% for a service earning $1M is worth about 0.09% × $1M = **$900**. If the extra nine costs more than that in engineering and infrastructure, do not buy it. Set the SLO from what users need, and spend the remaining error budget on shipping features.

keyPoints: Cost Optimization is one of six Well-Architected pillars; it trades off against the others.
For small teams, engineering and on-call time usually costs more than the cloud bill.
Start with a modular monolith and one relational database; split only for a concrete reason.
Buy undifferentiated capabilities; build only differentiators or hard-requirement gaps; check exit cost.
An extra nine is worth it only if its value beats its cost (the $900 example).

gotchas.trap: Starting a three-person product as eight microservices "so it can scale".
gotchas.correct: Ship a modular monolith on managed services and split when a measured need appears.

gotchas.trap: Self-hosting a database cluster to save on the managed-service premium.
gotchas.correct: Count the on-call, upgrade, backup and failover work; it usually costs more than the premium.

gotchas.trap: Targeting 99.99% because it sounds professional.
gotchas.correct: Derive the SLO from user need and compare the cost of the extra nine with its value.
