flashcards.front: What separates a functional from a non-functional requirement?
flashcards.back: Functional: what the system does (features). Non-functional: how well it does it (latency, availability, durability, RTO/RPO, throughput, cost); these drive most architecture choices.

flashcards.front: Define SLI and SLO.
flashcards.back: SLI: a quantitative measure of service level (e.g. fraction of requests under 300 ms). SLO: a target for that SLI over a window (e.g. 99.9% over 30 days).

flashcards.front: How does an SLA differ from an SLO?
flashcards.back: An SLA is a contract with users that carries consequences (often financial) when missed; an SLO is an internal target for an SLI. The SRE book advises keeping internal SLOs tighter than what is advertised to users, as a safety margin.

flashcards.front: Define RTO and RPO.
flashcards.back: RTO: maximum acceptable time the application is unavailable after an incident. RPO: maximum acceptable duration of data loss.

flashcards.front: Average QPS for 100M requests per day?
flashcards.back: 100,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 1,157 req/s. Size for peak (average × peak factor), not average.

flashcards.front: Formula for storage estimation?
flashcards.back: Items per day × bytes per item × retention days × replication factor.

flashcards.front: 2,000 req/s × 250 KB responses = how many Gbps?
flashcards.back: 500 MB/s × 8 = 4 Gbps.

flashcards.front: Round-trip times from the SRE book?
flashcards.back: About 1 ms within a datacenter, about 45 ms across the US, about 70 ms New York to London.

flashcards.front: Composite availability of a 99.99% service with two independent 99.99% hard dependencies?
flashcards.back: 0.9999^3 ≈ 99.97%. Serial hard dependencies multiply.

flashcards.front: Availability of two independent redundant 99.9% components?
flashcards.back: 1 − 0.001 × 0.001 = 99.9999% ("add the nines"), only if failures are independent.

flashcards.front: Availability from MTBF and MTTR?
flashcards.back: MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). 150 days MTBF and 1 h MTTR ≈ 99.97%.

flashcards.front: Downtime allowed by 99.9% and 99.99% per 30 days?
What is an error budget?
flashcards.back: 1 − SLO. Shared by product and SRE; when it is spent, releases slow or stop per the error budget policy.

flashcards.front: Burn rate and budget consumed?
flashcards.back: Budget consumed = burn rate × window / SLO period. Error-rate threshold = burn rate × (1 − SLO); 14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44%.

flashcards.front: SRE Workbook fast-burn page rule for a 99.9% / 30-day SLO?
flashcards.back: Burn rate 14.4 over a 1 h long window with a 5 min short window (2% of budget).

flashcards.front: Why not average latency?
flashcards.back: Averages hide the tail; at a 100 ms mean, 1% of requests can still take 5 s. Use histograms and percentiles.

flashcards.front: Fan-out of 100 with each backend slow 1% of the time: share of slow requests?
State Little's law.
flashcards.back: L = λW: items in system = arrival rate × time in system. 2,000 req/s × 50 ms = 100 in flight.

flashcards.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
flashcards.back: Else (no partition), choose Latency or Consistency: the cost of strong consistency is paid on every request, not just during partitions.

flashcards.front: Read-your-writes vs linearizability?
flashcards.back: Read-your-writes: a session sees its own writes. Linearizability: every client sees every completed write, in real-time order. RYW is much cheaper.

flashcards.front: What does consistent prefix guarantee?
flashcards.back: Readers may lag, but never observe writes out of order.

flashcards.front: Default starting point for a new product's system of record?
flashcards.back: A relational database (for example PostgreSQL): ACID transactions, joins and constraints. Add other stores only where access patterns or life cycles clearly diverge.

flashcards.front: When does a key-value store fit?
flashcards.back: When every access is by a known key, the value is opaque to the store, and low latency matters most: sessions, caches, counters, feature flags.

flashcards.front: When does a wide-column (column-family) store fit?
flashcards.back: Very high write throughput with queries that always use a row key designed up front, such as IoT telemetry by (device, time bucket). Secondary indexes and ad hoc queries are limited.

flashcards.front: Where should large uploaded files live?
flashcards.back: In object storage. Keep the object key and metadata (owner, size, type, checksum) in the database.

flashcards.front: What is "derived data"?
flashcards.back: A store rebuilt from the system of record, such as a search index or cache. It is eventually consistent with the source and can be dropped and rebuilt.

flashcards.front: What does UUIDv7 contain, and why use it?
flashcards.back: A 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits (RFC 9562). Time ordering improves B-tree insert locality compared with random UUIDv4.

flashcards.front: Is PostgreSQL streaming replication synchronous by default?
flashcards.back: No. It is asynchronous by default, so a failover can lose transactions committed on the primary but not yet shipped.

flashcards.front: Minimum extra commit latency of synchronous replication?
flashcards.back: The round-trip time between primary and standby, per the PostgreSQL docs.

flashcards.front: Which synchronous_commit setting waits until the change is visible to queries on the standby?
flashcards.back: remote_apply. The default synchronous mode waits only for the standby to flush WAL.

flashcards.front: Read-your-writes anomaly and fix?
flashcards.back: A user does not see their own write because the read hit a lagging replica. Fix: read from the leader for a window after a write, or wait for the replica to replay the write LSN.

flashcards.front: Monotonic reads anomaly and fix?
flashcards.back: Successive reads hit replicas with different lag, so data appears and then vanishes. Fix: pin each user's reads to one replica.

flashcards.front: Quorum overlap condition in leaderless replication?
flashcards.back: R + W > N, for example N=3, W=2, R=2. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff weaken the guarantee.

flashcards.front: Why is last-write-wins risky for multi-leader conflicts?
flashcards.back: It silently discards one of two concurrent updates, and it depends on wall clocks that drift.

flashcards.front: What does a version vector do?
flashcards.back: Keeps one counter per node so the system can tell whether two versions are ordered or concurrent (a conflict).

flashcards.front: Properties of a good shard key?
flashcards.back: Immutable, high cardinality, even data and load distribution, and aligned with the dominant query so most requests touch one shard.

flashcards.front: Why is hash(key) mod N painful to resize?
flashcards.back: Changing N reassigns most keys. Consistent hashing or fixed (virtual) partitions move only a small fraction.

flashcards.front: What is write sharding?
flashcards.back: Appending a random or computed suffix to a hot partition key so writes spread across partitions; reads query every suffix and merge.

flashcards.front: What does shuffle sharding achieve?
flashcards.back: Each customer gets a small random combination of workers, so a bad customer rarely shares its whole set with anyone else, shrinking blast radius.

flashcards.front: PostgreSQL default isolation level?
flashcards.back: Read Committed. Read Uncommitted behaves the same, so there are three distinct levels.

flashcards.front: How is PostgreSQL Repeatable Read implemented, and what can it still allow?
flashcards.back: As snapshot isolation. It still allows serialization anomalies such as write skew.

flashcards.front: What does SQLSTATE 40001 mean and how do you handle it?
flashcards.back: Serialization failure. Roll back and retry the whole transaction, ideally with backoff.

flashcards.front: Simplest fix for a lost update on a stock counter?
flashcards.back: A single atomic statement: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND qty >= 1, then check the affected row count.

flashcards.front: Optimistic concurrency over HTTP?
flashcards.back: Send If-Match with the ETag you read; the server answers 412 Precondition Failed if the resource changed (RFC 9110).

flashcards.front: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do?
flashcards.back: Locks the selected rows and skips rows locked by others, letting many workers claim jobs from a queue table without waiting.

flashcards.front: Cache-aside write order?
flashcards.back: Write the database, then invalidate the cache key. Keep a TTL as a backstop.

flashcards.front: What is request coalescing?
flashcards.back: Making sure only one request goes downstream for a given uncached key while other callers wait for its result. It prevents stampedes.

flashcards.front: Soft TTL vs hard TTL?
flashcards.back: Refresh after the soft TTL; if the downstream fails, keep serving the cached value until the hard TTL.

flashcards.front: What is a service "addicted to its cache"?
flashcards.back: One whose backend is sized for the miss rate, so a cold or flushed cache causes an outage. Prefer latency caches over capacity caches.

flashcards.front: Cache-Control: no-cache vs no-store?
flashcards.back: no-cache allows storage but requires revalidation before reuse; no-store forbids storing the response.

flashcards.front: What do private and s-maxage do?
flashcards.back: private: shared caches such as CDNs must not store the response. s-maxage: freshness lifetime for shared caches only, overriding max-age.

flashcards.front: Which RFC defines stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error?
flashcards.back: RFC 5861, not RFC 9111.

flashcards.front: Redis volatile-lru with no keys that have a TTL?
flashcards.back: It behaves like noeviction: writes that need memory return errors. allkeys-lru is the docs' suggested default for caches.

flashcards.front: L4 vs L7 load balancer?
flashcards.back: L4 balances TCP/UDP connections without parsing HTTP. L7 terminates HTTP(S) and can route by path or host, offload TLS, run a WAF and balance per request.

flashcards.front: Why must horizontally scaled instances be stateless?
flashcards.back: So any instance can serve any request. Session state lives in a shared store, so scale-in, crashes and deploys lose nothing.

flashcards.front: Main drawbacks of sticky sessions?
flashcards.back: Sessions are lost when the instance goes away, load skews toward instances holding heavy users, and new instances get little traffic.

flashcards.front: What makes a metric valid for target-tracking autoscaling?
flashcards.back: It measures how busy an instance is and changes proportionally with instance count (CPU, requests per target, or queue backlog per instance; not raw queue depth or latency).

flashcards.front: With several target-tracking policies, when does EC2 Auto Scaling scale out vs in?
flashcards.back: Out if any policy is ready to scale out; in only if all policies are ready to scale in. Availability is prioritized.

flashcards.front: Health-check "fail open"?
flashcards.back: When every target fails its health check, the load balancer keeps routing to all of them instead of none, so a bad dependency check cannot empty the fleet.

flashcards.front: Lame duck state (SRE)?
flashcards.back: A backend still serving but asking clients to send new requests elsewhere. It is used to drain gracefully after SIGTERM.

flashcards.front: How do you pick a timeout from latency data?
flashcards.back: From an acceptable false-timeout rate: tolerating 0.1% spurious timeouts means setting it near the downstream p99.9.

flashcards.front: Worst-case attempts when k layers each make a attempts?
flashcards.back: a^k. For example 4^3 = 64 (SRE) or 3^5 = 243 (Builders' Library).

flashcards.front: Where should retries happen in a deep call stack?
flashcards.back: At a single point, the layer directly above the failing backend. Overloaded servers should return "overloaded; don't retry".

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to backoff?
flashcards.back: Capped backoff alone keeps failed clients synchronized. Jitter randomizes waits so retries spread out instead of arriving as bursts.

flashcards.front: How to jitter scheduled jobs across a fleet?
flashcards.back: Use a consistent per-host offset (the same value every run on a host), not a new random value each time.

flashcards.front: SRE per-client retry budget?
flashcards.back: Retry only while retries are under 10% of requests. Combined with a 3-attempt per-request cap, it limits growth to about 1.1x instead of about 3x.

flashcards.front: Deadline propagation?
flashcards.back: Pass the remaining deadline downstream: a 30 s deadline with 7 s used leaves 23 s (minus a margin). Drop work whose deadline has passed.

flashcards.front: Circuit breaker states?
flashcards.back: Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: fail fast until a timer expires. Half-Open: a limited number of trial calls; successes close it, any failure reopens it.

flashcards.front: Bulkhead pattern?
flashcards.back: Partition resources (for example a connection pool per dependency, or instances per consumer) so one failing dependency or noisy client cannot exhaust shared capacity.

flashcards.front: Goodput vs throughput?
flashcards.back: Throughput is all requests sent. Goodput is requests served without error and fast enough to be useful. Load shedding protects goodput.

flashcards.front: Where and how should load be shed?
flashcards.back: As early and cheaply as possible (at the entry service), by criticality: sheddable traffic first, critical last.

flashcards.front: Fixed window rate limiter weakness?
flashcards.back: Counters reset at boundaries, so a client can send about 2x the limit across a window edge.

flashcards.front: Sliding window log vs sliding window counter?
flashcards.back: Log: exact, stores a timestamp per request (O(n) memory). Counter: weights the previous and current fixed windows, near-exact with two counters.

flashcards.front: Token bucket parameters?
flashcards.back: Refill rate (sustained requests per second) and capacity (maximum burst). API Gateway calls them rate and burst.

flashcards.front: Leaky bucket shaping vs policing?
flashcards.back: Shaping queues requests and forwards them at a fixed drain rate (delays bursts). Policing drops requests that exceed the drain rate.
429 Too Many Requests (RFC 6585): this client exceeded its quota. 503 Service Unavailable: the server is out of capacity. Both can carry Retry-After.

flashcards.front: Which HTTP methods are idempotent per RFC 9110?
flashcards.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE (safe) plus PUT and DELETE. POST and PATCH are not.

flashcards.front: Server response when an idempotency key is reused with a different payload?
flashcards.back: Reject it as a client error (the IETF draft suggests 422). Never process it as the same request.

flashcards.front: Server response when a retry arrives while the original request with that key is still processing?
flashcards.back: A conflict error (the IETF draft suggests 409), not a second execution.

flashcards.front: Idempotent consumer: how to avoid the crash window?
flashcards.back: Commit the dedup marker and the business side effects in the same transaction, and claim the key with an atomic insert-or-fail.

flashcards.front: Is the Idempotency-Key header an RFC?
flashcards.back: No. It is still an IETF Internet-Draft (httpapi WG). Describe it as a draft.

flashcards.front: At-most-once vs at-least-once: what decides which one a consumer gets?
flashcards.back: When it records its position. Saving the offset before processing gives at-most-once (messages can be lost); processing before saving gives at-least-once (messages can be redelivered).

flashcards.front: Where does Kafka guarantee message order?
flashcards.back: Only within a single partition. Records that must stay ordered need the same key, so that they land in the same partition.

flashcards.front: Classic consumer group with 6 partitions and 10 consumers: how many consumers are idle?
flashcards.back: 4. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer per group, so parallelism is capped by the partition count.

flashcards.front: What does Kafka exactly-once cover, and what does it not?
flashcards.back: Read-process-write pipelines within Kafka (idempotent producer plus transactions, with `read_committed` consumers). External destinations need cooperation: an idempotent write, or the offset stored with the output.

flashcards.front: Durable Kafka topic settings for RF=3?
flashcards.back: `acks=all` (the producer default) plus `min.insync.replicas=2` on the topic. The topic default for min ISR is 1.

flashcards.front: Idempotent Consumer pattern
flashcards.back: The consumer records processed message IDs (or uses an idempotent upsert) so that a redelivered message has no additional effect.

flashcards.front: The dual-write problem
flashcards.back: Updating a database and publishing a message as two separate writes. A crash between them leaves the two disagreeing, and reordering the writes only changes which way they disagree.

flashcards.front: Transactional outbox in one sentence
flashcards.back: Write the state change and an event row to an outbox table in one local transaction; a relay publishes the outbox rows to the broker afterwards.

flashcards.front: Why must consumers behind an outbox be idempotent?
flashcards.back: The relay can publish and then crash before marking the row as sent, so the event is published again. Publication is at-least-once.

flashcards.front: What is CDC, and what is the PostgreSQL mechanism for it?
flashcards.back: Change data capture: streaming committed changes from the database log as events. PostgreSQL provides logical decoding of the WAL through replication slots.

flashcards.front: Main weakness of two-phase commit
flashcards.back: Blocking: prepared participants hold locks and cannot decide on their own if the coordinator fails. It also requires every participant to be available.

flashcards.front: Saga
flashcards.back: A sequence of local transactions across services; if a step fails, compensating transactions semantically undo the steps already completed.

flashcards.front: Pivot transaction in a saga
flashcards.back: The point of no return. After it succeeds, the saga must complete, so the remaining steps are retryable and idempotent rather than compensated.

flashcards.front: Choreography vs orchestration
flashcards.back: Choreography: services react to each other's events with no coordinator (simple, but hard to track as it grows). Orchestration: a central coordinator directs the steps (explicit, but an extra component to run reliably).

flashcards.front: Semantic lock (saga countermeasure)
flashcards.back: An application-level flag such as `PENDING` on a record that a saga is changing, so that other operations know it is in flux.

flashcards.front: Event sourcing vs CQRS
flashcards.back: Event sourcing stores the events and derives state by replay. CQRS separates the write model from the read models. They pair well, but either can be used without the other.

flashcards.front: How many failures does a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate? A 4-node one?
flashcards.back: 5 nodes tolerate 2; 4 nodes tolerate only 1 (a majority of 4 is 3). 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures.

flashcards.front: Fencing token
flashcards.back: A monotonically increasing number issued with each lease or lock grant. The protected resource rejects writes that carry a token lower than the highest it has seen.

flashcards.front: Why measure lease and timeout durations with a monotonic clock?
flashcards.back: Wall clocks can jump (NTP steps, leap seconds, VM pauses). A monotonic clock only moves forward, so elapsed time stays correct.

flashcards.front: Lamport clock: what does L(a) < L(b) tell you?
flashcards.back: Only that b did not happen before a. a may have caused b, or they may be concurrent. Version vectors are needed to detect concurrency.

flashcards.front: Version vector
flashcards.back: One counter per node attached to each version. Comparing two vectors shows whether one descends from the other or whether they are concurrent, which is how conflicting writes are detected.

flashcards.front: gRPC vs JSON over HTTP: contract, protocol, payload?
flashcards.back: gRPC requires a .proto contract, runs on HTTP/2 and sends binary Protobuf. JSON HTTP APIs have an optional contract (OpenAPI) and human-readable payloads.

flashcards.front: Can browser JavaScript call a gRPC service directly?
flashcards.back: No. It needs gRPC-Web or a translating proxy.

flashcards.front: Which problem does GraphQL mainly target?
flashcards.back: Over-fetching and under-fetching. The client selects exactly the fields it needs, usually through one endpoint, and so avoids multiple round trips.

flashcards.front: Server-sent events: direction, media type, reconnect?
flashcards.back: One-way, from server to client. The media type is text/event-stream. EventSource reconnects automatically; the server can set the retry delay and event IDs.

flashcards.front: SSE connection limit over HTTP/1.1?
flashcards.back: About 6 open connections per browser per domain, shared across tabs. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams and avoids this.

flashcards.front: Three things a webhook receiver must assume
flashcards.back: Deliveries are at least once (duplicates happen), they can arrive out of order, and the sender retries if you do not acknowledge quickly. So dedupe by event ID and process asynchronously.

flashcards.front: Why is a large OFFSET slow?
flashcards.back: The skipped rows are still computed inside the server and then thrown away (PostgreSQL docs). Cursor/keyset pagination seeks directly to the next key.

flashcards.front: Cursor pagination: what goes in the cursor?
flashcards.back: An opaque encoding of the last row's position in a unique, stable sort order, for example (created_at, id). The next page asks for rows after that key.

flashcards.front: Breaking vs non-breaking API changes
flashcards.back: Non-breaking: adding an optional field, endpoint or parameter. Breaking: removing, renaming or retyping a field, or changing its meaning. Breaking changes need a new major version.

flashcards.front: RFC 9110: safe methods and idempotent methods
flashcards.back: Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. Idempotent: the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE. POST (and PATCH) are not idempotent.

flashcards.front: Which RFC defines Problem Details, and what is its media type?
flashcards.back: RFC 9457 (it obsoletes RFC 7807). The media type is application/problem+json, with members type (default about:blank), title, status, detail and instance.

flashcards.front: How does HTTP prevent lost updates?
flashcards.back: With conditional requests. The client sends If-Match with the ETag it read. If the resource changed in the meantime, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed.

flashcards.front: Which RFC defines 429 Too Many Requests?
flashcards.back: RFC 6585, not RFC 9110.

flashcards.front: RFC 9700: which OAuth grants are out?
flashcards.back: Do not use the implicit grant. The resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used. Use Authorization Code with PKCE (S256).

flashcards.front: RFC 10017: most secure architecture for browser apps?
flashcards.back: Backend for Frontend (BFF). The backend does the OAuth work and keeps the tokens; the browser holds only an HttpOnly session cookie.

flashcards.front: ID token vs access token
flashcards.back: An ID token (OIDC) tells the client who the user is; its aud contains the client_id. An access token (OAuth) is presented to an API and should be audience-restricted to that API.

flashcards.front: Two classic JWT signature attacks (RFC 8725)
flashcards.back: alg: none (signature stripped and accepted) and algorithm confusion (RS256 re-signed as HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret). The fix is an allowlist of algorithms.

flashcards.front: PostgreSQL RLS: who bypasses it?
flashcards.back: Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always do. Table owners do too, unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set. With RLS enabled and no policy, access is default-deny.

flashcards.front: Noisy neighbour: first-line mitigations
flashcards.back: Monitor resource usage per tenant, enforce per-tenant quotas through throttling or rate limiting (return 429), and isolate or move heavy tenants.

flashcards.front: Envelope encryption in one line
flashcards.back: A data key encrypts the data, and a key encryption key held in a vault or HSM encrypts the data key.

flashcards.front: OWASP Top 10:2025: which two categories are new?
flashcards.back: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. A01 is still Broken Access Control.

flashcards.front: Session ID after login?
flashcards.back: Issue a new session ID after login or any privilege change, which prevents session fixation. Set the cookie Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.

flashcards.front: URL shortener: why might you choose 302 over 301?
flashcards.back: RFC 9110 makes 301 heuristically cacheable, so browsers can skip your server on repeat clicks. A 302 is not cacheable by default, so every click reaches you and analytics stay accurate.

flashcards.front: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read for a feed
flashcards.back: Write (push): copy the post ID into every follower's feed at post time, so reads are fast but high-follower posts are expensive. Read (pull): merge at read time, so writes are cheap but reads are slow. The usual answer is a hybrid.

flashcards.front: Which pattern is a precomputed news feed an example of?
flashcards.back: Materialized View: a query-shaped, disposable copy of data that can be rebuilt from the source of truth.

flashcards.front: How should presence ("online now") be stored?
flashcards.back: As soft state driven by heartbeats: a fast key-value store with a per-key TTL. A user is online while their last heartbeat is younger than the timeout.

flashcards.front: Chat ordering: what scope of ordering do you guarantee?
flashcards.back: Per conversation, using a sequence number assigned when the message is persisted. Global ordering is unnecessary and becomes a bottleneck.

flashcards.front: Why use a separate queue per notification channel?
flashcards.back: Isolation. An SMS provider outage backs up only the SMS queue, while email and push keep flowing.

flashcards.front: How do notification workers avoid double-sends on retry?
flashcards.back: Give each notification a stable ID and make workers idempotent consumers that record what was sent and skip repeats.

flashcards.front: What is the Valet Key pattern?
flashcards.back: The API issues a short-lived, narrowly scoped token (such as a pre-signed URL) so the client reads or writes one object directly in storage, bypassing the app servers.

flashcards.front: What is the Claim Check pattern?
flashcards.back: Store a large payload in object storage and send only a reference to it through the queue.

flashcards.front: Asynchronous Request-Reply in one line
flashcards.back: Return 202 Accepted with a status URL. The client polls it, or gets a callback, until the long-running job completes.

flashcards.front: Autocomplete: three techniques to meet the per-keystroke latency budget
flashcards.back: Debounce or cancel on the client; serve precomputed top-k suggestions per prefix; cache the hot short prefixes.

flashcards.front: When a dedicated search engine is added, what is the consistency model of search results?
flashcards.back: Eventually consistent. The index is a derived copy fed asynchronously from the source-of-truth database, so monitor indexing lag and plan full reindexes.

flashcards.front: LLM gateway: correct response to a backend returning 429 with Retry-After
flashcards.back: Honour Retry-After, break the circuit for that backend, and retry on another backend in the pool that serves the same model and version.

flashcards.front: When does an LLM gateway NOT justify itself?
flashcards.back: When updating client configuration is as easy as changing gateway routing. The gateway then adds reliability, security, cost and maintenance burden for little gain.

flashcards.front: The two subsystems of every RAG reference architecture
flashcards.back: Data ingestion (parse, chunk, embed, index) and serving (retrieve, build prompt, generate).

flashcards.front: RED vs USE
flashcards.back: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is for request-driven services. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) is for resources such as CPU, disks, pools and queues.

flashcards.front: The four golden signals
flashcards.back: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation (SRE book, Monitoring Distributed Systems).

flashcards.front: Burn-rate formulas
flashcards.back: Budget consumed = burn rate × window ÷ period. Error-rate threshold = burn rate × (1 − SLO). For a 99.9% SLO, burn 14.4 over 1 h of 720 h = 2% of budget, at a 1.44% error rate.

flashcards.front: Why does a multiwindow burn-rate alert need a short window?
flashcards.back: The short window (for example 5 min for a 1 h alert) makes the alert stop firing soon after the problem is fixed. The long window provides significance.

flashcards.front: Head vs tail trace sampling
flashcards.back: Head sampling decides at trace start: cheap, but it can drop error traces. Tail sampling decides after seeing the spans: it can keep all errors and slow traces, at the cost of buffering.

flashcards.front: The six AWS Well-Architected pillars
flashcards.back: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability.

flashcards.front: SRE rule for whether an extra nine is worth it
flashcards.back: Only if its value exceeds its cost. Example: 99.9% to 99.99% on $1M revenue is worth about $900 (0.09% × $1M).

questions.scenario: A product manager says the new checkout "must be fast and basically never go down". The team is about to pick a database.
questions.stem: What should the engineer do first?
options: Turn each adjective into an SLO for the checkout journey: a percentile latency target, a success-rate target, a measurement point and a window
Choose the most scalable database available, since requirements can be refined after launch
Target 99.999% availability and 50 ms average latency so the system is safe for any future requirement
Ask the team to measure mean response time in staging and use that as the requirement
questions.explanation: Vague asks must become measurable targets before technology choices, because non-functional requirements drive the architecture. The SRE book defines an SLO as a target for a carefully defined SLI, and a target needs a measurement point and window to be checkable.
rationales: Correct: percentile latency and success-rate SLOs per journey make the requirement testable and drive design.
Picking technology before knowing the targets is backwards; the targets decide what fits.
Over-specifying nines is costly and restricts dependencies; mean latency also hides the tail.
Staging means describe the current build, not what users need, and averages hide tail latency.

questions.stem: Which of the following are non-functional requirements? (Select two.)
options: p99 latency of the search API stays under 300 ms over 28 days
A buyer can export their order history as CSV
No more than 5 minutes of committed data may be lost in a regional outage
An admin can deactivate a user account
questions.explanation: Latency targets and recovery point objectives describe how well the system behaves, so they are non-functional. Export and deactivation are features. Azure Well-Architected defines RPO as the maximum acceptable duration of data loss.
rationales: Correct: a latency SLO is a non-functional requirement.
This is a feature the system provides, so it is functional.
Correct: this is an RPO, a non-functional recovery target.
This is a feature, so it is functional.

questions.scenario: A team writes "the service must be 99.95% available" in a design doc. During review someone notes there is no SLI definition.

At least 99.95% of synthetic health-check pings succeed per day, regardless of user traffic
Average CPU utilisation below 70% so the service always has headroom to stay available
Server uptime as reported by the host monitoring agent, at least 99.95% per year, excluding planned maintenance

Health checks can pass while real requests fail; they are a weak proxy for user experience.
CPU is a saturation signal, not a measure of user-visible availability.
Host uptime can be 100% while users get errors, and excluding planned maintenance hides real unavailability.

About 100,000 req/s
About 35,000 req/s
About 3,500 req/s

This treats the daily total as if it arrived in about 1,000 seconds.
This is off by 10×, a common slip when rounding 86,400 to 10^4 instead of 10^5.

About 365 TB
About 1.1 PB
About 3.3 PB

This forgets the three replicas.

Peak egress is about 40 Gbps, so at least four servers are needed for bandwidth alone

Peak egress is about 500 Mbps, so one server has plenty of network headroom

questions.scenario: In a design review, the question is whether one PostgreSQL primary can absorb writes for a new feature. The author shows that average daily writes are 300 per second and the vendor advertises a much higher maximum.
questions.stem: What is the strongest way to answer the question?
options: Accept the design: average load is far below the advertised maximum
Defer the question and add autoscaling to the database tier later
Estimate peak write QPS from stated assumptions (users, actions per user, peak factor), compare it with a benchmark of this schema and workload on the target instance, and keep headroom
Shard the database from day one so capacity is never a question

A single primary does not autoscale writes; deferring hides the risk.
Correct: peak estimate versus measured capacity with headroom is the defensible check.

About 99.9%

This applies the redundancy formula, which is for parallel components.

questions.stem: What is the best assessment of the claim?

Correct: two 99.9% replicas always give six nines
Correct, as long as the load balancer itself is 99.9999% available
Wrong: redundancy lowers availability because there are more parts to fail

Only true for independent failures.
The load balancer matters, but it does not fix correlated replica failures.
Parallel redundancy raises availability when failures are independent; it is serial dependencies that multiply losses.

About 43 minutes
About 8.8 hours
About 7.2 hours

Lower the SLO for the rest of the month so the budget is no longer exceeded
Page the on-call engineer every hour until the month ends
Ship the features as planned, since the budget resets next month anyway

Moving the target to fit the outcome defeats the purpose of the SLO.

Ignoring an exhausted budget removes the incentive the budget creates.

questions.stem: Which alerting change follows the SRE Workbook's recommendation?

Raise the threshold to 5% errors for one minute
Replace error alerts with an average-latency alert
Page only once the entire monthly error budget has been consumed

A fixed high threshold misses slower burns that still exhaust the budget.
Averages hide the tail, and dropping error alerts loses the availability SLI.
By then the SLO is already missed; alerts must fire while there is still budget to protect.

An SLO is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI
An SLO is a contract with customers that pays service credits whenever it is missed
An SLI is the business penalty paid when the service misses its target

Service credits and penalties belong to the SLA, not the SLO or SLI.
rationales: Correct: consequences are what distinguish an SLA.
Correct: this is the SRE book's definition of an SLO.
That describes an SLA; an SLO is an internal target value or range for an SLI.
An SLI is a measurement, not a penalty.

questions.scenario: A component fails on average every 150 days and takes 1 hour to restore, giving about 99.97% availability. Making it fail less often would need a major redesign, but automated rollback could cut restore time to 30 minutes.
questions.stem: What availability does automated rollback give, and what does it show?
options: About 99.999%; halving MTTR adds a full nine
About 99.94%; faster rollback adds risk that lowers availability
About 99.97%; MTTR does not affect availability
About 99.986%; halving MTTR roughly halves unavailability, often more cheaply than raising MTBF

rationales: Halving MTTR halves unavailability; it does not divide it by 10.
This has the effect backwards.
MTTR is half of the availability formula.

questions.scenario: A dashboard shows mean API latency steady at 100 ms, yet support tickets about multi-second page loads keep rising.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation and fix?
options: Use the median instead of the mean, since it is more robust
The tickets are user-side network issues; the mean proves the service is fine
Increase the sampling interval so short spikes are smoothed out
The mean hides a slow tail; record latency histograms and alert on p99 or on the fraction of requests over a threshold
questions.explanation: The SRE book notes that at 1,000 rps with a 100 ms mean, 1% of requests could take 5 seconds. Distributions, not averages, reveal the tail that users feel.

A healthy mean does not rule out a slow tail.
Smoothing hides the problem further.
Correct: histograms and tail percentiles expose what the mean hides.

questions.stem: About what share of user queries will take over 1 s?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 63%
About 100%
questions.explanation: A query is slow if any of its 100 shards is slow: 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 0.63. This is the fan-out effect described in "The Tail at Scale", where a rare per-server delay becomes common at the request level.
rationales: This ignores fan-out; it is the per-shard rate.
This is roughly the figure for a fan-out of 10, not 100.
It approaches 100% only at much larger fan-out.

questions.scenario: A service receives 2,000 req/s. A downstream call normally takes 50 ms. The caller uses a pool of 300 worker threads and a 2 s timeout on the call. During an incident the downstream slows to 1 s per call.
questions.stem: What happens, and what is the best mitigation?
options: In-flight requests rise to about 300, which the pool exactly absorbs, so no action is needed
In-flight requests stay at about 100 because the arrival rate has not changed
Raise the timeout to 10 s so fewer calls fail
In-flight requests rise from about 100 to about 2,000, exhausting the 300-thread pool; bound concurrency to the dependency and set the timeout from its normal latency distribution
questions.explanation: By Little's law, in-flight = arrival rate × latency: 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 normally and 2,000 × 1 = 2,000 during the slowdown, far beyond 300 threads. The Builders' Library states this relation and recommends a separate concurrency bulkhead per dependency. Timeouts chosen from the downstream latency distribution and concurrency limits keep a slow dependency from consuming the caller.
rationales: Demand would be about 2,000, not 300; the pool saturates and requests queue or fail.
Concurrency depends on latency as well as arrival rate.
A longer timeout raises concurrency even further.
Correct: Little's law shows the 20× concurrency jump that exhausts the pool.

questions.scenario: To survive bursts, an engineer configures a request queue 10 times the size of the server's thread pool. Each request takes about 100 ms to handle. Clients time out after 500 ms.
questions.stem: Why is this a poor choice under sustained overload, and what is better?
options: The queue should be unbounded so no request is ever rejected
Replace the queue with more retries from clients
A full queue adds about 1 s of wait, so the server spends capacity on requests whose clients already timed out; keep the queue small (about half the thread pool or less) and reject early
It is fine: a larger queue always increases throughput
questions.explanation: The SRE book gives this example: a queue of 10× the thread count at 100 ms per request adds about 1 s of queueing when full, and it recommends small queues for steady traffic. Queues turn overload into latency; they do not add capacity.
rationales: An unbounded queue can grow until memory is exhausted, and every request in it is late.
Retries add load to an already overloaded server.
Correct: this matches the SRE book's queue sizing guidance.
Queues do not add capacity; they only add waiting time.

questions.scenario: An architect argues that because network partitions between their two regions happen only a few minutes per year, CAP is irrelevant and they should make every write synchronously replicated to both regions.
questions.stem: Which point best captures what this argument misses?
options: CAP says the system will lose data during partitions no matter what is chosen
Nothing; with rare partitions, synchronous cross-region replication is free
Partitions cannot happen between cloud regions
PACELC: even without a partition, strong consistency across regions costs latency on every write, roughly a cross-region round trip
questions.explanation: PACELC adds the normal-case trade-off: else, latency or consistency. The Azure Cosmos DB consistency documentation frames its levels with PACELC and notes that strong consistency raises write latency because data must replicate and commit across large distances.
rationales: CAP is about refusing requests versus serving possibly stale data, not guaranteed data loss.
Synchronous cross-region commits add tens of milliseconds per write.
Inter-region links can and do partition.
Correct: the latency cost is paid on every request, not only during partitions.

questions.scenario: Users edit their profile on a site backed by a leader database with asynchronous read replicas. After saving, the page reloads from a replica and sometimes shows the old bio, which generates support tickets. Other users seeing the old bio for a few seconds is acceptable.
questions.stem: What is the weakest consistency guarantee that fixes the complaint?
options: Eventual consistency
Consistent prefix across all replicas
Linearizability for all reads from all clients
Read-your-writes within the user's session
questions.explanation: The requirement is only that a user sees their own write, which is the read-your-writes session guarantee. Cosmos DB's session level provides exactly this within a session, and it can be implemented by reading from the leader or waiting for a follower to catch up to the session's last written version.
rationales: This is what produces the bug.
Consistent prefix stops out-of-order reads but still allows stale reads after the user's own write.
This works but is stronger and costlier than needed, since other users may lag.
Correct: the user must see their own write; others may see stale data briefly.

questions.scenario: In a discussion thread, readers in another region occasionally see a reply before the post it answers, because the two writes replicated in a different order.
questions.stem: Which guarantee most directly prevents this, without requiring every read to be strongly consistent?
options: Read-your-writes
Linearizability for the reply write only
Consistent prefix (or causal) consistency, so readers never see later writes without the earlier ones
Eventual consistency with a shorter replication delay
questions.explanation: Consistent prefix means readers may lag but never observe writes out of order; causal consistency means causally related operations (a reply after the post it answers) appear in the same order to all processes. Either fixes the anomaly without making every read strongly consistent. The Cosmos DB documentation reserves eventual consistency for data that needs no ordering guarantees, such as likes or nonthreaded comments.
rationales: Read-your-writes protects the writer's own view, not other readers in another region.
Making one write linearizable does not order it against the post for remote readers.
Correct: ordering guarantees fix out-of-order visibility.
Faster replication makes the anomaly rarer but does not remove it.

questions.stem: Which statements about consistency models are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Under linearizability, once a write completes, any later read from any client returns that value or a newer one
Under plain eventual consistency, a client can read a value older than one it read earlier
Causal consistency is stronger than linearizability because it tracks dependencies
Session consistency guarantees that all clients see each other's writes immediately
questions.explanation: Linearizability respects real-time order across all clients. The Cosmos DB documentation notes that with eventual consistency a client might read values older than those it read in the past. Causal is weaker than linearizable, and session guarantees apply within one session.
rationales: Correct: this is the real-time ordering property of linearizability.
Correct: eventual consistency gives no monotonic-read guarantee.
Linearizability implies causal ordering; causal is the weaker model.
Session guarantees cover a single session (or shared session token), not all clients.

questions.scenario: A four-person startup is building B2B invoicing: customers, invoices, line items, payments and monthly reports. One engineer proposes MongoDB for invoices, Cassandra for payments and Elasticsearch for reports "so each part can scale independently". Expected load in year one is a few hundred requests per second.

options: Use the three proposed stores, each owned by the service that writes to it.
Use one PostgreSQL database as the system of record, with jsonb for variable invoice fields, and add stores later for a measured need.
Use a key-value store for everything, keyed by invoice ID, and compute reports in application code.
Use Elasticsearch as the single store, because it can index every field for reporting.
questions.explanation: Invoices, payments and reports need multi-row transactions, joins and constraints, which are relational strengths. The Azure data store guide advises combining models only where access patterns or life cycles clearly diverge, and at a few hundred requests per second nothing here diverges. jsonb absorbs the flexible fields without a second system.
rationales: Three stores add three operational surfaces and cross-store consistency problems, such as a payment recorded without its invoice, with no load that needs them.
Correct. Relational fits the transactional core, and specialised stores can be added when a real access pattern requires them.
Key-value access by ID cannot do joins or multi-row transactions, so reporting and payment integrity move into fragile application code.
A search index is derived data, not a transactional system of record; it lacks multi-row ACID transactions for payments.

questions.scenario: A course platform lets instructors upload lecture videos from 50 MB to 4 GB. Today the API server receives the upload and inserts the bytes into a bytea column. Database backups have grown to hours and API memory spikes during uploads.
questions.stem: What is the best change?

Keep the bytes in PostgreSQL but move the videos table to its own tablespace on faster disks.
Store each video in a document database as a base64-encoded field next to its metadata.
Compress the videos with gzip before inserting them so the bytea column stays small.

Object stores such as S3 document strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE, so a metadata row can safely point at an object. Direct uploads with pre-signed URLs also take the bytes off the API servers.

A tablespace changes where the bytes sit, not that multi-gigabyte blobs still inflate backups and flow through the API.
Base64 increases size by about a third, and document stores are not built for multi-gigabyte values.
Video is already compressed, so gzip gains almost nothing, and the bytes still flow through the database and API.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce site has 40 million products in PostgreSQL. Product managers want typo-tolerant search, relevance tuning per category and facet counts (brand, price band) on every query. The team measured PostgreSQL full text search and found it does not meet the facet and typo-tolerance requirements at their latency target.

Write each product update to PostgreSQL and to the search engine from the API handler, in that order.
Keep PostgreSQL as the system of record and feed a dedicated search index from it through an outbox or change data capture, accepting short index lag.
Add a LIKE '%term%' query with a B-tree index on product name to handle typos.

questions.scenario: A fleet of 2 million sensors sends a reading every 10 seconds (about 200,000 writes per second). Every query is "readings for device X between time A and time B". There are no joins and no multi-row transactions.
questions.stem: Which storage model and key design fit best?
options: A relational table with an auto-increment primary key and a secondary index on device_id.
A document store with one document per device that appends each reading to an array.
A key-value store keyed by reading ID, scanning all keys to answer time-range queries.
A wide-column store with a row key of (device_id, time bucket) and readings sorted by timestamp within the row.

A (device, time bucket) key matches the only query and spreads writes across devices. Bucketing by time keeps any single row from growing without bound.

One ever-growing document per device hits document size limits and rewrites a large document on every reading.
Key-value access is by exact key; answering a time range by scanning keys is a full scan.
Correct. The row key matches the access pattern and the model is built for high write throughput.

questions.stem: Which two characteristics of a workload indicate that a key-value store is a good fit? (Select two.)
options: Every read and write addresses a single item by a known key.
Reports join several entities and filter on many different columns.
Values are treated as opaque blobs and the main requirement is very low latency, as with sessions or caches.
Business rules require updating several related records atomically.

Joins, multi-column filters and multi-record atomic updates are relational strengths. Choosing a key-value store for those pushes the logic into the application.

Multi-entity joins and flexible filters point to a relational or analytical store.
Correct. Opaque values with tight latency targets are a classic key-value workload.
Multi-record atomicity points to a relational database with ACID transactions.

questions.scenario: To offload a busy primary, an app sends all SELECTs to two asynchronous PostgreSQL streaming replicas. Users now report that after saving their profile, the page that loads next sometimes shows the old values. Refreshing a few seconds later shows the new values.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Switch the replicas to synchronous replication with the default synchronous_commit setting.
Add a third replica so each replica receives less read traffic and lags less.
For a short window after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary, or wait until the replica has replayed the write's LSN.
Cache the profile page in a CDN for five minutes so the old values stop flickering.
questions.explanation: This is a read-your-writes violation caused by asynchronous replication lag, which the PostgreSQL docs describe as a small delay between commit on the primary and visibility on the standby. Routing a user's post-write reads to the primary, or waiting for the replica to replay past the write's LSN, fixes it without moving all reads back. The default synchronous mode waits for WAL flush, not for apply.
rationales: Default synchronous commit waits for the standby to flush WAL, not to apply it, so the stale read can still happen while every commit gets slower.
More replicas may reduce load, but asynchronous lag never reaches zero, so the anomaly remains.
Correct. It targets exactly the reads that need freshness and keeps the rest on replicas.
A CDN cache would show stale profile data for longer and could serve one user's page to another.

questions.scenario: A payments ledger runs PostgreSQL with one asynchronous streaming standby in another availability zone. The primary's disk fails and the team promotes the standby. Reconciliation finds 14 payments confirmed to customers that are missing from the new primary. The business requires that a confirmed payment is never lost on a single-server failure.
questions.stem: Which change meets the requirement?
options: Take WAL archive backups every 5 minutes instead of every hour.
Promote the standby faster with automated failover so fewer transactions are in flight.
Configure synchronous replication to at least one standby, accepting at least one primary-standby round trip on each commit.
Add two more asynchronous standbys so at least one is likely to have the latest data.
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs state that with asynchronous replication, committed transactions not yet replicated are lost if the primary crashes, in proportion to the replication delay. Synchronous replication makes each commit wait until the standby confirms the WAL is on its disk, so data is lost only if both fail together. The cost is commit latency of at least the round-trip time.
rationales: More frequent archiving shrinks the loss window but does not eliminate it.
Failover speed does not change which transactions reached the standby before the crash.
Correct. A commit is confirmed only once a standby has durably received it.
Asynchronous standbys can all lag behind the primary; "likely" does not meet a never-lose requirement.

questions.scenario: A leaderless key-value store runs with N=3 replicas per key. To minimise latency the team configured W=1 and R=1. Users occasionally read a value older than one they just wrote, even when no node has failed.
questions.stem: Which configuration change makes every read overlap the latest acknowledged write in normal operation?
questions.explanation: Quorum reads overlap quorum writes when R + W > N. With N=3, W=2 and R=2 gives 4 > 3, so at least one replica in every read set holds the latest acknowledged write. W=1 with R=2 and W=2 with R=1 both sum to 3, which does not exceed N.
rationales: Correct. 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so read and write quorums always intersect.
1 + 2 = 3, not greater than N, so a read can miss the single replica that took the write.
R=0 is not a read; writing to all three also fails whenever any replica is down.
2 + 1 = 3, not greater than N, so the single replica read may be the one that missed the write.

sources.title: Patterns of Distributed Systems — martinfowler.com

questions.scenario: A note-taking app runs a leader in Europe and one in the US, each accepting writes and replicating to the other. A user edits the same note on a laptop in Paris and a phone in New York while offline-tolerant sync is in progress. Currently the system keeps the version with the later server timestamp.
questions.stem: What is the main problem with this approach, and the better alternative?
options: Timestamps are too coarse; switching to nanosecond timestamps would make the winner correct.
Replication is too slow; synchronous replication between the regions would remove all conflicts without other cost.
Multi-leader replication cannot work for notes; the app must move to leaderless quorums with R + W > N.
Last-write-wins silently discards one concurrent edit; detect concurrency with version vectors and merge or surface both versions.
questions.explanation: Two leaders can accept concurrent writes to the same record, and last-write-wins resolves that by throwing one away, using wall clocks that may drift. Version vectors keep one counter per node and show whether two versions are ordered or concurrent, so concurrent edits can be merged or shown to the user. Routing each note to one home leader is another valid design.
rationales: Finer timestamps still pick one edit and drop the other, and clock skew can exceed the resolution anyway.
Cross-region synchronous replication adds large latency to every write and breaks the offline-tolerant use case.
Leaderless replication also faces concurrent writes and still needs version tracking; quorums do not merge edits.
Correct. It identifies the data loss and names the standard detection mechanism.

sources.title: Patterns of Distributed Systems — martinfowler.com

questions.scenario: A feed service reads comments from a pool of five asynchronous replicas behind a round-robin load balancer, because the primary cannot absorb the read load on its own. A user refreshes a thread three times: the newest comment appears, disappears, then appears again.
questions.stem: Which change most directly fixes this experience?
options: Increase the load balancer's health-check frequency for the replicas.
Lower the replicas' max_standby_streaming_delay so they cancel long queries.
Send all comment reads to the primary.
Pin each user's reads to one replica, for example by hashing the user ID to a replica.
questions.explanation: The user is seeing non-monotonic reads: consecutive requests land on replicas with different lag. Pinning a user to one replica means their view only moves forward. Sending every read to the primary would also remove the anomaly, but the scenario says the primary cannot absorb that load.
rationales: The replicas are healthy; health checks do not change how far each one lags.
That setting affects how standby queries conflict with WAL replay, not which replica a user reads from.
The primary was offloaded because it cannot carry the read load, so moving every read back to it trades the anomaly for an overload; pinning fixes the anomaly while keeping the replicas' capacity.
Correct. A single replica's state only moves forward, so reads become monotonic for that user.

sources.title: Hot standby — PostgreSQL docs
Patterns of Distributed Systems — martinfowler.com

questions.stem: A team is enabling PostgreSQL synchronous replication. Which two statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Each commit waits at least the round-trip time between the primary and the synchronous standby.
With the default synchronous_commit setting, queries on the synchronous standby always see a commit as soon as the client receives success.
With synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)', commits wait for confirmation from any two of the three listed standbys.
Once synchronous replication is enabled, cascading standbys downstream also become synchronous.
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs give the minimum extra wait as the primary-standby round trip, and describe ANY n quorum syntax for waiting on any n of the listed standbys. The default synchronous mode waits for WAL flush, not replay, so standby queries can still briefly lag; remote_apply waits for visibility. The docs also state cascading replication is currently asynchronous.
rationales: Correct. The docs state the minimum wait is the round-trip time.
Default synchronous commit confirms durability on the standby, not that it has applied the change; that needs remote_apply.
Correct. This is the quorum-based form of synchronous_standby_names.
The docs say synchronous replication settings have no effect on cascading replication, which is asynchronous.

questions.scenario: A multi-tenant project-management SaaS is outgrowing one database. Almost every query is scoped to one tenant ("tasks in tenant T where ..."). There are 30,000 tenants of varied size. The team is choosing a shard key.
questions.stem: Which shard key is the best starting choice?
options: An auto-increment task ID with range-based sharding.
task.created_at, so recent tasks are on the same shard.
task.status (open, in progress, done), so status filters hit one shard.
tenant_id, hashed or mapped through a lookup table, with very large tenants moved to dedicated shards.
questions.explanation: The Azure Sharding pattern asks for an immutable, high-cardinality key that spreads load evenly and matches the dominant query so most requests hit one shard. tenant_id meets all four here. The same pattern suggests giving volatile or high-value tenants their own shards to handle skew.
rationales: Monotonic IDs under range sharding concentrate inserts on the last shard, and tenant queries span all shards.
A timestamp is monotonic, so all new writes hit the newest shard, and tenant queries fan out.
Three values is very low cardinality and status changes often, so rows would move between shards.
Correct. Tenant-scoped queries stay on one shard, and a lookup map lets you move large tenants.

sources.title: Sharding pattern — Azure Architecture Center

questions.scenario: A cache cluster assigns keys with node = hash(key) % 8. Traffic doubled, so the team adds a ninth node. Immediately the database behind the cache is overwhelmed as the hit rate collapses.
questions.stem: What design would have avoided this?
options: Using a stronger hash function, such as SHA-256 instead of a 32-bit hash.
Adding the new node during off-peak hours so the miss rate matters less.
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, or many fixed partitions mapped to nodes, so a resize moves only a small fraction of keys.
Doubling to 16 nodes instead of adding one, so the modulus stays a power of two.
questions.explanation: With hash mod N, changing N reassigns most keys, which here is a near-total cache flush. The Azure Sharding pattern notes that consistent hashing arranges the hash space so only a small fraction of keys move when the shard count changes. The Builders' Library caching article likewise says to make sure a cache fleet can be scaled up without downtime or mass cache invalidation.
rationales: Hash quality affects evenness, not how many keys move when N changes.
Timing reduces the impact but still remaps most keys and still overloads the database once traffic returns.
Correct. Only keys in the affected part of the ring, or partitions moved to the new node, change location.
Going from 8 to 16 with modulo still remaps about half of all keys.

sources.title: Sharding pattern — Azure Architecture Center
Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library

questions.scenario: A social app stores a like counter per post in a partitioned key-value store keyed by post_id. A celebrity post receives about 40,000 likes per second and requests for it are throttled, while overall table capacity is only 20% used.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix for the write throttling?
options: Raise the table's total provisioned throughput fivefold.
Move the counter to a secondary index on post_id.
Switch the counter to a strongly consistent read mode.
Split the counter into many sub-keys (post_id#0 to post_id#N-1), increment a random one, and sum them on read or in a periodic roll-up.
questions.explanation: A single key lives on one partition, and partitioned stores such as DynamoDB document a per-partition throughput ceiling, so total capacity is not the bottleneck. Write sharding with suffixes spreads one logical key across many partitions. The cost is that reads must gather and merge the shards.
rationales: Table-wide capacity does not lift the per-partition ceiling that one hot key is hitting.
An index on the same hot key inherits the same hot partition, and indexes add write work.
Read consistency mode does not affect write throughput, and strongly consistent reads cost more.
Correct. This is the documented write-sharding technique for hot partition keys.

questions.scenario: An audit-event store is range-sharded by event timestamp: each shard holds one week. Dashboards query the last 24 hours. Every week one shard runs at 100% CPU while the others sit idle.
questions.stem: Which key design best balances writes while still supporting time-range queries?
options: Shrink the range to one day per shard so each hot period is shorter.
Shard by event_id from an auto-increment sequence instead of by timestamp.
Move to geographic sharding by the region where each event occurred.
Use a composite key: a hash bucket (for example source_id modulo 32) as the shard key, with timestamp as the sort key inside each shard.
questions.explanation: Range sharding on a monotonically increasing value sends every new write to the newest shard, which the Azure Sharding pattern calls out. A hashed bucket spreads writes across shards while time ordering within each bucket keeps range scans efficient. A 24-hour query then fans out to 32 buckets, which is a bounded cost.
rationales: Smaller ranges still put all current writes on one shard; they just rotate faster.
A sequence is also monotonic, so it has the same newest-shard hotspot.
Geographic sharding is for residency and latency and is often uneven; it does not address the time hotspot.
Correct. Writes spread across buckets and each bucket stays ordered by time.

sources.title: Sharding pattern — Azure Architecture Center

questions.scenario: A shared rendering service runs 8 workers. Occasionally one customer sends a malformed request that crashes any worker that handles it, and retries spread the crash across all 8 workers, taking every customer down.
questions.stem: Which approach most reduces the number of other customers affected by one bad customer?
options: Shuffle sharding: give each customer a random combination of 2 of the 8 workers, so few customers share both of the bad customer's workers.
Round-robin all requests across all 8 workers so the load from any one customer is spread thin.
Split the 8 workers into 4 fixed shards of 2 and assign customers to shards by hash.
Add 8 more workers so the crashes take longer to reach every worker.
questions.explanation: With 8 workers there are 28 distinct pairs, so a bad customer's pair overlaps completely with only a small share of customers, and most others still have a healthy worker. Plain sharding with 4 shards would take out a quarter of customers. Spreading every request across every worker is what let one customer reach the whole fleet.
rationales: Correct. Shuffle sharding limits the blast radius to customers who share the exact combination.
Round-robin is the current failure mode: every worker sees the poison request.
Fixed shards help, but every customer on the same shard is fully affected, about 25% here versus far fewer with shuffle sharding.
More workers only delays the spread; retries still reach all of them.

sources.title: Shuffle sharding — Amazon Builders' Library

questions.stem: A team is choosing a shard key for a large orders table. Which two properties should the key have? (Select two.)
options: It increases monotonically, so new rows are easy to locate.
It has high cardinality and spreads both data and request load evenly.
It matches the dominant query so most requests can be served by a single shard.
It reflects order status, so active orders sit together on fast hardware.
questions.explanation: The Azure Sharding pattern lists immutable, high-cardinality, evenly distributed and aligned with dominant queries as the traits of an effective shard key. It warns specifically against monotonically increasing values, low-cardinality attributes and volatile attributes. Order status is both low-cardinality and volatile.
rationales: Monotonic keys create hotspots on the newest shard.
Correct. Even distribution of data and load is a core requirement.
Correct. Single-shard queries avoid expensive fan-out.
Status has few values and changes over an order's life, causing hotspots and cross-shard moves.

questions.scenario: A flash-sale endpoint runs in PostgreSQL at the default isolation level. The handler does SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = $1, checks qty > 0 in application code, then runs UPDATE stock SET qty = $computed WHERE sku = $1. Under load the shop sells 130 units of a 100-unit item.
questions.stem: What is the simplest correct fix?
options: Wrap the SELECT and UPDATE in an explicit BEGIN/COMMIT block at the default isolation level.
Add a unique index on sku so concurrent updates conflict.
Replace both statements with UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = $1 AND qty > 0, and treat zero affected rows as sold out.
Cache qty in Redis and decrement it there before writing to PostgreSQL.
questions.explanation: The default level, Read Committed, allows lost updates in read-modify-write code: two transactions read the same qty and both write back. A single UPDATE that computes from the current row value and checks the condition makes the decrement atomic. The affected row count tells the handler whether it got a unit.
rationales: A transaction at Read Committed still lets both sessions read the same value before either writes.
sku is already the row identifier; a unique index does not make concurrent updates conflict.
Correct. The row is updated atomically against its current value, with the stock check in the same statement.
This adds a second source of truth and a dual write without fixing the race in the database.

sources.title: Transaction isolation — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: A hospital scheduling app requires at least one doctor on call per shift. The "go off call" transaction runs at REPEATABLE READ: it counts on-call doctors for the shift, and if the count is 2 or more, sets the current doctor's on_call = false. Two doctors on the same shift click "go off call" at the same moment, and both succeed, leaving nobody on call.
questions.stem: Which change prevents this anomaly?
options: Move the transaction to READ COMMITTED so each statement sees the latest committed data.
Add a CHECK constraint that on_call is not null.
Run the count query twice inside the same transaction to confirm the result.
Run the transaction at SERIALIZABLE and retry the whole transaction when it fails with SQLSTATE 40001.
questions.explanation: This is write skew: both transactions read the same set and update different rows, which snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL Repeatable Read) allows. Serializable detects the read/write dependency and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, and the app must retry it in full. Locking the shift's doctor rows with FOR UPDATE is the pessimistic alternative.
rationales: Read Committed is weaker and still allows both transactions to see a count of 2.
A per-row CHECK cannot express a rule across rows and does not address the race.
Within one snapshot the second count returns the same stale answer.
Correct. Serializable prevents serialization anomalies such as write skew, with a retry on 40001.

sources.title: Transaction isolation — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: After switching a transfer service to SERIALIZABLE, logs show occasional errors: "could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions" (SQLSTATE 40001). A developer proposes catching the error and re-running only the UPDATE statement that failed.
questions.stem: What is the correct handling?
options: Roll back and re-run the entire transaction from its first statement, with a bounded number of retries and backoff.
Re-run only the failing UPDATE, since the earlier reads already succeeded.
Drop back to READ COMMITTED for transfers because SERIALIZABLE is unreliable.
Add SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT to every read so the error cannot occur.
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs say applications using Repeatable Read or Serializable must be prepared to retry transactions that fail with serialization errors, and the retry must include the reads because their results may now differ. Serialization failures are the expected way SSI prevents anomalies, not a malfunction. Bounded retries with backoff keep contention from spinning.
rationales: Correct. Whole-transaction retry is the documented handling for 40001.
The earlier reads are part of the conflict; reusing their results would reintroduce the anomaly.
The errors mean Serializable is doing its job; dropping the level re-allows the anomalies.
NOWAIT turns waits into immediate lock errors, adds pessimistic locking everywhere, and still does not remove the need for retries.

sources.title: Transaction isolation — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: An admin UI lets staff edit a customer record; people often keep the form open for 10 minutes. Occasionally two staff edit the same customer and the second save silently overwrites the first. One proposal is to SELECT ... FOR UPDATE when the form opens and commit on save.
questions.stem: What is the better approach?
options: Adopt the proposal, with a 15-minute lock timeout.
Run the save at SERIALIZABLE isolation.
Add a version column (or ETag); on save, update only WHERE version matches and return a conflict (for example 412 Precondition Failed with If-Match) if it does not.
Save every field change immediately as the user types so there is no long-lived form.
questions.explanation: Long think time with rare conflicts is the case for optimistic concurrency: detect the conflict at save time instead of locking. Over HTTP, RFC 9110 conditional requests use If-Match with an ETag and answer 412 Precondition Failed when the resource has changed. Holding a database lock across human think time blocks other work and ties up connections.
rationales: Holding a row lock and an open transaction for minutes blocks other writers and pins a connection per open form.
The save is a separate short transaction; Serializable cannot see that the form was loaded minutes earlier from stale data.
Correct. Conflicts are detected cheaply and the second editor can reload and merge.
Per-keystroke saves still interleave two editors' changes and greatly increase write load.

sources.title: HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110) — RFC Editor
Explicit locking — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: A team uses a PostgreSQL jobs table as a work queue. Ten workers each run SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE, then process the job. Throughput barely improves beyond one worker.
questions.stem: What change lets the workers claim jobs in parallel?
options: Remove FOR UPDATE so workers do not block one another.
Use FOR SHARE instead of FOR UPDATE.
Raise the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE.
Add SKIP LOCKED so each worker skips rows already locked by another worker.
questions.explanation: All ten workers try to lock the same first ready row, so nine wait. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes each worker skip locked rows and take the next one. The PostgreSQL docs describe this as a way to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers on a queue-like table.
rationales: Without a lock, several workers can pick and process the same job.
Share locks let several workers hold the same row, so they would process the same job.
Serializable adds aborts and retries but does not stop workers contending for the same row.
Correct. This is the documented queue-table use of SKIP LOCKED.

sources.title: SELECT locking clause — PostgreSQL docs

questions.stem: Which two statements about PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ level are accurate? (Select two.)
options: It is implemented as snapshot isolation.
It is PostgreSQL's default isolation level.
A transaction at this level can fail with a serialization error when it tries to update a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction.
It prevents write skew, so business rules across rows need no explicit locks.
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs state Repeatable Read is implemented as snapshot isolation and that updates to concurrently modified rows fail with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update". The default level is Read Committed. Snapshot isolation still allows serialization anomalies such as write skew, and the docs warn that business rules at this level need explicit locks.
rationales: Correct. The docs name the technique as Snapshot Isolation.
The default is Read Committed.
Correct. This is SQLSTATE 40001 at Repeatable Read.
Write skew is a serialization anomaly that Repeatable Read allows; only Serializable prevents it.
