questions.scenario: A cache-aside implementation updates a product like this: (1) SET the new value in Redis, (2) UPDATE the row in PostgreSQL. When the database rejects an update (for example on a constraint violation), customers keep seeing the rejected price until the key expires.
questions.stem: What is the recommended write path?
options: Keep the order but wrap both steps in a Redis MULTI/EXEC transaction.
Write only to Redis and let a background job copy values to PostgreSQL.
Update PostgreSQL first, then delete the cache key, and keep a TTL on every entry as a backstop.
Update PostgreSQL first, then remove the TTL from the key so it is never refetched.
questions.explanation: The Azure Cache-Aside pattern writes the change to the data store and then invalidates the cached item, so the next read reloads the committed value. Setting the cache first can publish a value the database never accepted. A TTL bounds the damage if an invalidation is ever missed.
rationales: MULTI/EXEC is atomic within Redis only; it cannot roll back when PostgreSQL rejects the write.
This is write-behind with Redis as the source of truth, risking lost writes and moving integrity checks out of the database.
Correct. The database decides, and the cache is cleared only for committed changes.
Removing the TTL means any missed invalidation leaves stale data forever.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center

questions.scenario: The home page config is cached under one key with a 60-second TTL across 300 API servers. Every minute, when it expires, the database sees a spike of hundreds of identical queries and p99 latency jumps.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause most directly?
options: Lower the TTL to 10 seconds so each spike is smaller.
Coalesce requests so only one fetch per key goes to the database while other callers wait, and refresh before expiry (soft TTL) with jitter.
Add read replicas so the database can absorb the spike.
Switch Redis to the allkeys-lfu eviction policy.
questions.explanation: This is a thundering herd on one hot key. The Builders' Library article recommends request coalescing so only one request is outstanding for an uncached resource. Refreshing on a soft TTL with jitter keeps the hot key from ever expiring under load.
rationales: A shorter TTL makes the herd happen six times as often.
Correct. Coalescing removes duplicate fetches and early refresh avoids the expiry cliff.
Replicas absorb the symptom at extra cost; every server still stampedes on expiry.
Eviction policy decides what is removed when memory is full; this key is expiring by TTL.

sources.title: Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library

questions.scenario: An API has a 95% cache hit rate, so its database was sized for about 10% of peak traffic to save cost. A Redis failover flushes the cache during peak hours; the database saturates, requests time out, retries pile on, and the outage lasts 40 minutes even after Redis returns.
questions.stem: Which lesson and change best address this failure?
options: The service had become dependent on the cache for capacity; size the backend for a cold cache or add admission control and load shedding when the hit rate drops.
Redis needs a longer TTL so that fewer keys are missing after a failover.
The cache should use write-through instead of cache-aside so it is always full.
Add more Redis replicas so that a failover never happens.
questions.explanation: The Builders' Library calls this a service "addicted to its cache": modal behaviour where the system works only while the hit rate stays high. The SRE book similarly advises preferring latency caches over capacity caches. The fix is to ensure the backend survives a cold cache, or to throttle and shed load deliberately while the cache warms.
rationales: Correct. It names the cache-as-capacity hazard and plans for the cold-cache mode.
TTL length is irrelevant when the whole cache is flushed.
Write-through fills only keys that are written, and a flush still empties the cache.
Replicas reduce failover frequency but cannot rule out a flush, cold start or key-distribution shift.

sources.title: Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library
Addressing cascading failures — Google SRE book

questions.scenario: An account page shows a user's billing address and last four card digits. The site is behind a CDN. A developer set Cache-Control: no-cache on the response "so nothing caches it". A security review flags the header.
questions.stem: Which header should the response use?
options: Cache-Control: no-cache, must-revalidate
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0
Cache-Control: s-maxage=0
Cache-Control: no-store
questions.explanation: RFC 9111 defines no-cache as permission to store with mandatory revalidation before reuse, so it does not keep the response out of caches. no-store is the directive that forbids any cache from storing the response. For per-user content that is not sensitive, private would keep shared caches out while allowing the browser to cache.
rationales: must-revalidate governs stale responses; together with no-cache it still allows storage.
public explicitly allows shared caches to store the response.
s-maxage=0 affects only shared caches' freshness and still allows storage, including in the browser.
Correct. no-store prevents storing the response anywhere.

questions.scenario: A single-page app ships main.js and styles.css behind a CDN with max-age=86400. After each deploy the team issues a CDN invalidation, but some users still load new HTML with old JavaScript for a while, and invalidations are slow and sometimes forgotten.
questions.stem: What is the most robust approach?
options: Set max-age=0 on all assets so every request goes to the origin.
Name assets by content hash (for example main.3f9a2c.js) with a long max-age and immutable, and serve the HTML with a short lifetime or no-cache.
Keep the same names but invalidate /* after every deploy.
Add a ?t=<timestamp of request> query parameter in the browser for each asset fetch.
questions.explanation: MDN describes cache busting: put a version or hash in the URL of content that never changes and give it a long max-age, with immutable to avoid reload revalidation. CloudFront documents versioned file names as an alternative to invalidation. The HTML then has to stay short-lived so it can reference the new names.
rationales: This discards the CDN's benefit for assets and loads the origin on every request.
Correct. New releases get new URLs, so old and new assets never mix and no invalidation is needed.
Invalidating everything is slow, costs requests, and still races with browsers holding cached HTML or assets.
A per-request timestamp makes every URL unique, which defeats caching entirely.

sources.title: HTTP caching — MDN Web Docs

questions.stem: A pricing service caches responses from a flaky downstream catalogue. Which two techniques keep it serving useful answers and avoid hammering the catalogue during a downstream outage? (Select two.)
options: Use a soft TTL for refresh and a longer hard TTL, serving the last good value while refreshes fail.
Set the TTL to zero during incidents so every request gets the freshest data.
Cache "not found" and error responses with their own, shorter TTL (negative caching).
On every cache miss, retry the downstream call immediately until it succeeds.
questions.explanation: The Builders' Library article describes soft and hard TTLs, where the cache keeps serving an item while the downstream is unavailable, and negative caching of errors with a different TTL. It notes that failing to cache negative responses has caused higher failure rates. Disabling the cache or retrying aggressively sends more traffic to a failing dependency.
rationales: Correct. Soft/hard TTL serves stale but useful data through downstream failures.
A zero TTL turns every request into a downstream call at the worst moment.
Correct. Negative caching stops repeated misses from reaching the downstream.
Immediate retries amplify load on a struggling dependency.

sources.title: Caching challenges and strategies — Amazon Builders' Library

questions.scenario: A Redis instance used only as a cache is configured with maxmemory and the volatile-lru policy. The application stores cache entries without a TTL. When memory fills, writes start failing with out-of-memory errors.
questions.stem: What explains this and what is the usual fix?
options: Redis cannot evict while replicas are connected; remove the replicas.
LRU in Redis is approximate, so it fails under memory pressure; switch to allkeys-random.
maxmemory is too low; set it to 0 so Redis never needs to evict.
volatile-lru evicts only keys with a TTL, so with none it behaves like noeviction; switch to allkeys-lru (or set TTLs on entries).
questions.explanation: The Redis docs state the volatile-* policies evict only keys with an expiration and behave like noeviction when no keys have one, and noeviction returns errors on commands that add data. For caches the docs suggest allkeys-lru as a good default. Setting TTLs on cache entries also makes them evictable.
rationales: Connected replicas do not stop the primary from evicting; the failure is that volatile-lru finds no keys with a TTL to evict.
Sampling-based LRU is an approximation but works; the failure is that no keys are eligible.
maxmemory 0 means no limit on 64-bit systems, so Redis grows until the host runs out of memory.
Correct. This matches the documented volatile-* behaviour and the recommended default.

questions.scenario: A gRPC service runs behind a Layer-4 TCP load balancer. Clients open one long-lived HTTP/2 connection each and multiplex all calls over it. After autoscaling adds instances, the new instances sit nearly idle while the old ones run hot.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Switch to Layer-7 (or client-side) balancing that distributes individual requests rather than connections
Enable session affinity on the L4 load balancer
Lower the autoscaling CPU target so even more instances are added
Move to larger instance types so each instance can absorb more connections
questions.explanation: An L4 balancer chooses a backend per TCP connection. A long-lived multiplexed connection keeps sending every request to the same instance, so new instances get nothing. An L7 balancer terminates HTTP and can balance per request, which spreads load onto new capacity.
rationales: Correct: request-level balancing is what multiplexed protocols need.
Affinity pins traffic even more tightly to existing instances.
More instances do not help when existing connections never move to them.
Bigger instances treat the symptom and still leave new capacity idle.

questions.scenario: A web shop stores shopping carts in each application instance's memory and uses sticky sessions. Every scale-in event produces support tickets about emptied carts.
questions.stem: Which change fixes the root cause while keeping autoscaling?
options: Increase the sticky-session cookie lifetime
Disable scale-in during business hours
Move cart state to a shared external store so instances are stateless
Replicate each instance's memory to a standby instance
questions.explanation: The root cause is state held in a disposable instance. Externalizing carts to a shared store (a database or cache cluster) lets any instance serve any request, so scale-in and crashes lose nothing. Affinity tweaks only change which users are hurt.
rationales: A longer cookie keeps users pinned but the state still dies with the instance.
This avoids the symptom at the cost of elasticity, and crashes still lose carts.
Correct: stateless instances are the prerequisite for horizontal scaling.
Per-instance replication is complex and still couples users to specific machines.

questions.scenario: A worker fleet in an Auto Scaling group consumes jobs from a queue. The team proposes a target-tracking policy on the queue's raw visible-message count with a target of 500.
questions.stem: What is the best guidance?
options: Use the raw message count; it is the most direct signal of work waiting
Track the load balancer latency metric instead, since it rises with load
Use step scaling on CPU only, because queue metrics cannot drive autoscaling
Track a custom backlog-per-instance metric (visible messages divided by running instances) with a target derived from acceptable processing delay
questions.explanation: Target tracking needs a metric that changes proportionally with the number of instances. The AWS docs say raw queue depth does not, but a messages-per-instance metric can work. Latency is also called out as not proportional.
rationales: Raw depth does not shrink in proportion as instances are added, so the policy misbehaves.
Latency rises with load but does not change proportionally to fleet size, so the AWS docs say it does not work for target tracking.
Queue-derived metrics can drive scaling when normalized per instance.
Correct: backlog per instance is proportional to fleet size.

questions.scenario: A load balancer spans two availability zones. Zone A has 2 registered targets and zone B has 8. DNS sends half of client traffic to the balancer node in each zone. Cross-zone load balancing is disabled.
questions.stem: What share of total traffic does each zone-A target receive?
questions.explanation: With cross-zone disabled, each node sends its 50% only to targets in its own zone. Zone A's 50% splits over 2 targets (25% each) and zone B's over 8 (6.25% each). With cross-zone enabled, all 10 targets would get 10%.
rationales: That is the cross-zone-enabled share.
Correct: 50% / 2 targets.
That is the share of each zone-B target.
That is the whole zone's share, not one target's.

questions.scenario: An API fleet's health check queries the shared database. During a brief database blip, every instance failed its check at once. The team is redesigning health checking and shutdown.
questions.stem: Which two practices should they adopt? (Select two.)
options: Rely on fail-open behaviour so that when all targets fail health checks, traffic still goes to all of them
Make the liveness check call every downstream dependency so that any dependency problem removes the instance
On SIGTERM, enter a draining (lame duck) state: stop taking new requests, finish in-flight ones, then exit
Run health checks only every few minutes to reduce their load on the database
questions.explanation: The Builders' Library describes fail-open load balancers, which route to every target when all fail checks, so a shared dependency blip cannot empty the fleet. The SRE book's lame duck state lets a task drain gracefully before shutdown. Deep checks on every dependency cause exactly the fleet-wide removal seen here.
rationales: Correct: fail open stops health checks from taking down the whole fleet.
This is what turned a database blip into a total outage.
Correct: draining avoids failing in-flight requests at shutdown.
Slow checks delay the detection of genuinely bad hosts.

questions.scenario: A dependency's latency is p50 = 20 ms, p99 = 120 ms and p99.9 = 400 ms. The caller can tolerate about 0.1% of otherwise-good calls timing out. The HTTP client currently uses a 30 s default timeout.
questions.stem: Which timeout best follows the false-timeout-rate approach?
options: 40 ms (2x the median)
Keep 30 s so that no good call is ever cut off
120 ms (the p99)
About 400 ms (the p99.9)
questions.explanation: The Builders' Library chooses timeouts from an acceptable false-timeout rate: tolerating 0.1% maps to the downstream p99.9. A 30 s timeout lets threads and connections pile up during a slowdown, and a median-based value fails many healthy calls.
rationales: This would time out a large share of good calls and trigger retries.
A huge timeout ties up resources during slowdowns and risks cascading failure.
p99 gives about a 1% false-timeout rate, 10x the tolerance.
Correct: p99.9 matches a 0.1% false-timeout budget.

questions.scenario: A request passes edge → API → order service → inventory service → database. Each of the four callers makes up to 3 attempts (1 try plus 2 retries) on failure. The database starts timing out.
questions.stem: In the worst case, how many database attempts can one user request cause, and what is the structural fix?
options: 12; add jitter at every layer
81; retry at a single layer and have lower layers return a do-not-retry signal
64; raise the database connection limit
243; increase every timeout
questions.explanation: Retries multiply: four layers with 3 attempts each give 3^4 = 81 attempts at the bottom. Both the Builders' Library and the SRE book recommend retrying at a single point (the layer directly above the failing backend) and propagating "overloaded; don't retry" upward.
rationales: Attempts multiply rather than add, and jitter does not reduce the count.
Correct: 3^4 = 81, fixed by single-layer retries.
64 is 4^3, a different configuration; more connections feed the overload.
243 is 3^5; longer timeouts do not reduce amplification.

questions.scenario: After a 20-second database failover, thousands of mobile clients retry every 1 second exactly. The database recovers but is immediately knocked over again by synchronized waves of requests.
questions.stem: Which client change most directly addresses this?
options: Remove client timeouts so requests wait for the database instead of retrying
Retry every 250 ms so requests succeed sooner after recovery
Increase the maximum retry count from 3 to 10
Capped exponential backoff with jitter, plus a limit on retries
questions.explanation: Fixed-interval retries keep clients synchronized and form a retry storm. Exponential backoff reduces the rate, the cap bounds waits, and jitter de-correlates clients so arrivals spread out. A retry limit bounds the extra load.
rationales: Unbounded waits hold resources and do not reduce offered load.
Faster retries increase the load on a recovering dependency.
More retries mean more amplification.
Correct: backoff, cap, jitter and a retry limit together break the storm.

questions.scenario: A backend cluster is partially overloaded. Client libraries currently retry any failed request up to 3 times, and retries at several layers multiply.
questions.stem: Which two mechanisms from the SRE guidance best bound retry-driven load growth? (Select two.)
options: A per-client retry budget that allows retries only while they stay below about 10% of requests
Raising the per-request limit to 5 attempts so more requests eventually succeed
Retrying only at the layer immediately above the overloaded backend, which returns an explicit "overloaded; don't retry" error
Switching retries from exponential backoff to immediate retry for lower latency
questions.explanation: The SRE book caps attempts per request and adds a per-client 10% retry budget, which cuts worst-case growth from about 3x to about 1.1x. It also says to retry only at the layer directly above and to signal "overloaded; don't retry" so higher layers do not multiply attempts.
rationales: Correct: the retry budget bounds aggregate retry load.
More attempts increase amplification during overload.
Correct: single-layer retries stop multiplication across the stack.
Immediate retries add load at the worst moment.

questions.scenario: A user-facing request has a 2 s deadline. The gateway spends 1.6 s waiting on an authentication call, then calls a downstream service whose client is configured with a fixed 3 s timeout.
questions.stem: What should the gateway do?
options: Use the fixed 3 s timeout, because the downstream service may need it
Retry the downstream call twice within the 3 s timeout to improve success odds
Propagate the remaining budget (about 0.4 s, minus a small margin) and skip the call if the deadline has already passed
Reset the deadline to 2 s for the downstream call so it gets a full budget
questions.explanation: The SRE book recommends deadline propagation: pass the remaining time downstream, less a margin, so no work continues after the caller has given up. Fixed or reset timeouts waste capacity on answers nobody will read.
rationales: The user stops waiting at 2 s, so work beyond that is wasted.
Retries inside an expired budget only add load.
Correct: propagate the remaining deadline and drop expired work.
Resetting the deadline ignores the time already spent.

questions.scenario: Ten thousand hosts each run an hourly job at minute :00 that calls a configuration service, which is overloaded for the first seconds of every hour.
questions.stem: Which approach does the Builders' Library recommend for spreading this scheduled work?
options: Have each host pick a new random delay every hour
Give each host a consistent offset derived from something stable, such as its host ID
Scale the configuration service to absorb the full top-of-hour peak
Run the job every minute so each run is smaller
questions.explanation: The article adds jitter to periodic work, but for scheduled jobs it uses a consistent method that produces the same number every time on the same host. That spreads load evenly and keeps behaviour reproducible, unlike a fresh random value per run.
rationales: This spreads load, but the article prefers a consistent per-host value so behaviour is predictable.
Correct: a stable per-host offset spreads load reproducibly.
This pays for a peak that jitter can remove.
More frequent runs keep the synchronized pattern and add calls.

questions.scenario: A circuit breaker around a payment provider opened after repeated failures. Its open timer has just expired.
questions.stem: Per the Circuit Breaker pattern, what should happen next?
options: Close immediately and send all traffic to the provider
Stay open until an operator resets it manually
Close, but halve the failure threshold
Enter Half-Open, let a limited number of trial calls through, close after enough successes and reopen on any failure
questions.explanation: After the open timeout, the breaker moves to Half-Open and admits a limited number of requests. Consecutive successes close it; any failure reopens it and restarts the timer. This keeps a recovering service from being flooded.
rationales: A flood of traffic can knock a recovering service over again.
The pattern automates recovery detection; manual resets are not required.
This is not part of the pattern and skips the trial phase.
Correct: this is the Half-Open behaviour.

questions.scenario: A client wraps all calls to a 16-shard data store in one circuit breaker. When one shard fails, the breaker opens and the client stops using all 16 shards.
questions.stem: What is the best redesign?
options: Use a separate circuit breaker per shard so healthy shards stay reachable
Raise the shared breaker's failure threshold so one shard cannot trip it
Remove the breaker and rely on retries
Keep one breaker but shorten its open timeout to a few milliseconds
questions.explanation: The Azure pattern warns against one breaker over multiple independent providers: merging their errors cuts off healthy shards too. Scoping breakers to each independent failure unit isolates the bad shard.
rationales: Correct: breakers should match independent failure units.
A higher threshold delays protection for every shard.
Retries alone keep hammering the failing shard.
Rapid flapping still blocks healthy shards and adds noise.

questions.scenario: A checkout service calls payments, inventory and a slow recommendations service through one shared pool of 50 HTTP connections. When recommendations hangs, all 50 connections wait on it and checkout fails entirely.
questions.stem: Which change best prevents this?
options: Increase the shared pool to 500 connections
Add retries to the payments call
Autoscale checkout on CPU
Give each dependency its own connection pool and timeout (bulkheads), so a hung dependency exhausts only its own pool
questions.explanation: The Bulkhead pattern assigns a connection pool per downstream service so that one failing dependency affects only the work using that pool. A bigger shared pool just takes longer to fill, and CPU is not the bottleneck.
rationales: A hung dependency eventually fills any shared pool.
Payments is healthy; its calls are starved of connections.
Threads are blocked on I/O, so CPU stays low and does not trigger scaling.
Correct: isolating pools contains the failure.

sources.title: Bulkhead pattern — Azure Architecture Center

questions.scenario: In an overload test, a service's availability falls toward zero as offered load rises past capacity. Latency grows until every client times out. The team wants goodput to plateau instead.
questions.stem: Which approach fits?
options: Queue all excess requests in an unbounded FIFO queue so none are rejected
Reject excess requests early and cheaply (for example 503 once in-flight requests pass a limit), prioritizing critical traffic
Increase client timeouts so slow responses still count as successes
Retry failed requests server-side before returning errors
questions.explanation: Load shedding keeps accepted requests fast, so goodput stays near capacity while extra throughput is rejected. Shedding should happen as early as possible and by criticality, and the SRE book suggests returning errors when in-flight requests exceed a limit.
rationales: An unbounded queue raises latency for everyone and serves requests whose clients already left.
Correct: early, prioritized shedding preserves goodput.
Longer timeouts hold more resources and deepen the collapse.
Server-side retries add load during overload.

questions.scenario: A product page calls a recommendations service that is currently failing. The product details, price and stock come from healthy services.
questions.stem: Which two responses are appropriate graceful degradation? (Select two.)
options: Render the page without the recommendations widget
Return HTTP 500 for the whole page so clients retry later
Have the open circuit breaker return a meaningful default, such as a cached list of best-sellers
Block the page until recommendations recover
questions.explanation: The SRE book advises serving degraded results when necessary, and the Azure Circuit Breaker pattern allows the open state to return a meaningful default value. Failing or blocking the whole page turns an optional feature into an outage.
rationales: Correct: omit the optional feature.
This fails the core function because of an optional dependency.
Correct: a fallback value keeps the page useful.
Blocking ties up resources and gives users nothing.

questions.scenario: During a spike, a service's FIFO work queue grows to several minutes of backlog. Most queued requests come from clients that timed out long ago, yet workers process them oldest-first.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Bound the queue, drop requests whose deadline has passed, and prefer LIFO or CoDel-style handling during overload
Add more workers and keep the unbounded FIFO queue
Persist the queue to disk so no request is lost
Increase the client timeout to match the queue delay
questions.explanation: The SRE book recommends bounded queues and LIFO or CoDel under overload, and the Builders' Library warns about insurmountable backlogs. Serving expired requests is pure waste, while fresh requests still have waiting clients.
rationales: Correct: bounded queues and deadline-aware ordering stop wasted work.
Workers would still spend time on dead requests first.
Durability does not help when the answers are no longer wanted.
Minutes-long timeouts give users a terrible experience and hold resources.

questions.scenario: An API limits each key to 100 requests per minute with a fixed-window counter. Logs show one key sent 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, and all 200 were admitted.
questions.stem: What explains this, and which algorithm removes it with near-exact accuracy and constant memory per client?
options: Clock skew between servers; fix it with NTP
A bug in the counter; a correct fixed window never admits more than 100 in 60 s
The fixed window resets at the boundary, allowing about 2x the limit; a sliding window counter fixes this
Fixed windows always admit exactly the limit; switch to a sliding window log, which uses less memory
questions.explanation: Fixed windows reset at each boundary, so a client can send nearly twice the limit across a window edge. A sliding window counter weights the previous window's count by its overlap and gives near-exact limits with two counters. A sliding window log is exact but stores every timestamp.
rationales: This happens even on a single server with a perfect clock.
Admitting 2x across a boundary is inherent to fixed windows.
Correct: boundary bursts are the fixed window's weakness.
A sliding log needs O(n) memory, not less.

questions.scenario: A partner API should sustain an average of 10 requests per second per client but tolerate short bursts of up to 50 requests after idle periods.
questions.stem: How should a token bucket be configured?
options: Refill 50 tokens per second, capacity 10
Refill 10 tokens per second, capacity 10
Refill 60 tokens per second, capacity 60
Refill 10 tokens per second, capacity 50
questions.explanation: The refill rate sets the sustained throughput and the capacity sets the largest burst. API Gateway describes its throttling the same way: a rate of tokens added per second and a burst equal to bucket capacity.
rationales: This swaps the two parameters: it allows 50 per second sustained and only 10 in a burst.
This allows no burst beyond the steady rate.
This allows 6x the intended sustained rate.
Correct: rate 10/s, burst 50.

questions.scenario: A legacy downstream system breaks if it receives more than 20 requests in any second. Callers are bursty, but occasional added delay is acceptable and dropping requests is not, up to a bounded backlog.
questions.stem: Which limiter fits best?
options: A token bucket with a large capacity
A fixed-window counter of 20 per second
A leaky bucket used for shaping: queue requests and forward them at a fixed drain rate, dropping only when the queue is full
A sliding window log that rejects anything over 20 per second
questions.explanation: A shaping leaky bucket queues arrivals and releases them at a constant rate, so the downstream sees a smooth flow and bursts are delayed rather than dropped. Token buckets intentionally allow bursts, and the window limiters reject rather than delay.
rationales: Large capacity means large bursts, which this downstream cannot take.
This can admit about 40 across a boundary and rejects instead of delaying.
Correct: shaping smooths bursts into a steady rate.
This is exact, but it polices (drops) rather than shapes.

questions.scenario: A tenant's limit is 1,000 requests per second across 10 gateway instances. Each instance enforces a local limit of 100 rps. Because of connection reuse, this tenant's traffic lands on only 2 instances and it is throttled at about 200 rps.
questions.stem: Which design best enforces the true tenant-wide limit?
options: Raise each instance's local limit to 1,000 rps
Keep a per-tenant counter in Redis, read it with GET and write it back with SET from each gateway
Remove server-side limiting and ask tenants to self-limit
Keep a per-tenant counter in a shared store, updated with an atomic check-and-increment such as a Redis Lua script
questions.explanation: Splitting a quota evenly across servers fails when traffic is uneven. A shared counter fixes that, but only if the check and update are atomic: separate GET and SET is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race that lets concurrent requests exceed the limit. Redis runs Lua scripts atomically.
rationales: The tenant could then reach 10,000 rps across all instances.
Non-atomic read-modify-write races under concurrency, exactly when limits matter.
Self-limiting gives no protection against misbehaving tenants.
Correct: a shared, atomically updated counter.

questions.scenario: A multi-tenant API has plenty of spare capacity, but one tenant has exceeded its per-minute quota.
questions.stem: Which response is most appropriate?
options: 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error
429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After
400 Bad Request
questions.explanation: 429 (defined in RFC 6585) signals that this client has sent too many requests and may include Retry-After. The Builders' Library notes that quota-exceeded responses are 4xx because the client exceeded its quota, not because the server is out of capacity, which is what 503 means.
rationales: 503 implies a server capacity problem, which is not the case here.
Nothing failed on the server.
Correct: the client exceeded its quota.
The request is well-formed; only its rate is the issue.

questions.scenario: A batch job ingests 10,000 records into a service throttled at a fixed capacity. It sends everything, retries whatever is rejected and repeats. The job finishes but sends 30,000 records and logs 20,000 errors.
questions.stem: What does the Rate Limiting pattern recommend?
options: Write records to a durable queue and have job processors dequeue at a controlled rate within the service's limit
Retry rejected records immediately with more parallel threads
Buffer all records in application memory until the service accepts them
Ask for the throttle to be removed for batch jobs
questions.explanation: The Azure pattern shows blind retry-on-error tripling the work. It recommends sending records to a durable messaging system and draining them at a controlled rate under the throttle. In-memory buffering risks losing data if the app stops.
rationales: Correct: controlled-rate consumption avoids wasted, rejected calls.
More parallel retries raise the rejection rate.
The pattern warns that buffered data can be lost if the app stops responding.
The throttle protects the shared service; work within it.

questions.scenario: A client sends POST /payments to charge a card. The connection times out with no response, so the client cannot tell whether the charge happened. The API supports idempotency keys.
questions.stem: What should the client do?
options: Retry with a new idempotency key so the server treats it as a fresh attempt
Retry the same request with the same idempotency key
Query the payments list and, if no charge appears, send a new charge
Switch to PUT so the retry is automatically idempotent
questions.explanation: The idempotency key identifies the logical operation. Reusing it lets the server recognize the retry and return a response equivalent to the original instead of charging again. A new key, or check-then-charge while the first attempt may still be in flight, risks a double charge.
rationales: A new key makes the retry a different operation, which can double-charge.
Correct: same operation, same key.
The original may still be processing or not yet visible, so this can double-charge.
Changing the method does not make the server's charge logic idempotent.

questions.scenario: A server receives POST /transfers with an idempotency key it already completed for a $100 transfer. The new request carries the same key but an amount of $1,000.
questions.stem: How should the server respond?
options: Process it as a new $1,000 transfer
Return the stored $100 response as if it were a normal retry
Update the stored transfer to $1,000
Reject it as a client error indicating the key was reused with a different payload (the IETF draft suggests 422)
questions.explanation: A key must not be reused with a different payload. The Builders' Library returns a validation error when a known token arrives with different parameters, assuming the intent differs. The Idempotency-Key draft suggests 422 Unprocessable Content.
rationales: This defeats the key's purpose and can create unintended transfers.
Silently returning the old result hides a client bug and a mismatch of intent.
Mutating a completed operation through a retry is unsafe.
Correct: reject key reuse with a different payload.

questions.scenario: A mobile client retries POST /orders with the same idempotency key 300 ms after the first attempt. The first attempt is still running on another server.
questions.stem: What should the server do with the second request?
options: Process it in parallel; the database will sort out duplicates
Return 200 with an empty body
Queue it and execute it after the first finishes
Respond with a conflict error (the IETF draft suggests 409) without executing it again
questions.explanation: The draft distinguishes a retry after completion, which gets a response consistent with the original, from a concurrent retry, which gets a resource-conflict error, suggested as 409. Claiming the key atomically, for example with a unique insert, prevents two executions.
rationales: Parallel execution is exactly how duplicates happen.
A fake success misleads the client about the order's state.
Executing it later still runs the operation twice.
Correct: report the conflict and execute once.

questions.scenario: A consumer reads at-least-once order events and writes ledger entries to Postgres. Today it checks a dedup table, processes the event, then inserts the event ID in a separate step. A crash between steps caused duplicate ledger entries.
questions.stem: Which two changes follow the Idempotent Consumer pattern? (Select two.)
options: Insert the dedup marker in the same database transaction as the ledger entries
Claim the key with an atomic conditional write, such as an insert that fails on conflict
Use the event's correlation ID, shared by related events, as the dedup key
Acknowledge the message before processing so it is never redelivered
questions.explanation: The Azure pattern says to commit the dedup marker and the side effects atomically, which removes the crash window, and to claim keys with an atomic conditional write so concurrent redeliveries cannot both proceed. It warns against correlation IDs, which identify groups of messages.
rationales: Correct: one transaction means a redelivery either sees the marker or safely reprocesses.
Correct: atomic claim stops concurrent duplicates.
Correlation IDs are shared across messages and would suppress legitimate ones.
Early acks turn at-least-once into at-most-once and lose events on crash.

questions.scenario: A platform team is adding automatic retries on connection resets to its HTTP reverse proxy. The proxy has no knowledge of application-level idempotency keys.
questions.stem: Which policy is consistent with RFC 9110?
options: Auto-retry GET only; DELETE is not idempotent because a second call returns 404
Auto-retry all methods, since resets usually happen before the server acts
Auto-retry POST and PATCH only, because they are most likely to fail
Auto-retry only idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE
questions.explanation: RFC 9110 says a proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests. PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not. Idempotency concerns the effect on the server, so a different status code on a repeated DELETE does not make it non-idempotent.
rationales: DELETE is idempotent; the response may differ but the effect does not.
A reset can happen after the server acted, and the RFC forbids this for non-idempotent methods.
These are exactly the methods that must not be auto-retried.
Correct: these are the idempotent methods.

questions.scenario: A ledger service consumes `account-transactions` from a Kafka topic with 12 partitions. Producers currently send records with no key, and the team sees debits applied before the credits that preceded them for the same account.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Use the account ID as the record key so that all of an account's records go to one partition.
Reduce the consumer group to a single consumer while keeping keyless producers.
Sort each poll batch by producer timestamp before applying it.
Turn on exactly-once transactions in the producer.
questions.explanation: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so records that must stay ordered need a common key. Keying by account ID keeps per-account order and still spreads accounts across partitions.
rationales: Correct. Same key, same partition, ordered delivery for that account.
Keyless records are still spread across partitions, so even a single consumer gets no cross-partition order, and all parallelism is lost.
Producer timestamps come from different machines' wall clocks, and a batch does not include later polls.
Transactions provide atomicity and deduplication, not ordering across partitions.

questions.scenario: A notification consumer has auto-commit enabled and commits offsets as soon as records are polled. It sends an email for each record. After a pod is OOM-killed mid-batch, customers report missing emails, but no one received a duplicate.
questions.stem: Which delivery semantic is the consumer effectively providing, and what change moves it to at-least-once?
options: At-least-once; switch to committing before processing.
At-most-once; increase the partition count so that fewer records are in flight.
Exactly-once; no change is needed.
At-most-once; commit offsets only after each email is sent, and make sending idempotent.
questions.explanation: Saving the position before processing means a crash skips the uncommitted work, so messages are lost but never redelivered. That is at-most-once. Committing after processing gives at-least-once, which then requires idempotent handling of redeliveries.
rationales: Committing before processing is what causes the loss. It is at-most-once.
More partitions do not change when the offset is committed.
Lost messages rule out exactly-once.
Correct. Process, then commit, and dedupe on a message ID.

questions.scenario: A stream job reads `payments` from Kafka and writes balances into PostgreSQL. The team enabled the idempotent producer and Kafka transactions and expects no double-applied payments. During a consumer rebalance, a few payments are applied twice.

Set `isolation.level=read_uncommitted` so that the consumer sees records sooner.
Lower `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` to 1 on the consumer.
Kafka transactions were misconfigured; with the right setting they also cover writes to PostgreSQL.
questions.explanation: The Kafka docs state that exactly-once for other destination systems generally requires cooperation with those systems. Either the database write is idempotent, or the offset commits atomically with the output, so a reprocessed record has no extra effect.
rationales: Correct. Effectively-once at the sink needs idempotence or offsets stored with the output.
`read_uncommitted` is the default and would also expose aborted data. It does not deduplicate.
That is a producer setting about request pipelining, and it is not related to sink duplicates.
Kafka transactions cannot enlist an external database.

questions.scenario: An image-thumbnail topic has 6 partitions consumed by a classic consumer group. To clear a backlog, an engineer scales the group from 6 to 10 instances, but throughput does not change.
questions.stem: Why?
options: Consumers share each partition round-robin, but the broker's `linger.ms` limits the rate.
Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer per group, so 4 instances get no partitions.
Kafka throttles consumer groups larger than the replication factor.

Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and have a relay publish it.
Wrap both calls in a try/catch that retries the publish three times.
Publish the event from a database trigger that calls the broker's HTTP API.

Retry the shipment step (idempotently) until it succeeds, then send the email.
Skip the shipment and send the email.
Hold a lock on the inventory row until the shipment service recovers, as in 2PC.

Increase the saga's retry count.

Return an opaque cursor encoding the last (created_at, id) and query for rows after that key using an index

questions.explanation: RFC 10017 presents browser architectures in decreasing order of security, with the BFF first, because tokens never reach JavaScript that an XSS bug could exploit. RFC 9700 says not to use the implicit grant, and says the password grant MUST NOT be used.
rationales: RFC 9700 and RFC 10017 both say not to use the implicit grant. Use Authorization Code with PKCE.
Short expiry reduces the window, but any injected script can still read tokens from localStorage.
Correct. RFC 10017 ranks the BFF as the most secure: tokens stay server-side, and the browser gets a Secure, HttpOnly cookie.
RFC 9700 says the ROPC grant MUST NOT be used. It also exposes user credentials to the client.

questions.scenario: An API accepts JWT access tokens from your identity provider, which also issues tokens for other APIs in the company. A penetration test finds that the API accepts a token whose header says "alg": "none", and that it also accepts tokens minted for a different internal API.
questions.stem: Which two validation changes fix these findings? (Select two.)
options: Verify signatures only with an allowlisted algorithm configured for this issuer, never the alg from the token header
Reject tokens whose aud claim does not identify this API
Fetch the verification key from the jku URL in the token header so key rotation works automatically
Skip signature checks for requests that arrive over TLS from the internal network
questions.explanation: RFC 8725 says libraries must let callers specify the allowed algorithms, which defeats alg:none and algorithm-confusion attacks. Where one issuer serves several relying parties, the token must carry aud, and the recipient must reject a token whose audience is missing or is not its own.
rationales: Correct. An algorithm allowlist stops alg:none and RS256-to-HS256 substitution.
Correct. Validating the audience stops tokens issued for another API from being replayed here.
jku is attacker-controlled. Following it blindly enables SSRF and lets the attacker supply their own key.
TLS protects the channel, not the token's authenticity. Internal callers can still present forged tokens.

questions.stem: Which flow should the app use?

Implicit grant, because the app has no backend
Resource owner password credentials, so the app shows its own login form
Authorization Code with PKCE using the S256 method, with an exactly matched registered redirect URI
questions.explanation: A mobile app is a public client. RFC 9700 requires PKCE for public clients, recommends the S256 challenge method (which does not expose the verifier), and requires exact matching of redirect URIs. It also rules out the implicit and password grants.
rationales: A secret shipped in an app binary can be extracted. Client credentials also act as the app, not as the user.
RFC 9700 says not to use the implicit grant.
RFC 9700 says the ROPC grant MUST NOT be used.

options: ID tokens are not signed, so the signature check is meaningless
The API should decode the token without verifying it to save latency
The ID token's audience is the client application; the API should require an access token issued for the API's own audience
Bearer tokens must only be sent in a query string parameter

Skipping verification makes forgery trivial.

Query strings leak into logs and referrers. Tokens belong in the Authorization header.

questions.scenario: A server-rendered web app issues a session cookie to anonymous visitors, so they can fill a cart, and keeps the same session ID after the user logs in. A security review flags this.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the review finding?

Move the session ID into localStorage so the server does not have to set cookies
Make the session ID longer but keep it the same across login
Encode the user ID in the cookie in base64 instead of a random session ID
questions.explanation: Keeping the pre-login session ID enables session fixation: an attacker who planted or learned that ID inherits the logged-in session. OWASP's session guidance is to renew the session ID after any privilege change and to protect the cookie with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
rationales: Correct. Renewing the ID at login defeats fixation, and the cookie attributes limit theft and cross-site sending.
localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug can steal the ID.
Length does not help if the attacker already knows the ID before login.
A base64 user ID is not a secret. Anyone can forge it.

questions.scenario: A SaaS app stores every tenant's invoices in one PostgreSQL table with a tenant_id column. The team enabled row level security and created a tenant policy, but tests show that each tenant still sees every row. The application connects as the role that created the table.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: RLS only applies to SELECT, so writes leak; add a trigger
Table owners bypass RLS by default; connect as a separate non-owner role, or set FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on the table
RLS requires a policy for every tenant ID; create one policy per tenant
With no policy match PostgreSQL allows all rows; add a default-deny policy
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs say table owners normally bypass row security unless the table is altered with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass it. An app that connects as the owner therefore sees all rows despite the policy.
rationales: Policies can apply to SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. The symptom here is reads of every row.
Correct. The owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, so use a dedicated application role.
One policy keyed on a per-request tenant value is the normal design. Per-tenant policies do not fix an owner bypass.
With RLS enabled and no policy, access is already default-deny. The issue is who bypasses RLS.

Vertically partitioned: pool the small tenants on shared infrastructure and give the enterprise tenants dedicated deployments
A separate schema per tenant with per-tenant column customisations, so each customer can extend the data model

It keeps the long tail cheap and gives regulated customers dedicated resources, while a fully siloed approach would multiply cost and operational work for a small team.

A shared table does not meet a contractual requirement for dedicated data stores.

questions.scenario: In a pooled multi-tenant service, one tenant starts a large nightly import that saturates the shared database. p99 latency for every other tenant triples. Total traffic is within what the database handles on a normal day.
questions.stem: Which mitigation addresses the root cause with the least collateral damage?
options: Enforce per-tenant quotas or throttling on the import path and monitor resource use per tenant
Add a single global rate limit on the API that applies to all tenants combined
Increase client retry counts so failed requests from other tenants eventually succeed
Disable the database connection pool so each request gets its own connection
questions.explanation: This is the noisy neighbour antipattern: one tenant's activity degrades the others on shared resources. Per-tenant resource governance, through throttling or rate limiting, plus per-tenant monitoring contains the heavy tenant without penalising everyone else.
rationales: Correct. Per-tenant quotas limit the tenant causing the load, and per-tenant metrics show who that is.
A global limit lets the heavy tenant use up the shared allowance, so other tenants get rejected too.
More retries add load to a saturated resource and make the contention worse.
Removing pooling multiplies connections and puts more pressure on the database.

questions.scenario: A pooled SaaS API serves GET /projects/{id}. Today the service reads the tenant from an X-Tenant-Id request header and filters on it in application code. A reviewer wants defence in depth against cross-tenant reads.
questions.stem: Which two changes most strengthen tenant isolation? (Select two.)
options: Derive the tenant ID on the server from the authenticated token or session, not from a client-supplied header
Enforce tenant filtering in the database with a row-level security policy keyed on the per-request tenant setting
Hide other tenants' project IDs in the UI so users cannot guess them
Use UUIDs for project IDs so cross-tenant IDs are hard to guess, and drop the tenant filter

Taking the tenant from the authenticated identity closes that gap, and RLS adds a second, database-enforced check that still holds if application code forgets a filter.
rationales: Correct. The server must decide which tenant a caller belongs to. Clients can set any header they like.
Correct. RLS enforces isolation in the database as a second layer behind the application's checks.
Hiding IDs in the UI is not access control. Attackers call the API directly.
Unguessable IDs are not authorization. A leaked or logged ID would still expose another tenant's data.

questions.scenario: A developer accidentally pushed a production database password and a third-party API key to a public Git repository. The commit was noticed an hour later.
questions.stem: Which two actions should the team take? (Select two.)
options: Rotate or revoke both credentials immediately and review access logs for misuse
Move the credentials into a secrets manager with access control, auditing and automated rotation
Rewrite Git history to remove the commit; no other action is needed once it is gone
Base64-encode the secrets in the config file so they are no longer readable
questions.explanation: Once a secret is exposed, assume it is compromised. Revoke or rotate it, and check for misuse. OWASP's secrets guidance is to centralise secrets in a managed store with access control, auditing and automated rotation, so they never live in code again.
rationales: Correct. Rotation or revocation makes the leaked values useless, and the logs show whether anyone used them.
Correct. A secrets manager with rotation stops this from happening again and shortens credential lifetimes.
Clones, forks and caches may already hold the secret. Rewriting history does not revoke it.
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it.

questions.scenario: A logged-in user of a multi-tenant billing app changes the URL from /api/invoices/1041 to /api/invoices/1042 and downloads another company's invoice. Authentication works correctly.
questions.stem: Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category does this fall under, and what is the fix?
options: A05 Injection: sanitise the invoice ID parameter
A07 Authentication Failures: require multi-factor authentication
A04 Cryptographic Failures: encrypt invoice IDs in URLs
A01 Broken Access Control: check on every request that the invoice belongs to the caller's tenant
questions.explanation: The user is correctly authenticated but can reach an object they are not entitled to. That is an object-level authorization failure, under A01 Broken Access Control, the top category in OWASP Top 10:2025. The fix is an ownership or tenant check on every object access.
rationales: Nothing is being injected. The ID is valid input that points to an object the user should not see.
Authentication already worked. MFA does not stop a legitimate user from reading another tenant's object.
Obscuring IDs does not replace an authorization check.
Correct. Missing object-level authorization is broken access control, so enforce the tenant and ownership check server-side.

questions.scenario: A team encrypts customer documents at rest. Their first design stores the single AES key in a column of the same database that holds the encrypted documents, so the app can read both with one query.
questions.stem: Which design is the recommended improvement?
options: Hard-code the key in the application binary instead of the database
Use envelope encryption: data keys encrypt the documents, and a key encryption key held in a key vault or HSM, with its own access control and audit, encrypts the data keys
Skip encryption at rest because TLS already protects the data
Store the key in the same database but in a different table
questions.explanation: Azure's encryption-at-rest guidance uses a key hierarchy: data encryption keys protect the data and are themselves encrypted by a key encryption key kept in a secure store with identity-based access control and auditing. Keeping the key next to the ciphertext means one database leak exposes both.
rationales: Keys in binaries leak through builds and repositories, and rotation needs a redeploy.
Correct. Envelope encryption separates the keys from the data and makes key rotation practical.
TLS protects data in transit. It does nothing for stolen disks, snapshots or backups.
A different table in the same database leaks together with the data.

questions.scenario: A new thumbnail service needs to read images from one object-storage bucket and write thumbnails to another. To ship quickly, the team proposes reusing an existing role that has full administrator access to the account.
questions.stem: What should a design review require instead?
options: Keep the admin role but enable logging so misuse can be detected later
A dedicated role for the service, allowed only to read from the source bucket and write to the thumbnail bucket, with temporary credentials
A long-lived access key for the service stored in an environment variable
Share one role across all services, so permissions are managed in one place
questions.explanation: AWS Well-Architected SEC03-BP02 says identities should be permitted only the smallest set of actions needed for the task. A per-service role scoped to two buckets, using temporary credentials, limits the blast radius if the service is compromised.
rationales: Logging detects problems after the fact. It does not reduce what a compromised service can do.
Correct. Scoped, per-service permissions with temporary credentials are what least privilege means in practice.
Long-lived keys are harder to rotate and easy to leak, and they still need a scoped policy.
A shared role gives every service the union of all permissions, the opposite of least privilege.

questions.scenario: A marketing team wants a link shortener. Their main requirement is accurate click counts per link, including repeat clicks from the same browser.
questions.stem: Which redirect response best fits this requirement?
options: A 301 redirect with a one-year max-age so the CDN can serve redirects cheaply
A 301 Moved Permanently redirect with no cache headers, because it is the "correct" status for short links
A 200 OK page containing JavaScript that changes window.location after logging
A 302 Found redirect, because it is not cacheable by default, so each click reaches the shortener
questions.explanation: RFC 9110 lists 301 as heuristically cacheable, so browsers and caches may reuse it without contacting the shortener, which hides repeat clicks. A 302 is not cacheable unless headers say so, so each click is observed. Long-lived caching of a 301 makes the analytics problem worse.
rationales: Long caching is cheapest, but it is the opposite of what accurate click counting needs.
A 301 is heuristically cacheable even without headers, so repeat clicks may never reach the server.
This works, but it adds a page load and breaks non-browser clients. A 302 meets the requirement directly.
Correct. Without explicit freshness, a 302 is not reused from cache, so the server sees every click.

questions.scenario: A social app precomputes each user's home feed by inserting post IDs into every follower's feed list when a post is created. A handful of creators have tens of millions of followers. Each of their posts causes a multi-minute write backlog that delays everyone's feeds.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Switch every account to fan-out on read so no feed is precomputed
Keep fan-out on write for ordinary accounts, but fetch posts from very high-follower accounts at read time and merge them into the precomputed feed
Add more feed-writer workers until the backlog for a creator post clears in seconds
Store full post bodies in each feed entry so readers never need a second lookup
questions.explanation: The hybrid keeps fast precomputed reads for the common case and removes the multi-million-write spike caused by a few accounts. Pure fan-out on read makes every feed read expensive, and scaling writers keeps paying the spike on every post. Storing post bodies multiplies storage and makes edits and deletes rewrite millions of entries.
rationales: This fixes write spikes but makes every read merge many sources, which hurts a read-heavy feed.
Correct. Push for most accounts and pull for the few huge ones removes the hot spot while keeping reads fast.
This throws capacity at a structural hot spot. The write amplification remains, and the cost scales with follower counts.
Denormalising post bodies makes the write amplification and the edit or delete problem worse.

questions.scenario: A chat service has 2 million concurrently connected clients that send a presence heartbeat every 30 seconds. The current design runs `UPDATE users SET last_seen = now()` on the primary PostgreSQL database for each heartbeat, and write latency for messages is rising.
questions.stem: What is the best redesign for presence?
options: Add a read replica so presence reads move off the primary
Increase the heartbeat interval to 10 minutes to cut writes
Store presence as keys with a TTL slightly longer than the heartbeat interval in an in-memory store, and treat a missing key as offline
Batch heartbeats into a nightly job that updates last_seen
questions.explanation: Presence is soft state. Heartbeats plus a timeout are the standard way to detect liveness, and a TTL key models that directly without primary-database writes. At this scale the heartbeats amount to about 67,000 writes per second, which the replica option does not reduce. Very long intervals or nightly batches make presence useless.
rationales: The load is writes. A replica does not reduce writes on the primary.
This cuts load, but presence becomes up to 10 minutes stale, which defeats the feature.
Correct. TTL keys in a fast store model heartbeat liveness cheaply and keep the primary database free for messages.
Nightly updates cannot answer "is this user online now".

questions.scenario: You are designing a notification service that sends email, SMS and mobile push. Requirements: an outage at the SMS provider must not delay email or push, and a retried job must never send the same notification twice.
questions.stem: Which two design choices directly address these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Publish each event once and route it to separate per-channel queues, each with its own workers
Assign every notification a stable ID and have workers record sent IDs and skip duplicates
Have the order service call the three providers synchronously in the checkout request
Use a single shared queue and worker pool for all channels to maximise utilisation

rationales: Correct. Separate queues and workers per channel give failure isolation.

Use PostgreSQL full text search with a tsvector column and a GIN index, and revisit if relevance or load needs outgrow it
Run `ILIKE '%term%'` queries against the articles table
Export articles nightly to object storage and search the files with a serverless function

questions.stem: Which combination is the most effective fix?

Return the full catalogue to the browser once and filter it in JavaScript
Debounce and cancel stale requests on the client, and serve top-k suggestions per prefix from a precomputed structure with hot short prefixes cached
Move autocomplete to a nightly batch email of popular searches

questions.scenario: Users upload videos of up to 4 GB. Today the browser POSTs the file to the API servers, which stream it to object storage. During upload peaks, API latency for unrelated endpoints spikes.
questions.stem: What is the recommended change?
options: Increase the API servers' request body limit and timeout
Give the browser long-lived storage account credentials so uploads bypass the API
Have the API issue a short-lived, single-object, write-only pre-signed URL so the browser uploads directly to object storage
Base64-encode uploads in JSON so the API can validate them in memory

Long-lived broad credentials in a browser can be extracted and abused.

questions.stem: Which two changes best fit this workload? (Select two.)

Enqueue a message containing a reference to the stored object, and run scan, transcode and thumbnail as separate stages with their own queues and idempotent workers

Honour Retry-After by breaking the circuit for that deployment, and retry the request on another deployment in the pool
Return 500 to the client so it knows the backend failed
Route the request to a deployment of the newer model version, which has spare quota

Enforce per-task and per-tenant caps on steps, tokens, wall-clock time and spend, and stop cleanly when a cap is hit
Split the agent into five cooperating agents so each loop is shorter
Increase the HTTP timeout to 20 minutes

Correct. Explicit budgets bound cost when the agent misbehaves.
More agents add overhead and cost without bounding loops.
Long timeouts keep the fragility and still lose work on deploys.

questions.scenario: Users of an LLM chat feature complain it "feels slow". Responses average 600 output tokens and are returned only when complete. Finance also wants lower model spend.
questions.stem: Which statement about streaming the response is correct?
options: Streaming has no effect on perceived latency because total generation time is unchanged
Streaming cuts both latency and cost, because fewer tokens are generated
Streaming increases cost because each chunk is billed as a separate request
Streaming improves perceived latency because the first tokens appear sooner, but it does not reduce the tokens billed
questions.explanation: Streaming changes when the user sees output, reducing time to first token, not how much is generated. To cut spend, use other levers: shorter contexts, routing simple tasks to a smaller model, caching or output limits.
rationales: Users perceive the first visible output, which streaming makes arrive much sooner.
The same tokens are generated, so cost is unchanged.
Streaming does not turn one generation into many billed requests.
Correct. It improves time to first token with the same token count.

questions.scenario: An on-call engineer is paged several times a week for "CPU > 85% on api-7". Most of these pages show no user impact. Meanwhile, a recent outage in which 3% of checkout requests failed for 40 minutes produced no page.
questions.stem: What is the best change to the alerting strategy?
options: Lower the CPU threshold to 75% so problems are caught earlier
Page on user-facing symptoms such as SLO error-budget burn, and move CPU to dashboards for diagnosis
Add alerts for memory, disk and network on every host as well
Page on the average latency across all endpoints
questions.explanation: The SRE book advises paging on symptoms rather than causes. Burn-rate alerts on the checkout SLO would have caught the 3% failure, while CPU is a cause that often has no user impact. More cause-based alerts and averages increase noise and hide tail problems.
rationales: This adds more non-actionable pages.
Correct. Symptom-based SLO alerts page on what users feel, and causes help diagnosis.
This multiplies cause-based noise.
Averages hide tail latency and per-endpoint failures.

questions.scenario: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. You want a fast-burn page that fires when 2% of the monthly error budget has been consumed within one hour.
questions.stem: What burn rate and error-rate threshold should the 1-hour window use?
options: Burn rate 2; error rate above 0.2%
Burn rate 14.4; error rate above 1.44%
Burn rate 14.4; error rate above 14.4%
Burn rate 6; error rate above 0.6%
questions.explanation: Budget consumed equals burn rate × window ÷ period, so 0.02 = b × 1/720 gives b = 14.4. The error-rate threshold is burn rate × (1 − SLO) = 14.4 × 0.001 = 1.44%. This matches the SRE Workbook's recommended first row.
rationales: A burn rate of 2 over 1 h consumes only about 0.28% of the budget.
Correct. Burn rate 14.4 over 1 h of 720 h consumes 2%, at an error rate of 1.44%.
The burn rate must be multiplied by the error budget (0.1%), not used as a raw error percentage.
Burn rate 6 is the 6-hour row (5% of budget).

questions.scenario: Your 1-hour burn-rate page correctly fired during a 10-minute outage. After the fix, it kept firing for most of the next hour, and on-call could not tell whether the fix had worked.
questions.stem: What change does the SRE Workbook recommend for this problem?
options: Shorten the long window to 5 minutes
Also require a short window (for example 5 minutes) to exceed the same burn rate, so the alert resets soon after recovery
Raise the burn-rate threshold to 30
Silence the alert for an hour after it fires
questions.explanation: Multiwindow alerts fire only when both the long window and a short window, about one-twelfth of the long one, exceed the threshold. The long window keeps significance, and the short window drops below threshold soon after recovery, so the alert clears.
rationales: A 5-minute long window alone is noisy and pages on short blips.
Correct. A long and a short window together give both precision and fast reset.
This delays detection and does not change how long the alert stays on.
Silencing hides a recurrence and does not show whether the fix worked.

questions.scenario: A team is building dashboards for an API service and the PostgreSQL connection pool behind it. They want a consistent checklist for each.
questions.stem: Which pairing is most appropriate?
options: USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for the API endpoints, and RED (rate, errors, duration) for the connection pool
RED (rate, errors, duration) for the API endpoints, and USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for the connection pool
Average latency only, for both
Log volume per minute for the API, and CPU for the pool
questions.explanation: RED suits request-driven services, and USE suits resources such as pools, CPUs, disks and queues. When RED shows the API slowing, USE on the pool shows whether it is saturated, for example by waiters queuing for connections.
rationales: These are reversed. A pool has utilisation and saturation, while an endpoint has rate and duration.
Correct. RED is for services and USE is for the resources behind them.
Averages hide the tail and say nothing about saturation.
Neither metric tracks errors or saturation directly.

questions.scenario: A team head-samples 5% of traces in OpenTelemetry to control cost. When rare errors occur, the relevant traces are usually missing.
questions.stem: What is the best approach?
options: Raise head sampling to 50%
Use tail sampling in a collector so traces with errors or high latency are always kept, plus a small sample of the rest
Disable tracing and rely on logs
Add the request ID as a metric label so failing requests can be found
questions.explanation: OpenTelemetry notes that head sampling decides before the trace completes, so it cannot ensure that traces containing errors are sampled. Tail sampling decides after seeing the spans, so errors and slow traces can be kept while overall volume stays low.
rationales: This costs ten times more and still drops half of the error traces.
Correct. Tail sampling keeps the traces you need, at the cost of buffering in the collector.
This loses cross-service timing, which is the reason to trace.
Per-request labels create unbounded metric cardinality.

questions.scenario: A three-engineer team is starting a new B2B product with uncertain demand. The tech lead proposes eight microservices, a self-managed message broker cluster and a service mesh "so we will not need to re-architect later".
questions.stem: What is the most cost-aware recommendation?
options: Proceed; re-architecting later always costs more than building for scale now
Self-host everything on a single VM to minimise the cloud bill
Use microservices but skip observability to save cost
Start with a modular monolith on a managed relational database and managed queue, and split services only when a measured need appears
questions.explanation: For a small team, operational complexity and people's time usually dominate cost. The SRE book treats complexity as a cost to justify. Managed services offload undifferentiated work, and a modular monolith keeps boundaries without network hops.
rationales: This is premature distribution. It pays the costs of distributed systems before there is any need.
A single self-managed VM minimises the bill but adds operations work and creates a single point of failure.
Distributed systems without observability are much harder to run.
Correct. It keeps the system simple and offloads undifferentiated work, while leaving room to split later.

questions.scenario: A service earning about $1M per year runs at 99.9% availability. Leadership asks for 99.99%. Engineering estimates the extra nine needs a second region and about $150k per year in infrastructure and staffing.
questions.stem: Using the SRE book's reasoning, what is the best response?
options: Approve it; four nines is the industry standard
Decline for now; the extra nine is worth roughly 0.09% × $1M ≈ $900 per year in recovered revenue, far below its cost, unless other impacts justify it
Approve it, because availability gains always pay for themselves
Decline, because 99.99% is impossible with cloud services
questions.explanation: The SRE book frames an extra nine as worth funding only if its value exceeds its cost, and uses this very calculation (0.09% of $1M ≈ $900). AWS also notes that higher availability constrains dependencies and slows change. Reputational or contractual factors could change the answer, but they must be stated explicitly.
rationales: Targets should come from user need and economics, not from convention.
Correct. The value of the extra nine is tiny compared with its cost.
Each extra nine typically costs more than the previous one.
It is achievable, just expensive.

questions.scenario: A small team must add transactional email (receipts and password resets) to its product. Options are to build an SMTP sending fleet with IP reputation management, or to use a managed email delivery service.
questions.stem: Which two considerations best support a sound build-vs-buy decision here? (Select two.)
options: Whether email delivery is a differentiator for the product, or undifferentiated work a provider already does well
How the provider's pricing grows with the team's growth driver, and the cost of exiting (data export, templates, switching providers)
Whether building it would be an interesting engineering challenge
Whether the managed service's monthly bill is higher than the raw cost of servers
questions.explanation: Buy undifferentiated capabilities and build differentiators. Then check how the price scales and what it costs to leave. Comparing only the bill against raw server cost ignores on-call and engineering time, which usually dominate for small teams.
rationales: Correct. Differentiation is the core build-vs-buy question.
Correct. Pricing shape and exit cost decide whether buying stays a good deal.
Engineering interest is not a business justification.
This ignores the people cost of running deliverability yourself.
